**Surat al-Anbiya' is Makki according to all scholars, and it has one hundred and twelve verses. In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.**

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿The reckoning of mankind has drawn near, yet they are heedless and turn away. No fresh reminder comes to them from their Lord but they listen to it while playing, their hearts diverted. And those who did wrong confer secretly: "Is this not but a human like yourselves? Will you then submit to magic while you see it?"﴾

**His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿The reckoning of mankind has drawn near﴾.** Ibn Mas'ud said: "Al-Kahf, Maryam, Ta-Ha and al-Anbiya' are among the first of the ataq (the old, precious surahs), and they are from my tilad." He means by tilad what is old and has been earned and preserved of the Qur'an, like the inherited wealth (al-mal al-tilad).

It is also narrated that a man among the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was building a wall, when another man passed by him on the day this surah was revealed. The one who was building the wall said: "What has been revealed of the Qur'an today?" The other said: "There was revealed: ﴿The reckoning of mankind has drawn near, yet they are heedless and turn away.﴾" So he shook his hand free of the building and said: "By Allah, I will never build again, since the reckoning has drawn near."

"Has drawn near" means the time has come near when they will be called to account for their deeds. As for "for mankind," Ibn 'Abbas said: "The intended meaning of 'mankind' here is the polytheists, as evidenced by His statement, ﴿but they listen to it while playing﴾, up to His statement, ﴿Will you then submit to magic while you see it?﴾" It was also said: "Mankind" is a general term, even if what is referred to at that time was the disbelievers of Quraysh; this is indicated by the verses that follow. Whoever knows that the Hour has drawn near will have a short hope, his soul will be at ease with repentance, and he will not incline toward this world. So what has passed is as though it had never been, once it is gone, and everything that is coming is near. Death is inevitable, and each person's death is the establishment of his own hour. The Resurrection is also near in comparison with the time that has passed, for what remains of this world is less than what has gone.

Al-Dahhak said: The meaning of ﴿The reckoning of mankind has drawn near﴾ is their punishment, meaning the people of Makkah, because they were slow to accept what they had been promised of punishment, in denial. Their killing took place on the day of Badr.

Al-Nahhas (said): In speech it is not permissible to say "has drawn near the reckoning of them for mankind," lest a pronoun precede its noun, which is not permissible when one intends to delay it.

**(And they are heedless and turn away)** is a subject and predicate (mubtada' and khabar). The accusative is permissible outside the Qur'an as a circumstantial state (hal). In this there are two meanings: first, "and they are heedless and turn away" means: they are occupied with this world rather than the Hereafter. Second: they are heedless of preparing for the reckoning and of what Muhammad ﷺ brought. This wāw, according to Sibawayh, has the meaning of "when," and it is what the grammarians call the wāw of circumstance (wāw al-hal), as Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿There covered you a security, a slumber overtaking a party of you, while another party was concerned only for themselves﴾ [Al 'Imran: 154]. [[See vol. 4, p. 242.]]

**His statement, may He be exalted: (No fresh reminder comes to them from their Lord).** "Fresh" (muhdath) is an adjective of "reminder" (dhikr). Al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' permitted "muhdathan" (in the accusative) with the meaning "no reminder comes to them fresh," in the accusative as a circumstantial state. Al-Farra' also permitted the nominative "muhdathun" as an adjective of "dhikr," because if you delete "min" you would put "dhikrun" in the nominative: "no reminder comes to them from their Lord that is fresh," meaning in the descent and the recitation of Jibril to the Prophet ﷺ, for he would receive a surah after a surah and a verse after a verse, as Allah sent it down to him at one time after another, not because the Qur'an is created.

It was also said: The reminder is what the Prophet ﷺ reminds them of and admonishes them with. He said "from their Lord" because the Prophet ﷺ speaks only by revelation, so the admonition and warning of the Prophet ﷺ are a reminder, and it is fresh. Allah, may He be exalted, said: ﴿So remind; you are only a reminder﴾ [al-Ghashiyah: 21]. [[See vol. 20, p. 37.]] It is said: "So-and-so is in a gathering of remembrance (majlis al-dhikr)."

It was also said: The reminder is the Messenger himself. This was said by al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl, based on what is in the context of the verse: ﴿Is this not but a human like yourselves?﴾ [al-Anbiya': 3]. Had He meant by the reminder the Qur'an, He would have said: "Is this not but the fables of the ancients?" The evidence for this interpretation is His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿And they say, "Indeed, he is a madman." And it is not but a reminder to the worlds﴾ [al-Qalam: 51–52], meaning Muhammad ﷺ. And He said: ﴿Allah has sent down to you a reminder, a messenger﴾ [al-Talaq: 10–11].

**"But they listen to it"** means Muhammad ﷺ, or the Qur'an from the Prophet ﷺ, or from his community. **"While playing"**: the wāw here is the wāw of circumstance, indicated by "their hearts diverted." The meaning of "playing" (yal'abun) is "amusing themselves" (yalhun). It was also said: "they occupy themselves." If its interpretation is taken as amusement, then what they amuse themselves with has two possibilities: first, their own pleasures; second, listening to what is recited to them. If its interpretation is taken as occupation, then what they occupy themselves with has two possibilities: first, this world, because it is play, as Allah, may He be exalted, said: ﴿The life of this world is but play and amusement﴾ [Muhammad: 36]. [[See vol. 16, p. 257.]] Second, they occupy themselves with disparaging it and objecting to it. Al-Hasan said: Whenever the reminder was renewed for them, they persisted in ignorance. It was also said: they listen to the Qur'an mockingly.

**His statement, may He be exalted: (Their hearts diverted)**, meaning: their hearts are heedless, turned away from the remembrance of Allah, occupied from reflection and understanding. It derives from the Arabs' saying: "I forgot (lahaytu) about the matter when I left it, and I was distracted from it (salawtu 'anhu), I forget (ulha) to forgetting (lihyan)." "Diverted" (lahiyah) is an adjective that precedes the noun, and it is required that an adjective follow the noun it qualifies in all the i'rab (grammatical inflection). When the adjective precedes the noun, it takes the accusative, as in His statement: ﴿their eyes humbled﴾ [al-Qalam: 43], ﴿and its shades close over them﴾ [al-Insan: 14] [[See vol. 19, p. 136.]], and "their hearts diverted." A poet said:

*For 'Izzah, a desolate campsite...*
*gleams, as though its traces were the embroidery in the sheaths of swords.* [[This is Kuthayyir 'Izzah; i.e., its traces appear and become clear, like the embroidery in the sheaths of swords, which are the linings of scabbards, singular khallah.]]

He intended: "a desolate campsite (talal muwhish)."

Al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' permitted "lahiyatun qulubuhum" in the nominative, with the meaning "their hearts are diverted." Others permitted the nominative as a second predicate (khabar ba'da khabar), or by supposing an implied subject (mubtada').

Al-Kisa'i said: The meaning may also be: "except that they listen to it with their hearts diverted."

**(And those who did wrong confer secretly)**: that is, they conferred among themselves in denial. Then He specified who they are, saying: **"those who did wrong,"** that is, those who associated partners with Allah. "Those who did wrong" is a substitute (badal) for the wāw in "confer" (asarru), and it refers back to the people mentioned earlier. One does not stop at this statement at "the secret conference (al-najwa)" [20:62]. Al-Mubarrad said: It is like your saying: "Indeed those who are in the house have departed, the sons of 'Abd Allah," so "the sons" is a substitute for the wāw in "departed." It was also said: it is in the nominative by way of disparagement, meaning "they are those who did wrong." It was also said: it is by omitting the verb "say," the estimated meaning being: "those who did wrong say," and the verb was omitted, like His statement: ﴿and the angels enter upon them from every gate, "Peace be upon you"﴾ [al-Ra'd: 23–24]. Al-Nahhas chose this view and said: The evidence for the correctness of this answer is that what follows is ﴿Is this not but a human like yourselves?﴾ [al-Anbiya': 3]. A fourth view: it is in the accusative with the meaning "I mean those who did wrong." Al-Farra' permitted it to be in the genitive, with the meaning "the reckoning of those who did wrong has drawn near for mankind," and one does not stop at this point at "the secret conference," but one stops at the three preceding possibilities. So these are five views. Al-Akhfash permitted the nominative according to the dialect of one who says: "The fleas have eaten me (akaluni al-baraghith)," and this is good. Allah, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Then they became blind and deaf, many of them﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 71] [[See vol. 6, p. 247.]]. A poet said:

*By you, the contest gained what lies beyond the efforts, so the arrows were guided to the targets.*

Another said: [[This is al-Farazdaq satirizing 'Amr ibn 'Afra'. Diyaf: a place in al-Jazirah, and they are the Nabateans of al-Sham. Al-Salit: olive oil.]]

*But he is a Diyafi, whose father and mother, his relatives in Hawran, press olive oil.*

Al-Kisa'i said: There is inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir) in it; its sense is: "And those who did wrong confer secretly."

Abu 'Ubaydah said: "Asarru" here is one of the words with opposite meanings (al-adhdad), so it may mean that they concealed their speech, and it may mean that they revealed it and made it public.

**His statement, may He be exalted: (Is this not but a human like yourselves?)**, meaning: they conferred among themselves and said: "Is this remembrance, which is the Messenger, or is this one who calls you, not but a human like yourselves, who is not distinguished from you by anything, who eats food and walks in the markets as you do?" They did not know that Allah, may He be exalted, made clear that He sends to them none but a human, so that they may understand and He may teach them.

**(Will you then submit to magic)**: that is, what Muhammad ﷺ brought is magic, so how do you come to him and follow him? So Allah informed His Prophet, peace be upon him, of what they had conferred about. In the language, "magic" (sihr) is anything that is deceptive and has no reality and no soundness.

**(While you see it).** [It was said its meaning is: that he is a human like you, like "while you understand" (wa antum ta'qilun), because intellect is sight of things (al-'aql al-basar bi-l-ashya'). It was also said: the meaning is: "Will you accept magic while you know that it is magic?" It was also said: the meaning is: "Will you turn to falsehood while you recognize the truth?" The meaning of the statement is reproach.] [[From manuscripts b, j, z, t, k, and y.]]

If its interpretation is taken as occupation, then what they occupy themselves with has two possibilities: first, this world, because it is play, as Allah, may He be exalted, said: ﴿The life of this world is but play and amusement﴾ [Muhammad: 36]. [[See vol. 16, p. 257.]] Second, they occupy themselves with disparaging it and objecting to it. Al-Hasan said: Whenever the reminder was renewed for them, they persisted in ignorance. It was also said: they listen to the Qur'an mockingly.

**His statement, may He be exalted: (Their hearts diverted)**, meaning: their hearts are heedless, turned away from the remembrance of Allah, occupied from reflection and understanding. It derives from the Arabs' saying: "I forgot (lahaytu) about the matter when I left it, and I was distracted from it (salawtu 'anhu), I forget (ulha) to forgetting (lihyan)." "Diverted" (lahiyah) is an adjective that precedes the noun, and it is required that an adjective follow the noun it qualifies in all the i'rab (grammatical inflection). When the adjective precedes the noun, it takes the accusative, as in His statement: ﴿their eyes humbled﴾ [al-Qalam: 43], ﴿and its shades close over them﴾ [al-Insan: 14] [[See vol. 19, p. 136.]], and "their hearts diverted." A poet said:

*For 'Izzah, a desolate campsite...*
*gleams, as though its traces were the embroidery in the sheaths of swords.* [[This is Kuthayyir 'Izzah; i.e., its traces appear and become clear, like the embroidery in the sheaths of swords, which are the linings of scabbards, singular khallah.]]

He intended: "a desolate campsite (talal muwhish)."

Al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' permitted "lahiyatun qulubuhum" in the nominative, with the meaning "their hearts are diverted." Others permitted the nominative as a second predicate (khabar ba'da khabar), or by supposing an implied subject (mubtada').

Al-Kisa'i said: The meaning may also be: "except that they listen to it with their hearts diverted."

**(And those who did wrong confer secretly)**: that is, they conferred among themselves in denial. Then He specified who they are, saying: **"those who did wrong,"** that is, those who associated partners with Allah. "Those who did wrong" is a substitute (badal) for the wāw in "confer" (asarru), and it refers back to the people mentioned earlier. One does not stop at this statement at "the secret conference (al-najwa)" [20:62]. Al-Mubarrad said: It is like your saying: "Indeed those who are in the house have departed, the sons of 'Abd Allah," so "the sons" is a substitute for the wāw in "departed." It was also said: it is in the nominative by way of disparagement, meaning "they are those who did wrong." It was also said: it is by omitting the verb "say," the estimated meaning being: "those who did wrong say," and the verb was omitted, like His statement: ﴿and the angels enter upon them from every gate, "Peace be upon you"﴾ [al-Ra'd: 23–24]. Al-Nahhas chose this view and said: The evidence for the correctness of this answer is that what follows is ﴿Is this not but a human like yourselves?﴾ [al-Anbiya': 3]. A fourth view: it is in the accusative with the meaning "I mean those who did wrong." Al-Farra' permitted it to be in the genitive, with the meaning "the reckoning of those who did wrong has drawn near for mankind," and one does not stop at this point at "the secret conference," but one stops at the three preceding possibilities. So these are five views. Al-Akhfash permitted the nominative according to the dialect of one who says: "The fleas have eaten me (akaluni al-baraghith)," and this is good. Allah, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Then they became blind and deaf, many of them﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 71] [[See vol. 6, p. 247.]]. A poet said:

*By you, the contest gained what lies beyond the efforts, so the arrows were guided to the targets.*

Another said: [[This is al-Farazdaq satirizing 'Amr ibn 'Afra'. Diyaf: a place in al-Jazirah, and they are the Nabateans of al-Sham. Al-Salit: olive oil.]]

*But he is a Diyafi, whose father and mother, his relatives in Hawran, press olive oil.*

Al-Kisa'i said: There is inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir) in it; its sense is: "And those who did wrong confer secretly."

Abu 'Ubaydah said: "Asarru" here is one of the words with opposite meanings (al-adhdad), so it may mean that they concealed their speech, and it may mean that they revealed it and made it public.

**His statement, may He be exalted: (Is this not but a human like yourselves?)**, meaning: they conferred among themselves and said: "Is this remembrance, which is the Messenger, or is this one who calls you, not but a human like yourselves, who is not distinguished from you by anything, who eats food and walks in the markets as you do?" They did not know that Allah, may He be exalted, made clear that He sends to them none but a human, so that they may understand and He may teach them.

**(Will you then submit to magic)**: that is, what Muhammad ﷺ brought is magic, so how do you come to him and follow him? So Allah informed His Prophet, peace be upon him, of what they had conferred about. In the language, "magic" (sihr) is anything that is deceptive and has no reality and no soundness.

**(While you see it).** [It was said its meaning is: that he is a human like you, like "while you understand" (wa antum ta'qilun), because intellect is sight of things (al-'aql al-basar bi-l-ashya'). It was also said: the meaning is: "Will you accept magic while you know that it is magic?" It was also said: the meaning is: "Will you turn to falsehood while you recognize the truth?" The meaning of the statement is reproach.] [[From manuscripts b, j, z, t, k, and y.]]

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 4–6:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿He said: "My Lord knows the word in the heaven and the earth"﴾. That is, nothing is hidden from Him of what is said in the heaven and the earth. In the codices of the people of Kufa it is "Qala Rabbi" (He said: "My Lord..."), meaning Muhammad said, "My Lord knows the word," that is, He knows what you have whispered together. It has been said that the first reading (qala, "he said," in the past tense) is preferable, because they had kept this saying secret, so God, Mighty and Majestic, revealed it to His Prophet ﷺ and commanded him to say it to them. Al-Nahhas said: "Both readings are sound, and they are like two verses, and in them there is the benefit that the Prophet ﷺ was commanded and that he said as he was commanded."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Rather, they said: "Confused dreams"﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: That is, they said that what he brings is "confused dreams." Others said: That is, they said it is a mixture like confused dreams, that is, jumbled visions seen in sleep. This is the meaning given by Mujahid and Qatada, and from it is the saying of the poet:

"Like a bundle of dream that its dreamer was deceived by."

Al-Qutabi said: It refers to false dreams, and in this regard is the saying of the poet:

"Tales of Tasm, or a mirage in a desert plain, shimmering for the night traveler, and confused dreams of a dreamer."

Al-Yazidi said: Adghath (confused dreams) are what has no interpretation. This has already been discussed in "Yusuf" (see vol. 9, p. 200 onward).

When they saw that the matter was not as they had said, they shifted from that, and they said: ﴿Rather, they said﴾, then they shifted from that too and said: "Rather, he is a poet." That is, they are bewildered and do not settle on anything: they said once "magic," and once "confused dreams," and once "he has fabricated it," and once "poet." It has also been said: that is, one group said he is a magician, another group said it is confused dreams, another group said he has fabricated it, and another group said he is a poet. And "iftira'" (fabrication) means invention, which has been mentioned before.

﴿So let him bring us a sign as the earlier ones were sent﴾. That is, as Moses was sent with the staff and other signs, and like the she-camel of Salih. They knew that the Qur'an is neither magic nor a dream, but they said: "He ought to bring a sign that we propose." And it was not for them to propose after they had seen one sign. Also, if they do not believe in a sign of the kind in which they are the most knowledgeable of people, and in which there is no room for doubt, how will they believe in another sign? Even if he were to heal the blind-born and the leper, they would say: "This is a matter of medicine, and that is not our craft." Their request was only obstinacy, since God had already given them signs that were sufficient. God, Mighty and Majestic, made clear that if they were believers He would have granted them what they asked, by His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And had God known any good in them, He would have made them hear. And had He made them hear, they would have turned away while they were refusing﴾ [al-Anfal: 23].

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿No town believed before them, which We destroyed﴾. Ibn Abbas said: He means the people of Salih and the people of Pharaoh.

﴿Which We destroyed﴾: he means that their destruction was in Our knowledge. ﴿Will they then believe?﴾: he means will they affirm. That is, they did not believe in the signs and so they were uprooted. Thus, if these people saw what they proposed, they would not believe either, because of the decree already passed that they would not believe. Their punishment was delayed only because We knew that among their descendants there would be one who believes. And "min" is extra in His saying "min qaryah" (from a town), like His saying: ﴿Then not one of you could withhold him from Us﴾ [al-Haqqah: 47].

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 7–10:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We sent not before you except men to whom We revealed⦗[[(yūḥā) with the ya' is the reading of Nafi'.]]⦘ — to them.﴾ This is a rebuttal of their saying: ﴿Is this not but a human being like you?﴾ [al-Anbiya': 3], and a consolation to His Prophet ﷺ, meaning: He sent none before you except men.

﴿So ask the people of the reminder (ahl al-dhikr) if you do not know.﴾ He means the people of the Torah and the Gospel who believed in the Prophet ﷺ. This was said by Sufyan. He named them "people of the reminder" because they used to recount the reports of the prophets, which the Arabs did not know. The disbelievers of Quraysh used to consult the People of the Book regarding the matter of Muhammad ﷺ. Ibn Zayd said: by "the reminder" He meant the Qur'an, that is, ask the believing scholars among the people of the Qur'an. Jabir al-Ju'fi said: When this verse was revealed, 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "We are the people of the reminder." It has been established by tawatur (mass transmission) that the messengers were from among mankind. The meaning is: do not begin with denial and with your saying that the messenger ought to be an angel; rather, consult the believers so that they may explain to you the permissibility of the messenger being a human being. An angel is not called a man (rajul), because the word rajul applies to what has an opposite in its wording; you say: rajul and imra'ah (man and woman), and rajul and sabiy (man and boy). So His saying "men (rijalan)" [means] from the children of Adam. Hafs, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read: "nūḥī ilayhim (We reveal to them)."

Issue: The scholars have not disagreed that the common people must follow their scholars, and that they are the ones meant by Allah's saying, mighty and majestic: "So ask the people of the reminder if you do not know." They have also agreed that a blind person must rely on another whom he trusts to distinguish the qibla when it is unclear to him; likewise, one who has neither knowledge nor insight into the meaning of his religion must follow his scholar. Similarly, the scholars have not disagreed that the common people may not issue legal rulings (fatwa), due to their ignorance of the meanings by which permitting and forbidding are determined.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We did not make them bodies that do not eat food.﴾ The pronoun in "ja'alnāhum (We made them)" [10:73] refers to the prophets, meaning: We did not make the messengers before you to be outside the natures of human beings, not needing food and drink. ﴿And they were not immortal⦗(khalidin)⦘.﴾ He means they do not die. This is a reply to their saying: ﴿What is this but a human being like you?﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 33], and their saying: ﴿What is with this messenger that he eats food and walks in the markets?﴾ [al-Furqan: 7]. "Jasad" is a noun of genus, and for this reason He did not say "ajsad (bodies)." It was also said: He did not say "ajsad" because He intended: We did not make each one of them a body (jasad). The jasad is the body. One says from it: tajassada, just as one says from al-jism: tajassama. Al-jasad also means saffron or the like of dye, and it is blood as well. Al-Nabighah said:

"Nor by the Lord whose Ka'bah was anointed, [I swear]... and what was spilled upon the idols of blood."

[The verse's first hemistich is: "fa-la la-'umri alladhi masahat ka'batuhu"; he swears first by God, then by the blood that used to be poured upon the idols (ansab) in the Jahiliyyah.]

Al-Kalbi said: the jasad is the embodied thing in which there is a spirit, that eats and drinks. According to this view, what does not eat and drink is a jism. Mujahid said: the jasad is what does not eat and drink. According to this view, what eats and drinks is a nafs (soul). Mentioned by al-Mawardi.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then We fulfilled the promise to them⦗...⦘﴾, meaning the prophets: by delivering them, granting them victory, and destroying those who denied them.

(And whom We willed) — that is, those who affirmed the prophets.

(And We destroyed the transgressors) — that is, the polytheists.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed We have sent down to you a Book﴾ [10], meaning the Qur'an.

(In it is your reminder) [10] — it is in the nominative by the inchoative, and the clause is in the accusative position because it is an adjective (na't) for "kitab." The "dhikr" here is meant as honor (sharaf); that is, in it is your honor, like His saying: ﴿And indeed it is a reminder for you and your people﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 44]. Then He admonished them with a question whose meaning is reproach, saying, mighty and majestic: (Will you not then reason?). It was also said: "In it is your reminder" means the mention of the matter of your religion, the rulings of your law, and what you will come to in reward and punishment; will you not then reason about these things we have mentioned? Mujahid said: "In it is your reminder" means your speech/talk. It was also said: the noble qualities of your character and the excellence of your deeds. Sahl ibn 'Abd Allah said: acting upon what is in it is your life. I say: these sayings are of one meaning, and the first encompasses them all, for all of them are honor. The Book is an honor for our Prophet ﷺ, because it is his miracle, and it is an honor for us if we act upon what is in it. Its proof is his saying, upon him peace: "The Qur'an is a proof for you or against you."

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 21, verses 16–18:**

His words, exalted is He: ﴿And We did not create the heaven and the earth and what is between them in play.﴾ That is, in vain and without purpose. Rather, it is to alert to the fact that they have a Creator, Powerful, whose command must be obeyed, and that He recompenses the evildoer and the doer of good. That is, We did not create the heaven and the earth so that some people would wrong others, some would disbelieve, some would oppose what they were commanded, and then they would die without being recompensed, and without being commanded in this world to do good or forbidden from evil. This play that is negated of the Wise, its opposite is wisdom.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿If We had wished to take a pastime﴾. When a people believed that He had a child, He said: "If We had wished to take a pastime." And *al-lahw* (pastime) in the language of Yemen means the woman. This was said by Qatadah. And ʿUqbah ibn Abi Jasrah said, when Tawus, ʿAta', and Mujahid came asking him about His words, exalted is He, "If We had wished to take a pastime": "*Al-lahw* is the wife." This was also said by al-Hasan. Ibn ʿAbbas said: "*Al-lahw* is the child," and this was also said by al-Hasan. Al-Jawhari said: "*Al-lahw* is sometimes used as a euphemism for intercourse." I say: From this is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

Did Basbasah not claim today that I have grown old, and that such as I no longer do well at *al-lahw*?

Intercourse was called *lahw* only because it is a diversion for the heart, as he said:

[[This is Zuhayr ibn Abi Sulma, and the verse is from his Mu'allaqah, and its completion is:
"Pleasing to the eye of the beholder who observes."]]

And in them is a diversion for the friend and a sight (pleasing to the eye).

Al-Jawhari. His words, exalted is He: ﴿If We had wished to take a pastime﴾: they said "a woman," and it is said "a child."

(﴿We would have taken it from Us﴾) That is, from Our presence, not from your presence. Ibn Jurayj said: "From the people of the heaven, not from the people of the earth." It was said: He intended to refute those who said that the idols are the daughters of God; that is, how could your carved idols be a child of Ours? Ibn Qutaybah said: The verse is a refutation of the Christians.

(﴿If We were doers﴾) Qatadah, Muqatil, Ibn Jurayj, and al-Hasan said: The meaning is "We were not doers," like His words: ﴿You are only a warner﴾ [Fatir: 23], that is, you are only a warner. The *in* (إن) here carries the meaning of negation, and the speech is complete at His words: "We would have taken it from Us." It was also said that it is conditional, meaning: if We were doing that, but We are not doing that, because it is impossible for Us to have a child, for if that were the case, We would not have created a Paradise, nor a Fire, nor death, nor resurrection, nor reckoning. It was also said: If We had wished to take a child by way of adoption (*tabanni*, the taking of an adopted son), We would have taken him from Our presence among the angels. A group inclined to this view, because the will may be related to adoption, but taking a child by birth is impossible, and the will is not related to the impossible; this was mentioned by al-Qushayri.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿Rather, We hurl the truth against falsehood﴾. *Al-qadhf* means throwing, that is, We throw the truth against falsehood.

(﴿so it crushes it﴾) That is, it overpowers it and destroys it. The root of *al-damgh* is splitting the head until it reaches the brain, and from it comes *al-Damighah* [[See vol. 2, p. 7 onward.]]. Here "the truth" is the Qur'an, and "falsehood" is Satan, according to the view of Mujahid, who said: Everything in the Qur'an that concerns falsehood refers to Satan. It was also said: Falsehood is their lying and their description of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, with attributes not His, such as a child and other things. It was also said: By "the truth" He meant the proof, and by "falsehood" their doubts. It was also said: The truth is the admonitions, and falsehood is the sins, and the meanings are close. The Qur'an includes both proof and admonition.

(﴿then it vanishes﴾) That is, it perishes and is lost, as said by Qatadah.

(﴿And woe to you﴾) That is, the punishment in the Hereafter because of your describing the Lord with what is not permissible to describe Him with. Its parallel is: ﴿He will recompense them for their description﴾ [[See vol. 7, p. 95 onward.]] [al-An'am: 139], that is, for their lying. It was also said: "For what you describe" God with, of the impossible, which is His taking a child, glory be to Him.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 19–21:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And to Him belongs whoever is in the heavens and the earth﴾, meaning in ownership and creation. So how is it permissible to associate with Him that which is His servant and His creation?

(And those with Him) meaning the angels, whom you claimed to be the daughters of Allah.

(Are not too proud) i.e., do not disdain (to worship Him) and to humble themselves before Him.

(Nor do they tire) i.e., they do not grow weary; this is said by Qatadah. It is derived from al-hasir, which is the camel that has been left exhausted by fatigue and weariness. It is said: hasara al-ba'ir yahsiru husuran, meaning it became exhausted and weary; istahsara and tahassara are similar to it; and I made it weary (hasartuhu) hasran, which is transitive and intransitive; and ahsartuhu too, so he is hasir. Ibn Zayd said: they do not become bored. Ibn 'Abbas said: they do not disdain. Abu Zayd said: they do not tire. It is also said: they do not falter, as recorded by Ibn al-A'rabi, and the meaning is one.

(They glorify Him night and day) i.e., they pray, remember Allah and declare Him free of imperfection, constantly.

(Without slackening) i.e., they do not weaken and do not grow weary. They are inspired to glorify and sanctify (Allah) just as they are inspired to breathe. Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 22–24:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Had there been in them (the heavens and the earth) gods other than Allah, they would both have been ruined﴾. That is, had there been in the heavens and the earths gods other than Allah who were worshipped, they would both have been ruined. Al-Kisa'i and Sibawayh said: "illa" (except) here means "ghayr" (other than). When "illa" is placed in the position of "ghayr," the noun following it takes the i'rab (grammatical inflection) of "ghayr," as the poet said:

"And every brother who parts from his brother... by the life of your father, except the two Farqads (stars)."

Sibawayh also related: "Had there been with us a man except Zayd, we would have perished." Al-Farra' said: "illa" here is in the position of "siwa" (besides), and the meaning is: had there been in them gods besides Allah, their inhabitants would have been corrupted. Others said: that is, had there been in them two gods, the management would have been corrupted, because if one of them willed something and the other willed its opposite, one of them would be powerless. It was also said: the meaning of "lafasadata" is that they would have been laid waste, and those in them would have perished through the occurrence of dispute caused by the disagreement between the partners.

﴿Exalted is Allah, Lord of the Throne, above what they describe﴾. He declared Himself free of imperfection and commanded the servants to declare Him free of having a partner or a son. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He is not questioned about what He does, but they will be questioned﴾ is a crushing refutation of the Qadariyyah and others. Ibn Jurayj said: the meaning is that creation does not question Him about His decree concerning His creation, while He questions creation about their deeds, because they are servants. By this it is shown that whoever will be questioned tomorrow about his deeds, such as the Messiah and the angels, is not fit for divinity. It was also said: He is not held to account for His actions, while they are held to account. It is narrated from Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, that a man said to him: "O Commander of the Faithful, does our Lord love to be disobeyed?" He said: "Would our Lord be disobeyed by compulsion?" The man said: "Tell me, if He withheld guidance from me and granted me perdition, would He have done good to me or wronged me?" He said: "If He withheld from you your right, He would have wronged you; and if He withheld from you His bounty, then He gives it to whomever He wills." Then he recited the verse: "He is not questioned about what He does, but they will be questioned."

It is related from Ibn Abbas that he said: When Allah, Mighty and Majestic, sent Musa and spoke to him and revealed the Torah to him, he said: "O Allah, You are a Great Lord. If You willed to be obeyed, You would be obeyed; and if You willed that You not be disobeyed, You would not be disobeyed. You love to be obeyed, yet You are disobeyed in that. How is this, O Lord?" Allah revealed to him: "I am not questioned about what I do, but they will be questioned."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Or have they taken gods besides Him?﴾ He repeated the rebuke concerning taking gods besides Allah, as an intensification of the reproach. That is, their description is as previously mentioned regarding creation and giving life, so "am" (or) here means "hal" (is it that?) according to what has preceded. Let them bring proof for that. It was also said: the first (argument) is a rational argument, since He said: "they raise the dead" and give life to the dead, far-fetched! The second is an argument from transmitted revelation, i.e., bring your proof from this direction: in which Book was this revealed? In the Qur'an, or in the books sent down to the rest of the prophets?

﴿This is the reminder of those with me﴾ with sincere monotheism in the Qur'an, ﴿and the reminder of those before me﴾ in the Torah and the Gospel and the other books Allah sent down. So look: is there in any of these books that Allah commanded taking gods other than Him? The law-codes did not differ concerning matters related to monotheism; they differed only in commands and prohibitions. Qatadah said: the reference is to the Qur'an; the meaning: "This is the reminder of those with me" regarding what is obligatory for them of the lawful and the unlawful, "and the reminder of those before me" of the nations, of those who were saved by faith and perished by polytheism. It was also said: "the reminder of those with me" concerns the reward for them for faith and the punishment for disbelief, "and the reminder of those before me" concerns the previous nations, regarding what was done to them in this world and what will be done to them in the Hereafter. It was also said: the meaning of the statement is a warning and threat, i.e., do what you will, for soon the veil will be lifted. Abu Hatim related that Yahya ibn Ya'mur and Talhah ibn Musarrif recited "hadha dhikru man ma'iya wa dhikru man qablì" with tanwin and a kasra on the mim, and he claimed there was no basis for this. Abu Ishaq al-Zajjaj said concerning this reading: the meaning is, "This is a reminder of what has been sent down to me and of what is with me, and a reminder from before me." It was also said: a reminder existing from before me, i.e., I came with what the prophets before me came with.

﴿Nay, most of them do not know the truth﴾. Ibn Muhays and al-Hasan read "al-haqqu" with a raised vowel (al-haqqu), meaning "He is the truth" and "this is the truth." On this reading one stops at "la ya'lamun," but one does not stop there on the reading with the accusative.

﴿So they are turning away﴾, that is, from the truth, which is the Qur'an, so they do not reflect upon the proof of monotheism.

﴿that there is no god except Me, so worship Me﴾. That is, We said to all of them: there is no god but Allah. The reason (al-'aql) bears witness that He has no partner, and the transmitted report (al-naql) from all the prophets exists, and the proof is either rational (ma'qul) or transmitted (manqul). Qatadah said: No prophet was sent except with monotheism (al-tawhid), and the laws (al-shara'i') differ in the Torah, the Gospel and the Qur'an, but all of that rests on sincerity (al-ikhlas) and monotheism.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (*al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran*) on Surah 21, verses 26–29:

God's statement: ﴿And they say, "The Most Merciful has taken a son." Glory be to Him!﴾ It was revealed concerning Khuza'ah, when they said, "The angels are the daughters of God," and they worshipped them, hoping for their intercession on their behalf. Ma'mar related from Qatadah, who said: "The Jews said" (Ma'mar said in his narration), "or groups of people: 'Khatan is related to the jinn, and the angels are of the jinn.'" Then God, Mighty and Majestic, said: "Glory be to Him" (subhanahu), meaning, exalting Him above such things.

"Rather, they are servants" means: rather, they are servants, "honoured," meaning: it is not as these disbelievers claim. According to al-Zajjaj, the accusative (naṣb) is also permissible, in the sense of "Rather, He has taken honoured servants." Al-Farra' permitted it on the basis that it refers back to "a son," meaning: "Rather, We did not take them as a son, but We took them as honoured servants." The word "son" (walad) here is in the plural sense, though it may be singular or plural. It is also possible that the word walad is used generically, as one says, "So-and-so has wealth (mal)."

"They do not precede Him in speech" means they do not speak until He speaks, and they speak only what He commands them.

"And they act by His command" means they obey Him and carry out His orders. "He knows what is before them" means He knows what they have done and what they will do, according to Ibn Abbas. It is also related from him: "what is before them" is the Hereafter, and "what is behind them" is this world. The first interpretation was mentioned by al-Tha'labi, and the second by al-Qushayri.

"And they do not intercede except for those whom He approves." Ibn Abbas said: they are the people of the testimony that there is no god but God. Mujahid said: they are everyone whom God is pleased with. The angels will intercede on the Day of Resurrection, as is found in Sahih Muslim and elsewhere, and also in this world, for they seek forgiveness for the believers and for those on earth, as the revelation explicitly states, as will come.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 30–33:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Have not those who disbelieve seen that the heavens and the earth were a joined mass, and We parted them?﴾ [30] The common reading is "أَوَلَمْ" with the waw. Ibn Kathir, Ibn Muhaysin, Humayd and Shibl ibn Abbad read "أَلَمْ تَرَ" without the waw, and it is also so in the Mushaf of Makkah. "أَوَلَمْ يَرَ" means "يَعْلَمْ" (know). "الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا أَنَّ السَّماواتِ وَالْأَرْضَ كانَتا رَتْقاً" [30]. Al-Akhfash said: "كانتا" (were, dual) because they are two kinds, as the Arabs say: "هُمَا لِقَاحَانِ أَسْوَدَانِ" (they are two black stallion camels), and as Allah, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿Indeed, Allah holds the heavens and the earth lest they cease﴾ [Fatir: 41]. Abu Ishaq said: "كانتا" because the heavens are referred to in the singular "سماء" (sky), and because the heavens were one heaven, and likewise the earths. He said: "رَتْقاً" [30] and did not say "رَتْقَيْنِ" (two parts), because it is a verbal noun (masdar), and the meaning is: they were two possessors of a joined state. Al-Hasan read "رَتَقًا" with a fatha on the ta'. Isa ibn Umar said: it is correct and it is a dialect. "الرَّتْقُ" is closing, the opposite of "الفَتْق" (parting); one says "رَتَقْتُ الْفَتْقَ أَرْتُقُهُ فَارْتَتَقَ" (I sealed the rent, so it became sealed), meaning it joined together; and from it comes "الرَّتْقَاءُ" for a woman whose vulva is closed. Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, Ata, al-Dahhak and Qatadah said: it means they were one thing, stuck together, and Allah separated them by air. Likewise Ka'b said: Allah created the heavens and the earth one upon the other, then created a wind in their middle, and parted them by it, and made the heavens seven and the earths seven. A second view, held by Mujahid, al-Suddi and Abu Salih: the heavens were joined as one layer, and He parted them and made them seven heavens; likewise the earths were joined as one layer, and He parted them and made them seven. Al-Qutaybi, in his 'Uyun al-Akhbar, related from Isma'il ibn Abi Khalid, concerning Allah's saying, mighty and majestic: ﴿Have not those who disbelieve seen that the heavens and the earth were a joined mass, and We parted them﴾, that he said: the sky was created alone and the earth was created alone; from this He parted seven heavens and from that seven earths. He created the upper earth, made its inhabitants jinn and humans, split in it rivers, made fruits grow in it, put seas in it, and named it "رعاء" (Ra'a), its breadth being a five-hundred-year journey. Then He created the second, like it in breadth and thickness, and placed in it peoples whose mouths were like dogs' mouths, whose hands were human hands, whose ears were cows' ears, and whose hair was sheep's hair. When the Hour draws near, the earth will cast them out toward Yajuj and Majuj; the name of that earth is "الدَّكْمَاءُ" (al-Dakma'). Then He created the third earth, its thickness a five-hundred-year journey, and in it is air for the earth. The fourth: He created in it darkness and scorpions for the people of the Fire, like black mules, with tails like long horses' tails, eating one another, and they will be let loose upon the children of Adam. Then Allah created the fifth, like it in thickness, length and breadth; in it are chains, shackles and fetters for the people of the Fire. Then Allah created the sixth earth, named "مَادْ" (Mad); in it are black, dense stones, and from it the dust of Adam, peace be upon him, was created. Those stones will be raised on the Day of Resurrection, each stone like a great mountain, made of sulphur, hung upon the necks of the disbelievers, and they will blaze until they burn their faces and hands. This is His saying, mighty and majestic: ﴿Its fuel is people and stones﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 24]. Then Allah created the seventh earth, named "عَرَبِيَّةُ" (Arabiyah), and in it is Hell. In it are two gates: one named Sijjin, and the other named al-Falaq. As for Sijjin, it is open, and to it ends the book of the disbelievers, and upon it are presented the companions of the Table and the people of Pharaoh. As for al-Falaq, it is closed and will not be opened until the Day of Resurrection. It has passed in "al-Baqarah" that they are seven earths, between each two earths a five-hundred-year journey, and further explanation will come at the end of "al-Talaq", God willing. A third view, held by Ikrimah, Atiyyah, Ibn Zayd and also Ibn Abbas, as mentioned by al-Mahdawi: the heavens were a joined mass not raining, and the earth was a joined mass not producing growth; so He parted the sky by rain and the earth by vegetation. Its parallel is His saying, mighty and majestic: ﴿By the sky with its returning rain, and by the earth with its splitting﴾ [At-Tariq: 11–12]. Al-Tabari chose this view, because after it comes: "وَجَعَلْنا مِنَ الْماءِ كُلَّ شَيْءٍ حَيٍّ أَفَلا يُؤْمِنُونَ" [30] (And We made from water every living thing; will they not believe?). I say: by it the lesson is established through observation and direct sight, and for that reason He informed of it in more than one verse, to show the perfection of His power, and for resurrection and recompense. It was said:

It becomes easy for them when they are angry, the wrath of enemies and their humbling,
and the sealing of rents and the parting of knots, and the undoing and the tying of affairs.

Regarding His saying, exalted is He: (And We made from water every living thing) [30], there are three interpretations: first, that He created everything from water, said by Qatadah; second, the preservation of the life of everything by water; third, "And We made from the water of the loins every living thing," said by Qutrub, with "وَجَعَلْنا" meaning "خَلَقْنَا" (We created). Abu Hatim al-Busti related in his Musnad Sahih, from the hadith of Abu Hurairah, who said: I said, "O Messenger of Allah! When I see you my soul is content and my eye is comforted; inform me about everything." He said: "Everything was created from water." The hadith... Abu Hatim said: Abu Hurairah's words "inform me about everything" meant "about everything that was created from water," and the proof of the correctness of this is the Prophet's answer to him when he said: "Everything was created from water," though not everything is created from water. This is another argument apart from what preceded about the heavens and the earth being a joined mass. It was said: "the all" is sometimes mentioned to mean "some," as in His saying: ﴿and she has been given of everything﴾ [An-Naml: 23], and His saying: ﴿destroying everything﴾ [Al-Ahqaf: 25]. The correct view is generality, due to his saying, peace be upon him: "Everything was created from water." And Allah knows best.

(Will they not believe?) [30], that is: will they not affirm what they witness, and that these things did not exist by themselves, but by a Maker who brought them into being, and a Director who originated them, and that this Maker cannot be originated.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We placed in the earth firm mountains﴾, that is, fixed mountains.

(Lest it should shake with them) [31], that is, lest it shake with them and not move, so that settling upon it is complete; this is said by the Kufans. The Basrans said: the meaning is "lest it shake." "al-Mayd" is movement and turning; one says "مَادَ رَأْسُهُ" (his head spun), meaning it turned. It has passed fully in "al-Nahl".

(And We placed in it broad passages) [31], meaning in the mountains, according to Ibn Abbas. "al-Fijaj" are paths; "al-Fajj" is a wide road between two mountains. It was also said: "And We placed in the earth broad passages," meaning routes, and this is the choice of al-Tabari, because of His saying: (that they may be guided) [31], that is, that they may be guided to travel in the earth.

(Paths) [31] explains "al-Fijaj," because a fajj may be a traversed open road and may not be. It was also said: that they might be guided by reflecting upon them to their religion.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We made the sky a protected ceiling﴾ [32], that is, protected from falling and collapsing upon the earth; its evidence is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And He holds the sky from falling upon the earth except by His permission﴾ [Al-Hajj: 65]. It was also said: protected by the stars from the devils, said by al-Farra'; its evidence is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and We guarded it from every accursed devil﴾ [Al-Hijr: 17]. It was also said: protected from demolition and dissolution, and from anyone reaching it by a stratagem. It was said: protected so that it needs no pillar. Mujahid said: raised. It was also said: protected from polytheism and sins.

(And they, meaning the disbelievers, from its signs are turning away) [32]. Mujahid said: meaning the sun and the moon. He ascribed the signs to the sky because they are placed in it, and He ascribed the signs to Himself in several places, because He is their doer. He made clear that the polytheists were heedless of reflecting upon the heavens and their signs, of their night and day, their sun and moon, their spheres, winds and clouds, and what in them of the power of Allah, exalted is He; for had they looked and reflected, they would have known that it has one capable Creator, and it would be impossible for Him to have a partner.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And it is He who created the night and the day﴾ [33] He reminded them of another blessing: He made the night for them to rest in, and the day for them to move about in for their livelihoods.

(The sun and the moon) [33], that is, He made the sun a sign of the day and the moon a sign of the night, so that the months, years and reckoning may be known, as its explanation has passed in "Subhan".

(Each) [33], meaning of the sun, the moon, the stars, the planets, the night and the day, (in a sphere they swim) [33], that is, they run and travel swiftly like a swimmer in water. Allah, exalted is He, and He is the truest of speakers, said: "وَالسَّابِحاتِ سَبْحاً" (and those that glide with gliding). "Sabih" is said of a horse that stretches out its foreleg while running. Grammatically, He did not say "يُسَبِّحْنَ" or "تُسَبِّحُ": Sibawayh's view is that when He spoke of them with the verb of rational beings and placed them in obedience as rational beings, He spoke of them with the waw and nun; al-Farra' said likewise. This meaning has passed in "Yusuf". Al-Kisa'i said: He said "يَسْبَحُونَ" only because it is the end of a verse, as Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿We are a victorious host﴾ [Al-Qamar: 44], and did not say "مُنْتَصِرُونَ". It was also said: the running is attributed to the sphere, so it is ascribed to them. The more correct view is that the planets run in the sphere; there are seven spheres below the enveloping heavens, which are the domain of the angels and the causes of the sovereignty: the moon is in the lowest sphere, then Mercury, then Venus, then the sun, then Mars, then Jupiter, then Saturn; the eighth is the sphere of the zodiac, and the ninth is the outermost sphere. "al-Falak" is the singular of the spheres of the stars. Abu Amr said: it may be pluralized on the pattern "fu'l," like "asad" and "usud," and "khashab" and "khushb." The root of the word is from turning, and from it comes "falkat al-mighzal" (the whorl of a spindle), because of its roundness. From it one says "falaka thady al-mar'a tafliikan" (the woman's breast became round), and "tafallaka" meant "became round." In the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud: "I left my horse as if it were turning in a falak," as if, because of its turning, he likened it to the sky's falak upon which the stars turn. Ibn Zayd said: the spheres are the courses of the stars, the sun and the moon; he said: they are between the sky and the earth. Qatadah said: the falak is a rotation in the sky, turning the stars while the sky stays fixed. Mujahid said: the falak is like the shape of a millstone's iron, and it is its axis. Al-Dahhak said: its falak is its course and the speed of its travel. It was also said: the falak is a restrained wave, and the course of the sun and the moon is in it. And Allah knows best.

Regarding His saying, exalted is He: (And We made from water every living thing) [30], there are three interpretations: first, that He created everything from water, said by Qatadah; second, the preservation of the life of everything by water; third, "And We made from the water of the loins every living thing," said by Qutrub, with "وَجَعَلْنا" meaning "خَلَقْنَا" (We created). Abu Hatim al-Busti related in his Musnad Sahih, from the hadith of Abu Hurairah, who said: I said, "O Messenger of Allah! When I see you my soul is content and my eye is comforted; inform me about everything." He said: "Everything was created from water." The hadith... Abu Hatim said: Abu Hurairah's words "inform me about everything" meant "about everything that was created from water," and the proof of the correctness of this is the Prophet's answer to him when he said: "Everything was created from water," though not everything is created from water. This is another argument apart from what preceded about the heavens and the earth being a joined mass. It was said: "the all" is sometimes mentioned to mean "some," as in His saying: ﴿and she has been given of everything﴾ [An-Naml: 23], and His saying: ﴿destroying everything﴾ [Al-Ahqaf: 25]. The correct view is generality, due to his saying, peace be upon him: "Everything was created from water." And Allah knows best.

(Will they not believe?) [30], that is: will they not affirm what they witness, and that these things did not exist by themselves, but by a Maker who brought them into being, and a Director who originated them, and that this Maker cannot be originated.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We placed in the earth firm mountains﴾, that is, fixed mountains.

(Lest it should shake with them) [31], that is, lest it shake with them and not move, so that settling upon it is complete; this is said by the Kufans. The Basrans said: the meaning is "lest it shake." "al-Mayd" is movement and turning; one says "مَادَ رَأْسُهُ" (his head spun), meaning it turned. It has passed fully in "al-Nahl".

(And We placed in it broad passages) [31], meaning in the mountains, according to Ibn Abbas. "al-Fijaj" are paths; "al-Fajj" is a wide road between two mountains. It was also said: "And We placed in the earth broad passages," meaning routes, and this is the choice of al-Tabari, because of His saying: (that they may be guided) [31], that is, that they may be guided to travel in the earth.

(Paths) [31] explains "al-Fijaj," because a fajj may be a traversed open road and may not be. It was also said: that they might be guided by reflecting upon them to their religion.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We made the sky a protected ceiling﴾ [32], that is, protected from falling and collapsing upon the earth; its evidence is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And He holds the sky from falling upon the earth except by His permission﴾ [Al-Hajj: 65]. It was also said: protected by the stars from the devils, said by al-Farra'; its evidence is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and We guarded it from every accursed devil﴾ [Al-Hijr: 17]. It was also said: protected from demolition and dissolution, and from anyone reaching it by a stratagem. It was said: protected so that it needs no pillar. Mujahid said: raised. It was also said: protected from polytheism and sins.

(And they, meaning the disbelievers, from its signs are turning away) [32]. Mujahid said: meaning the sun and the moon. He ascribed the signs to the sky because they are placed in it, and He ascribed the signs to Himself in several places, because He is their doer. He made clear that the polytheists were heedless of reflecting upon the heavens and their signs, of their night and day, their sun and moon, their spheres, winds and clouds, and what in them of the power of Allah, exalted is He; for had they looked and reflected, they would have known that it has one capable Creator, and it would be impossible for Him to have a partner.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And it is He who created the night and the day﴾ [33] He reminded them of another blessing: He made the night for them to rest in, and the day for them to move about in for their livelihoods.

(The sun and the moon) [33], that is, He made the sun a sign of the day and the moon a sign of the night, so that the months, years and reckoning may be known, as its explanation has passed in "Subhan".

(Each) [33], meaning of the sun, the moon, the stars, the planets, the night and the day, (in a sphere they swim) [33], that is, they run and travel swiftly like a swimmer in water. Allah, exalted is He, and He is the truest of speakers, said: "وَالسَّابِحاتِ سَبْحاً" (and those that glide with gliding). "Sabih" is said of a horse that stretches out its foreleg while running. Grammatically, He did not say "يُسَبِّحْنَ" or "تُسَبِّحُ": Sibawayh's view is that when He spoke of them with the verb of rational beings and placed them in obedience as rational beings, He spoke of them with the waw and nun; al-Farra' said likewise. This meaning has passed in "Yusuf". Al-Kisa'i said: He said "يَسْبَحُونَ" only because it is the end of a verse, as Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿We are a victorious host﴾ [Al-Qamar: 44], and did not say "مُنْتَصِرُونَ". It was also said: the running is attributed to the sphere, so it is ascribed to them. The more correct view is that the planets run in the sphere; there are seven spheres below the enveloping heavens, which are the domain of the angels and the causes of the sovereignty: the moon is in the lowest sphere, then Mercury, then Venus, then the sun, then Mars, then Jupiter, then Saturn; the eighth is the sphere of the zodiac, and the ninth is the outermost sphere. "al-Falak" is the singular of the spheres of the stars. Abu Amr said: it may be pluralized on the pattern "fu'l," like "asad" and "usud," and "khashab" and "khushb." The root of the word is from turning, and from it comes "falkat al-mighzal" (the whorl of a spindle), because of its roundness. From it one says "falaka thady al-mar'a tafliikan" (the woman's breast became round), and "tafallaka" meant "became round." In the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud: "I left my horse as if it were turning in a falak," as if, because of its turning, he likened it to the sky's falak upon which the stars turn. Ibn Zayd said: the spheres are the courses of the stars, the sun and the moon; he said: they are between the sky and the earth. Qatadah said: the falak is a rotation in the sky, turning the stars while the sky stays fixed. Mujahid said: the falak is like the shape of a millstone's iron, and it is its axis. Al-Dahhak said: its falak is its course and the speed of its travel. It was also said: the falak is a restrained wave, and the course of the sun and the moon is in it. And Allah knows best.

God, Exalted is He, says: ﴿And We did not grant to any human before you immortality﴾, meaning lasting survival in this world. It was revealed when they said: "We await for Muhammad the vicissitudes of fate (rayb al-manun)." This is because the polytheists were rejecting his prophethood and saying: "He is a poet; we await for him the vicissitudes of fate, and perhaps he will die as the poet of Banu so-and-so died." So God the Exalted said: The prophets before you have died, and God has taken charge of His religion with victory and protection. Thus We preserve your religion and your law.

﴿Then if you die, will they be the immortals?﴾ Meaning: "Will they be [immortal]?" This is like the words of the poet:

*They soothed me and said, "O Khuwaylid, do not be alarmed,"*
*So I said, and I denied the faces, "They are they!"*

Meaning: "Are they they?" This is a rhetorical interrogative of denial. Al-Farra' said: The particle *fa* (then) was used to indicate a conditional, because it is the answer to their saying, "He will die." It is also permissible that it was brought in because the implied meaning is: "Will they be the immortals if you die?" Al-Farra' said: It is also permissible to omit the *fa* and to leave it implicit, because the *i'rab* (grammatical case-inflection) does not appear in *hum* (they), meaning: "If you die, they too will die, so there is no gloating over the death." It is read both *mit* and *mitta* with a kasra and a damma on the letter *mim*, and both are dialectal forms.

God, Exalted is He, says: ﴿Every soul shall taste death﴾. This has preceded in (Surat Al 'Imran) [See vol. 4, p. 297 onwards.] ﴿And We test you with evil and with good as a trial﴾. *Fitnatan* (as a trial) is a verbal noun not from the same root as the verb, meaning: We test you with hardship and ease, and with the lawful and the unlawful, so that We may see how you give thanks and how you are patient.

﴿And to Us you will be returned﴾, meaning: for recompense for your deeds.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 36:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when those who disbelieve see you, they take you only as a jest﴾, meaning: they do not take you except as a jest. Al-huzu (mockery) is ridicule, as has already been explained. They are the mockers mentioned earlier at the end of Surah al-Hijr [[See vol. 10, p. 62.]] in His saying: ﴿Indeed, We suffice you against the mockers﴾ [al-Hijr: 95]. They used to blame whoever denied the divinity of their idols, while they themselves denied the divinity of the Most Merciful, and this is the utmost ignorance. (Is this the one) meaning: they say, "Is this the one...?" So the verb of saying is elided, and it is the response of "idha" (when). His saying, "they take you only as a jest," is a parenthetical statement between "idha" and its response.

(Who mentions your gods) meaning: with evil and reproach. From this is the saying of 'Antarah:

"Do not mention my steed, nor what I have fed him, lest your skin become like the skin of a mangy camel." [[He said it to a woman of his from Bajila who was blaming him over a mare he preferred over his other horses and fed the milk of his camels.]]

Meaning: do not reproach my steed.

(And they, at the remembrance of the Most Merciful) meaning: with the Qur'an.

(They are disbelievers) The second "they" (hum) emphasizes their disbelief, meaning: they are the disbelievers, intensifying their description as disbelievers.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Qur'an) on Surah 21 (al-Anbiya'), verses 37–40:**

His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿Man was created of haste﴾. That is, he was constructed upon haste, so he was created hasty, as Allah, may He be exalted, said: ﴿It is Allah who created you from weakness﴾ [Ar-Rum: 54] [[See vol. 14, p. 46.]], meaning man was created weak. It is also said: man was created of evil, meaning wicked, if you exaggerate in describing him with it. It is also said: "You are only going and coming," meaning one who goes and comes; that is, the nature of man is haste, so he hastens toward many things even if they are harmful.

Then it was said: the intended "man" is Adam, peace be upon him. Sa'id ibn Jubayr and as-Suddi said: when the spirit entered the eyes of Adam, peace be upon him, he looked at the fruits of Paradise. When it entered his body he craved food, so he leapt, before the spirit reached his feet, hastily toward the fruits of Paradise. This is His statement: ﴿Man was created of haste﴾. It was also said: Adam was created on Friday at the end of the day, and when Allah brought his head to life he hastened and sought the completion of the breathing of the spirit into him before sunset. This was said by al-Kalbi, Mujahid and others.

Abu 'Ubaydah and many people of the meanings (ahl al-ma'ani) said: *al-'ajal* is clay in the language of Himyar. They recited:

*"And the palm grows between water and clay"* [[The first half of the verse:
"And the cedar (al-na'ba') in the hard rock is its place of growth,"
...]]

It was also said: the intended "man" is all of mankind. It was said: the intended one is an-Nadr ibn al-Harith ibn 'Alqamah ibn Kaladah ibn 'Abd al-Dar, according to the tafsir (exegesis) of Ibn 'Abbas; meaning, it is not fitting for one who was created from lowly clay to mock the signs of Allah and His messengers. It was also said: it is of the inverted form (al-maqlub), meaning that haste was created from man. This is the view of Abu 'Ubaydah. An-Nahhas said: this view should not be adopted in the Book of Allah, because inversion (al-qalb) occurs in poetry only out of necessity, as in the verse of al-Ju'di, whose first half is: "It was an obligation, what you say, as..." He said:

*"Adultery was an obligation of stoning"*

Its parallel is this verse: ﴿And man has always been hasty﴾ [Al-Isra: 11] [[In MSS b, j, t, k, y: its parallel. See vol. 10, p. 226.]], and it has passed in ﴿Subhan [Glory be to Him]﴾ [Al-Isra: 1] [[In MSS b, j, t, k, y: its parallel. See vol. 10, p. 226.]].

﴿I will show you My signs, so do not ask Me to hasten﴾. This strengthens the first view, that the nature of man is haste, and that he was created with a nature that cannot restrain itself, as the Prophet, peace be upon him, said, as has preceded in "Subhan". The intended "signs" are the miracles that testify to the truthfulness of Muhammad, peace be upon him, and the praiseworthy outcome that He granted him. It was also said: they are what they asked for of punishment; they wished to hasten it and said: ﴿When is this promise?﴾ [Yunus: 48], without knowing that for everything there is a predetermined term. It was revealed concerning an-Nadr ibn al-Harith. And His statement: ﴿If this is indeed the truth﴾ [Al-Anfal: 32] [[See vol. 7, p. 398.]].

Al-Akhfash Sa'id said: the meaning of ﴿Man was created of haste﴾ is: it was said to him "Be," and he was. So the meaning of ﴿so do not ask Me to hasten﴾ according to this view is that He who says to a thing "Be" and it is, is not hindered from manifesting what they sought to hasten of the signs.

﴿And they say, "When is this promise?"﴾ [Yunus: 48], meaning: the promised thing (al-mawʿud), as one says: "Allah is our hope (raja'una)," meaning our object of hope (marjuwwuna). It was also said: the meaning of "the promise" here is the threat (al-wa'id), that is, what threatens us of punishment. It was also said: it is the Resurrection.

﴿If you are truthful﴾, O assembly of believers.

His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿If only those who disbelieved knew﴾. Here "knowledge" (al-'ilm) means recognition (al-ma'rifah), so it does not require a second object, like ﴿You do not know them; Allah knows them﴾ [Al-Anfal: 60]. The answer to "law" (lau) is omitted, meaning: if they knew the time ﴿when they will not be able to keep the Fire away from their faces or from their backs, nor will they be helped﴾, and recognised it, they would not have hastened the threat. Al-Zajjaj said: meaning, they would have known the truth of the promise. It was also said: the meaning is that if they knew it, they would not have persisted in disbelief and would have believed. Al-Kisa'i said: it is an alert to the certainty of the occurrence of the Hour, meaning that if they knew it with certainty of knowledge, they would have known that the Hour is coming. This is indicated by ﴿But it will come upon them suddenly﴾ [40], meaning unexpectedly, that is, the Resurrection. It was said: the punishment. It was said: the Fire. So they will not be able to contrive a means, ﴿and it will confound them﴾ [40]. Al-Jawhari said: "bahhahu bahtan" means he took him by surprise; Allah, may He be exalted, said: "But it will come to them suddenly and confound them" [40]. Al-Farra' said: ﴿and it will confound them﴾ [40] means it will bewilder them. It is said: "bahhahu yabhatuhu" when he confronts him with something that bewilders him. It was also said: it will catch them unawares.

﴿So they will not be able to repel it﴾ [40], meaning to turn it away from their backs.

﴿Nor will they be reprieved﴾, meaning they will not be given respite or delay for repentance or excuse.

That is, he was constructed upon haste, so he was created hasty, as Allah, may He be exalted, said: ﴿It is Allah who created you from weakness﴾ [Ar-Rum: 54] [[See vol. 14, p. 46.]], meaning man was created weak. It is also said: man was created of evil, meaning wicked, if you exaggerate in describing him with it. It is also said: "You are only going and coming," meaning one who goes and comes; that is, the nature of man is haste, so he hastens toward many things even if they are harmful.

Then it was said: the intended "man" is Adam, peace be upon him. Sa'id ibn Jubayr and as-Suddi said: when the spirit entered the eyes of Adam, peace be upon him, he looked at the fruits of Paradise. When it entered his body he craved food, so he leapt, before the spirit reached his feet, hastily toward the fruits of Paradise. This is His statement: ﴿Man was created of haste﴾. It was also said: Adam was created on Friday at the end of the day, and when Allah brought his head to life he hastened and sought the completion of the breathing of the spirit into him before sunset. This was said by al-Kalbi, Mujahid and others.

Abu 'Ubaydah and many people of the meanings (ahl al-ma'ani) said: *al-'ajal* is clay in the language of Himyar. They recited:

*"And the palm grows between water and clay"* [[The first half of the verse:
"And the cedar (al-na'ba') in the hard rock is its place of growth,"
...]]

It was also said: the intended "man" is all of mankind. It was said: the intended one is an-Nadr ibn al-Harith ibn 'Alqamah ibn Kaladah ibn 'Abd al-Dar, according to the tafsir (exegesis) of Ibn 'Abbas; meaning, it is not fitting for one who was created from lowly clay to mock the signs of Allah and His messengers. *"Adultery was an obligation of stoning"*

Al-Qurtubi's commentary (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 41:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And messengers before you were certainly mocked﴾ 10. This is consolation and comfort for the Prophet ﷺ. It means: if these people mock you, then messengers before you were mocked too, so be patient as they were patient. Then He promised him victory, saying: (fa-haqa) meaning it encompassed and befell (bi-alladhina) those who disbelieved and (sakhiru minhum) mocked them and ridiculed them (ma kanu bihi yastahzi'un), meaning the recompense of their mockery.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 42–44:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Say: Who protects you by night and by day from the Most Merciful?﴾ (yaksa'ukum) means: guards you and preserves you. Al-kala'ah (protection) is al-hirasah (guarding) and al-hifz (preserving). One says: kala'ahu Allah kila'an (with a kasra), meaning He preserved him and guarded him. It is said: "Go in the protection of God" (idhhab fi kila'at Allah), and "I took precautions against them" (iktala'tu minhum), meaning I guarded myself. The poet, Ibn Harmah, said:

Indeed Sulaymá, and God protects her, has withheld something that would not diminish her.

Another poet said: [[It is Ka'b ibn Zuhayr, and its second half is:

I made my camel kneel and I took precautions for its eye
And I resolved within myself, i.e., "What should I do about my affair?"]]

I made my camel kneel and I took precautions for its eye.

Al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' related "Say: who protects you" (man yaklu'ukum) with a fatha on the lam and a sukun on the waw. They also related "man yaklaakum" with the hamza lightened in both cases, though the well-known reading is with the hamza pronounced fully, and it is the reading of the common people. As for "yaklaakum," it is an error for two reasons, as al-Nahhas mentioned: first, the substitution of the hamza occurs only in poetry; second, they say in the past tense "kulyatihi." Then it is said: the form of the utterance is that of a question, but its meaning is negation. Its implied sense: Say, there is no guardian for you ﴿by night﴾ when you sleep, ﴿and by day﴾ when you rise and conduct your affairs.

(from the Most Merciful) means: from His punishment and His might, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Who then will help me against God?﴾ [[See vol. 9, p. 58 onward.]] [Hud: 63], i.e., from the punishment of God. The address is to those among them who acknowledged the Creator, meaning: if you affirm that He is the Creator, then He is able to bring down the punishment you are seeking to hasten.

(Nay, they turn away from the remembrance of their Lord) means: from the Qur'an. It is also said: from the admonitions of their Lord, and it is said: from knowledge of Him.

(turning away) means: heedless, unmindful.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Or do they have gods who can protect them from Us?﴾ The meaning: "Do they have...?" The mim is a connecting particle.

(who can protect them from Us) means: from Our punishment.

(They are unable) means: those whom these disbelievers claimed would help them are unable (to help themselves), so how could they help their worshippers?

(Nor can they be companioned by Us) Ibn Abbas said: "They will be prevented." And it is related from him: "They will be granted protection," and this is the choice of al-Tabari. The Arabs say: "I am a neighbour (jar) and companion (sahib) to you from so-and-so," meaning: a protector from him. The poet said:

He calls out at the top of his voice, seeking refuge, so that he may be companioned from them, while the spears are at his back.

Ma'mar related from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, who said: "They will be helped" (yunsarun), meaning they will be protected. Qatadah said: meaning God will not accompany them with good, nor will He make His mercy their companion.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Nay, We gave these and their fathers enjoyment until life was prolonged for them﴾. Ibn Abbas said: he means the people of Makkah. That is, We spread out for them and their forefathers its blessings, and (life was prolonged for them) in favour, so they thought it would never leave them, and so they became deluded and turned away from contemplating the proofs of God, Mighty and Majestic.

(Do they not see that We come to the land, reducing it from its outlying parts?) That is, by granting you victory over it, O Muhammad, land after land, and conquering town after town around Makkah. Al-Hasan and others said this meaning. It is also said: by killing and taking captives; al-Kalbi related this. The meaning is one. The discussion of this has already been covered fully in "al-Ra'd" [[See vol. 9, p. 333.]].

(Are they then the victors?) meaning: the disbelievers of Makkah, after We have diminished their outlying parts. Rather, you will overcome them and prevail over them.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 45–46:

Allah's statement: ﴿Say: I only warn you by the Revelation﴾ means: I frighten you and caution you by the Qur'an.

(And the deaf will not hear the call) means: those whom Allah has made deaf in their hearts, whose hearing He has sealed, and over whose sight He has placed a veil, so that they do not understand the signs or hear the truth. Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami and Muhammad ibn al-Sumaiqa read "wa-la yusma'" with a damma on the yaa' and a fatha on the meem, in the passive (mā lam yusamma fā'iluhu, the form whose agent is not named), with "al-summu" in the nominative (raf'), meaning: Allah does not make them hear. Ibn 'Amir, al-Sulami also, Abu Haywa and Yahya ibn al-Harith read "wa-la tusma'" with a damma on the taa' and a kasra on the meem, with "al-summa" in the accusative (nasb), meaning: you, O Muhammad, do not make the deaf hear the call; so the address is to the Prophet ﷺ. Some of the grammarians rejected this reading and said: it should have been "idha ma tundhiruhum" (if you warn them). Al-Nahhas said: that is permissible, because the meaning is already known.

Allah's statement: ﴿And if a breath of the punishment of your Lord touches them﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: a portion. Qatadah said: a punishment. Ibn Kaysan said: a little and the least thing, derived from nafh al-misk (the scent of musk). He said: [[This is Qays ibn al-Khatim al-Ansari.]]

"And 'Amrah is among the chieftains of women, / her sleeves are scented with musk."

Ibn Juraij said: a share, as one says: "So-and-so bestowed on so-and-so a share of his gift (nafaha fulan li-fulan min 'ata'ihi)," when he gives him a portion of wealth. The poet said: [[This is by al-Rimah ibn Mayyadah, who praised al-Walid ibn Yazid ibn 'Abd al-Malik with it.]]

"When I came to you hoping for the bounty of your favour, / a breath reached me which made the Arabs content."

That is, the soul found it pleasant. In the language, the nafha is a small push, so the meaning is: even if the least of the punishment touches them.

(They will surely say: "Woe to us! Indeed we were wrongdoers") means: transgressors. So they will acknowledge (their fault) at a time when acknowledgement will not benefit them.
