Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 47:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We shall set up the scales of justice for the Day of Resurrection, so no soul will be wronged in anything at all﴾. "Al-mawazin" is the plural of "mizan" (scale, balance). It has been said: its apparent meaning indicates that every accountable person has a scale by which his deeds are weighed, so the good deeds are placed in one pan and the bad deeds in the other. It has also been said: it is possible that there are multiple scales for a single doer, with each scale weighing one category of his deeds, as the poet said:

"A king by whose justice the calamities are set right... so for every calamity there is a scale for it."

It is also possible that it is a single scale, expressed by a plural form. Al-Hafiz Abu al-Qasim al-Lalikai (al-Lalakai) transmitted in his Sunan from Anas, who raised it (to the Prophet ﷺ): "Indeed there is an angel appointed over the scale. A son of Adam is brought and stood between the two pans of the scale. If his side outweighs, the angel calls out with a voice that the creatures hear: 'So-and-so has been made happy with a happiness after which he will never be wretched, ever.' And if it is light, the angel calls out: 'So-and-so has been made wretched with a wretchedness after which he will never be happy, ever.'" And he transmitted from Hudhayfah, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "The one in charge of the scale on the Day of Resurrection is Jibril, peace be upon him." It has been said: the scale has two pans, strings, a tongue, and a pointer (al-shahayn), and the plural refers to these parts. Mujahid, Qatadah and al-Dahhak said: the mention of the scale is a figure of speech, and there is no actual scale; it is only justice. What the reports have come with, and what the great majority hold, is the first view. This has already been explained in "al-A'raf" (see vol. 7, p. 165), and also in "al-Kahf" (see vol. 10, p. 418). We have mentioned it fully in the book "al-Tadhkirah", and praise be to Allah.

"Al-qist" means justice, i.e., there is in it no diminishing and no wronging, as there is in the scales of this world. "Al-qist" is an attribute of the scales, and it is in the singular because it is a verbal noun (masdar). One says: "mizan qist" (a just scale), "mizanan qist" (two just scales), and "mawazin qist" (just scales), like "rijal 'adl" and "ridan" (just men, and contented). A group read "al-qisṭa" with the letter ص (ṣ). "Li-yawm al-qiyamah" means for the people of the Day of Resurrection. It has been said: the meaning is "on the Day of Resurrection". "Fa-la tuzlamu nafsun shay'an" means: nothing of the good deeds of the doer of good is reduced, and nothing is added to the evil of the doer of evil.

(﴿And if it be the weight of a grain of mustard seed﴾) Nafi', Shaybah and Abu Ja'far read "mithqalu habbatin" with a nominative ending here, and in "Luqman" (see vol. 14, p. 66 onwards), meaning "if it occurs or is present", so that "kana" is used in its complete sense (kana tammah) and does not need a predicate. The rest read "mithqala" with the accusative, meaning "and if the deed or that thing is a mithqal". The "mithqal" of a thing is its weight measured against its like.

(﴿We bring it﴾) With a short alif is the reading of the majority, meaning: We produce it and bring it forth to recompense for it and to give it its due. "Yujaʾu bihā" means the grain is brought; had he said "bihi" (with it, the mithqal), it would also be permissible. It has been said: the "mithqal" of the grain is nothing other than the grain itself, so He said: "We bring it." Mujahid and Ikrimah read "ātainā" with the long alif, meaning "We recompense it". One says: "ātā yu'ātī mu'ātāh".

(﴿And sufficient are We as reckoners﴾) That is, recompensing for what they have done of good and evil. It has been said: "hasibin" means that no one is quicker at reckoning than We. "Al-hisab" means counting. Al-Tirmidhi transmitted from A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her: that a man sat before the Prophet ﷺ and said: "O Messenger of Allah! I have slaves who lie to me, betray me and disobey me, and I curse them and beat them. So where do I stand regarding them?" He said: "Their betrayal, disobedience and lying of you will be reckoned, and your punishment of them. If your punishment of them is in proportion to their sins, it will be an even balance, neither for you nor against you. If your punishment of them is less than their sins, it will be a surplus in your favour. And if your punishment of them exceeds their sins, retaliation will be taken from you on their behalf for the excess." He said: So the man withdrew and began weeping and crying out. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Do you not read the Book of Allah, the Exalted: 'And We shall set up the scales of justice for the Day of Resurrection, so no soul will be wronged in anything at all'?" The man said: "By Allah, O Messenger of Allah, I find for myself and for these no better thing than parting from them. I call you to witness that they are all free." He said: a strange (gharib) hadith.

Al-Qurtubi's commentary (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 21, verses 48–50:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We had certainly given Moses and Aaron the Criterion (al-Furqan) and a light (diya')﴾. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas and Ikrimah that they read "al-Furqana diya'an" without the waw, as a circumstantial accusative (hal). Al-Farra' claimed that omitting the waw and including it are the same, as Allah, mighty and majestic, said: "Indeed, We adorned the lowest heaven with an adornment of the stars" [al-Saffat: 6] and "and as a guard" [al-Saffat: 7], meaning "a guard." Al-Zajjaj refuted this view, saying: the waw comes for a meaning, so it is not added superfluously. He said: the interpretation of "al-Furqan" is the Torah, because in it is the distinction (al-farq) between the lawful and the unlawful. He said: "diya'" is like "in it is guidance and light" [al-Ma'idah: 44, see vol. 6, p. 208]. Ibn Zayd said: "al-Furqan" here means victory over the enemies, its proof being the saying of Allah, exalted: ﴿And what We sent down upon Our servant on the Day of al-Furqan﴾ [al-Anfal: 41], meaning the Day of Badr. Al-Tha'labi said: this view is more consistent with the apparent meaning of the verse, because the waw enters upon "diya'," so the meaning of the verse would be: "And We had certainly given Moses and Aaron victory, and the Torah, which is light and remembrance."

(For those who fear their Lord in the unseen) — that is, while absent, because they have not seen Allah, exalted; rather they knew through reflection and reasoning that they have a capable Lord who recompenses deeds, so they fear Him in their inner hearts and in their solitude, where they are hidden from people.

(And they are fearful of the Hour) — that is, of its coming before repentance.

(Anxious) — that is, afraid and apprehensive.

(And this is a blessed Reminder that We have sent down) — meaning the Qur'an. (Do you then deny it?) — O assembly of the Arabs. It is a miracle; you are unable to produce anything like it.

Al-Farra' also permitted reading "wa-hadha dhikrun mubarakan anzalnahu," in the sense of "We have sent it down blessed."

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 21, verses 51–56:**

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We had certainly given Ibrahim his guidance (rushd) before,﴾ al-Farra' said: that is, We had given him his guidance (huda).

(Min qabl) means: from before prophethood, that is, We granted him success in reflection and reasoning, when the night covered him and he saw the star, the sun and the moon. It was also said: "min qabl" means before Musa and Harun. According to this view, rushd means prophethood. According to the first view, which is held by most of the exegetes, it is like His saying concerning Yahya: ﴿And We gave him judgment while still a boy﴾ [[See p. 74 of this part and what follows.]] [Maryam: 12]. Al-Qurazi said: "His rushd is his righteousness."

(And We were of him well-aware) means: he was worthy of being granted rushd and fit for prophethood.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿When he said to his father﴾ It has been said: the meaning is "Remember when he said to his father," so the sentence is complete at His saying "And We were of him well-aware." It has also been said: the meaning is "And We were of him well-aware when he said," so the sentence is connected and one does not stop at His saying "well-aware." "His father" is Azar, "and his people" are Nimrod and those who followed him.

(What are these images) means: the idols. The word timthal is a term applied to a made thing that is designed to resemble one of the creations of God the Exalted. One says: "I made the thing like (mathaltu) the thing," meaning I likened it to it, and the name of that which is likened is timthal.

(to which you are devoted) means: remaining steadfast in worshipping them.

(They said: We found our fathers worshipping them.) means: we worship them in imitation of our forebears.

(He said: Certainly you and your fathers have been in manifest error.) means: in loss through worshipping them, since they are lifeless objects that neither benefit nor harm and do not know.

(They said: Have you brought us the truth, or are you among the jesters?) means: Have you come to us with truth in what you say, or are you a joker who jests?

(He said: Rather, your Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth.) means: I am not a jester; rather, your Lord and the one who manages your affairs is the Creator of the heavens and the earth.

(Who originated them.) means: who created them and brought them into being.

(And I am of those who bear witness to that.) means: to the fact that He is the Lord of the heavens and the earth. "Shahid" (witness) makes the ruling clear, and from it comes ﴿God bears witness﴾ [[See vol. 4, p. 40 and what follows.]] [Ali 'Imran: 18], meaning "God makes clear." So the meaning is: "And I make clear by proof what I say."

**Al-Qurtubi's commentary (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 21, verses 57–58:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And by God, I will surely scheme against your idols﴾. He informs that he did not suffice with argument by tongue, but broke their idols, an act of one who trusts in God, prepared to endure what is disliked in defending the religion. The letter *ta'* in *Ta-llahi* (تَاللَّهِ) is specific in oaths to the name of God alone; the letter *waw* applies to every apparent (explicit) noun, and the letter *ba'* to every pronoun and noun, both explicit and implicit. The poet said:

*Ta-llahi yabqa 'ala al-ayyami dhu hiyadin*
*bi-mushmakhirrin bihi al-zhayyanu wa al-asu*

(He is Malik ibn Khalid al-Khunā'i al-Hudhali. Ḥayad (ḥīd) here (on the pattern of ʿinab): any protrusion on the mountain. Mushmakhirr: a high mountain. Ẓayyān: wild jasmine. Meaning: it does not remain.)

*By God, there remains over the days a crag*
*on a lofty mountain, where there is wild jasmine and myrtle.*

Ibn ʿAbbas said: that is, "And by the sanctity of God, I will surely scheme against your idols," i.e., I will plot against them. *Al-kayd* (scheming) is *al-makr* (deceit). One says *kadahu yakiduhu kaydan wa makidatan*, and likewise *al-mukayadah*. Sometimes war is called *kayd*; it is said: "So-and-so fought and did not meet any kayd." And everything you treat, you *kidah*.

*(After you have turned away, retreating)*: that is, departing and going away. They had a festival each year to which they gathered, and they said to Abraham: "If you came out with us to our festival, our religion would please you." This was narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, as will be explained in *al-Saffat* (ref. vol. 15, p. 94). Abraham said to himself: "And by God, I will surely scheme against your idols." Mujahid and Qatadah said: Abraham said this secretly, away from his people, and only one man heard it, the one who reported it about him. The singular may be spoken of with the plural form when what he reports is something others are pleased with, like His saying: ﴿They say: If we return to Medina, the mightier will surely expel the meaner from it﴾ (ref. vol. 18, p. 129) [al-Munafiqun: 8]. It was also said: he said it after the people had left, and only the weak remained, and they are the ones who heard him. Abraham had devised a way to stay behind from them with his saying: ﴿Indeed, I am ill﴾ [al-Saffat: 89], i.e., weak from movement.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So he made them into fragments (judhadhan)﴾: that is, crumbs. *Al-jadhdh* is breaking and cutting; *jadhadhtu al-shay'* means I broke and cut the thing. *Al-jidhadh* and *al-judhadh* are what is broken off from it, and the *dammah* (u-vowel) is more eloquent than its *kasrah*. So said al-Jawhari. Al-Kisa'i said: gold stones are called *judhadh*, because they are broken. Al-Kisa'i, al-A'mash and Ibn Muhaysin recited *jidhadhan* with a *kasrah* on the *jim*, meaning fragments and pieces, the plural of *jadhid*, which is crushed debris, like *khafif* and *khifaf*, *zarif* and *zirafin*. The poet said:

*Judhdhadha al-asnama fi mihrabiha*
*dhaka fi Allahi al-'Aliyyi al-muqtadiri*

The rest read with a *dammah*, and Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim preferred it. [Like] *al-huṭam* and *al-rufat*, the singular of which is *judhadhah*. This is the scheme he swore he would carry out against them. He said "so He made them," because the people believed their idols to be divine. Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Nahik and Abu al-Sammal recited *jadhadhan* with a *fatḥah* on the *jim*; *fatḥah* and *kasrah* are two dialects, like *al-ḥaṣād* and *al-ḥiṣād*. Abu Hatim said: the *fatḥah*, *kasrah* and *dammah* have the same meaning, as related by Qutrub.

*(Except a great one among them)*: that is, the greatest of the gods in creation, for he did not break it. Al-Suddi and Mujahid said: he left the largest idol and hung the axe with which he had broken the other idols around its neck, so that he could argue with it against them.

*(That perhaps they may return to it)*: that is, to Abraham's religion, once the proof is established against them. It was also said: "*Perhaps they may return to it*" means to the largest idol, "*they may return*" in questioning its breaking.

**Verses 59–61:** ﴿They said: "Who has done this to our gods? Indeed, he is one of the wrongdoers."﴾

The meaning is that when they returned from their festival and saw what had been done to their gods, they said, as an inquiry and an expression of denial: "Who has done this to our gods? Indeed, he is one of the wrongdoers." It has also been said that "man" (*man*) is not an interrogative here but a *mubtada'* (inchoative subject), and its predicate is "one of the wrongdoers," meaning that whoever did this is a wrongdoer. The first view is more sound, because of their words "We heard a youth mention them," which is the answer to "Who did this?" The pronoun in "They said" refers either to the weak people who heard Abraham or to the one previously mentioned. The meaning of "mention them" is that he disparaged and reviled them, so perhaps he is the one who did this.

People differ over the grammatical case of "Abraham" (*Ibrahim*). Al-Zajjaj said it is in the nominative because the sense is "It is said to him: he is Abraham," so it is the predicate of an omitted subject, and the sentence is a quotation. He also said it may be nominative as a vocative, and its final vowel is then a fixed ending (*bina'*), and it stands in the place of the passive subject. It has also been said that its nominative case is because it is the object of a verb whose subject is not named (*ma lam yusamma fa'iluh*), on the basis that "Abraham" is not taken as pointing to a person, but the uttering of it is taken as pointing to the word itself. That is, it is said to him this statement and this word, just as you say "Zayd is the pattern *fa'l*" or "Zayd is three letters." Thus you do not refer to the person, but by your utterance you refer to the word itself. In this way you say: "I said *Ibrahim*," and it is a correct object, which you have placed in the position of a saying and a speech. Therefore it is not impossible that the verb is then put in the passive. This is the preference of Ibn 'Atiyya regarding its nominative case. Al-Ustadh Abu al-Hajjaj al-Ishbili al-A'lam said: it is nominative by *al-ihmal* (being left without a governing agent). Ibn 'Atiyya said: when he saw that the various nominative explanations did not clarify the meaning they intended, he resorted to its being nominative without any governing element, just as bare, ungoverned position can make a noun nominative as a *mubtada'*.

*Al-fata* means a young man and *al-fatat* a young woman. Ibn 'Abbas said: God did not send any prophet except as a youth. Then he recited: "We heard a youth mention them."

**Verse 61:** ﴿They said: "Bring him before the eyes of the people, so that they may bear witness."﴾

Concerning this there is one issue. When the report reached Nimrod and the nobles of his people, they disliked seizing him without proof, so they said: "Bring him openly, in the sight of the people, so that they may see him, [so that] they may bear witness against him for what he said, and that this may be a proof against him." It has also been said that "so that they may bear witness" means witnessing his punishment, so that no one would venture into the like of what he did. Or it may mean that some people would bear witness that they saw him breaking the idols, or that they would bear witness to his disparagement of their gods, so that they would know that he deserves punishment.

I say: In this there is evidence that in earlier times no one was held to account on another's claim alone, because of His words: "Bring him before the eyes of the people, so that they may bear witness." The same rule applies in our law, and there is no disagreement about it.

**Allah's words, "They said: 'Did you do this to our gods, O Ibrahim?'"** Here there are four issues.

**The first issue:** Since the report was not widespread and no testimony had been established, they asked him whether he had done it or not. The sentence contains an ellipsis. So Ibrahim came when he was brought, and they said: "Did you do this to the gods?" Ibrahim answered them, by way of argument against them: "Rather, it was done by this, their biggest one" (*bal faʿalahu kabīruhum hādhā*). That is, he was jealous and angry that he should be worshipped alongside the smaller ones, so he did this to them for that reason. "If they can speak, then ask them." He made the act of the biggest one conditional on the speech of the others, as a warning to them about the corruption of their belief. It is as if he said: "Rather, he is the doer, if these ones can speak." On this interpretation there is an inversion in the phrase *fasʾalūhum in kānū yanṭiqūn* ("ask them, if they can speak"). It was also said that he meant: "Rather, their biggest one did it, if they can speak." This shows that whoever cannot speak, know, or act is not deserving of worship. His statement was a *maʿārīḍ* (an allusive, indirect form of speech, a technical term meaning speech that suggests a meaning without a plain lie), and in *maʿārīḍ* there is an escape from lying. That is, ask them if they speak, for they will confirm it. If they do not speak, then he is not the doer. Within this statement is an implicit acknowledgment that he himself was the doer, and this is the correct view, because he counted it against himself. This shows that it was an indirect expression. That is because they used to worship them and take them as gods besides Allah, just as Ibrahim said to his father: ﴿O my father, why do you worship what neither hears nor sees?﴾ [Maryam: 42] (see p. 110 of this part), and so on. Ibrahim said: "Rather, it was done by this, their biggest one," so that they would say that they do not speak, nor benefit, nor harm. Then he would say to them: "Why then do you worship them?" and the proof would be established against them by their own words. For this reason it is permissible among the scholars of the community to put forward falsehood together with an opponent, until he returns to the truth on his own, for that is more effective as proof and cuts off doubt. Likewise he said to his people: "This is my lord" (see vol. 7, p. 25), "and this is my sister," and "I am sick" (see vol. 15, p. 19 onward), and "Rather, it was done by this, their biggest one."

Ibn al-Samayqaʿ recited *bal faʿallahu* with a doubled *lām*, meaning "perhaps the doer was their biggest one." Al-Kisāʾī said: the pause is at *bal faʿalahu* (meaning: "whoever did it did it"), then one begins with *kabīruhum hādhā* ("their biggest one, this"). It was also said: "Do they deny that their biggest one did it?" This is a reproach in the form of a statement, meaning: whoever believes in worshipping them is obliged to attribute an act to them, and the meaning is: "Rather, their biggest one did it, according to what is incumbent upon you."

**The second issue:** Al-Bukhari, Muslim and al-Tirmidhi related from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Ibrahim the Prophet never lied except in three instances: ﴿I am sick﴾ [al-Saffat: 89], his saying to Sarah 'my sister,' and his saying 'Rather, it was done by this, their biggest one.'" (This is the wording of al-Tirmidhi, who said: a good, sound hadith.) In Muslim's *Sahih*, in the hadith of Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) in the story of Ibrahim, there occurs a mention of his statement about the star, "This is my lord." He said: "He mentioned his saying about the star, 'This is my lord.'" On this basis the lies would be four. However, the Messenger (peace be upon him) negated those by his saying: "Ibrahim the Prophet never lied except in three lies, two of them concerning the cause of Allah: his saying ﴿I am sick﴾ [al-Saffat: 89], and his saying 'Rather, it was done by this, their biggest one,' and one concerning Sarah's affair." This is the wording of Muslim. As for his saying about the star, ﴿This is my lord﴾ [al-An'am: 78], it is not counted as a lie, and it does not fall under lying, because, Allah knows best, at the time he said it he was in childhood, and that is not a state of obligation. Or he said it to his people as a question, in the form of rebuke and denial, and the interrogative hamza was omitted. Or it was said as an argument against his people, to point out that what changes is not fit to be a lord. All these aspects have already been explained fully in *al-Anʿam*, and praise be to Allah.

**The third issue:** The judge Abu Bakr ibn al-ʿArabi said: In this hadith there is a great point that breaks the back. It is that he (peace be upon him) said: "Ibrahim did not lie except in three lies, two of which were only to protect the religion of Allah: his saying ﴿I am sick﴾ [al-Saffat: 89] and his saying 'Rather, it was done by this, their biggest one.'" He did not count his saying "This is my sister" as being for the sake of Allah, even though he used it to repel something disliked. But since Ibrahim (peace be upon him) had a share in it, namely the protection of his bed and the defence of his family, he did not put it in the cause of Allah. This is because nothing is placed alongside Allah and His cause except pure deeds free from the worldly impurities. Allusive speech that goes back to the self, when it is purified for the religion, belongs to Allah, glory be to Him, as He said: ﴿Is it not for Allah that sincere obedience is due?﴾ [al-Zumar: 3] (see vol. 15, p. 232 onward). If this had come from us, it would have been for Allah, but the station of Ibrahim required this. And Allah knows best.

**The fourth issue:** Our scholars said: lying is reporting about a thing contrary to what it is. The more apparent view is that Ibrahim's statement, in what Allah related about him (peace be upon him), was an allusive form of speech. Even though these were allusions, good deeds, arguments and indications for the creation, they lowered his rank and reduced his station compared with Muhammad, and the one who said them felt shy of them, as is reported in the hadith of intercession. The prophets fear what others do not fear, out of reverence for Allah. What would befit his rank in prophethood and friendship (*khullah*, the special intimate friendship with Allah) is that he should openly declare the truth and speak it plainly whatever the circumstances. But he was granted a concession, and he accepted the concession, so what happened happened, and the story is well known. For this reason it came in the hadith of intercession: "I was only taken as a close friend (*khalīl*) from behind, from behind" (*min warāʾ warāʾ*), with the accusative on *warāʾ* in both instances, being indeclinable like *khamsata ʿashar* (fifteen). Similarly they said *jāri bayta bayta*. In some copies of Muslim it occurs as "*min warāʾu min warāʾu*" with *min* repeated. In that case the indeclinability on the fatha is not permitted, and each of them is rather indeclinable on the damma, because it has been cut off from the genitive construction while the implied noun remains in mind, like *qablu* and *baʿdu*. If the implied noun is not intended, it is declined with tanwin, except that *warāʾ* is not inflected (not diptotic), because its *alif* is a feminine marker, since they said in its diminutive *wurayʾa*. Al-Jawhari said: this is anomalous. On this basis the fatha is valid in both instances even with *min* present. The meaning is: "I was a close friend who came later than others." From this it is derived that intimate friendship was not realised in its full perfection except for the one for whom the praised station (*al-maqam al-mahmud*) was established on that day, as has been mentioned before, and that is our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ).

That is, ask them if they speak, for they will confirm it. If they do not speak, then he is not the doer. Within this statement is an implicit acknowledgment that he himself was the doer, and this is the correct view, because he counted it against himself. This shows that it was an indirect expression. That is because they used to worship them and take them as gods besides Allah, just as Ibrahim said to his father: ﴿O my father, why do you worship what neither hears nor sees?﴾ [Maryam: 42] (see p. 110 of this part), and so on. Ibrahim said: "Rather, it was done by this, their biggest one," so that they would say that they do not speak, nor benefit, nor harm. Then he would say to them: "Why then do you worship them?" and the proof would be established against them by their own words. For this reason it is permissible among the scholars of the community to put forward falsehood together with an opponent, until he returns to the truth on his own, for that is more effective as proof and cuts off doubt. Likewise he said to his people: "This is my lord" (see vol. 7, p. 25), "and this is my sister," and "I am sick" (see vol. 15, p. 19 onward), and "Rather, it was done by this, their biggest one."

Ibn al-Samayqaʿ recited *bal faʿallahu* with a doubled *lām*, meaning "perhaps the doer was their biggest one." Al-Kisāʾī said: the pause is at *bal faʿalahu* (meaning: "whoever did it did it"), then one begins with *kabīruhum hādhā* ("their biggest one, this"). It was also said: "Do they deny that their biggest one did it?" This is a reproach in the form of a statement, meaning: whoever believes in worshipping them is obliged to attribute an act to them, and the meaning is: "Rather, their biggest one did it, according to what is incumbent upon you."

**The second issue:** Al-Bukhari, Muslim and al-Tirmidhi related from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Ibrahim the Prophet never lied except in three instances: ﴿I am sick﴾ [al-Saffat: 89], his saying to Sarah 'my sister,' and his saying 'Rather, it was done by this, their biggest one.'" (This is the wording of al-Tirmidhi, who said: a good, sound hadith.) In Muslim's *Sahih*, in the hadith of Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) in the story of Ibrahim, there occurs a mention of his statement about the star, "This is my lord." He said: "He mentioned his saying about the star, 'This is my lord.'" On this basis the lies would be four. However, the Messenger (peace be upon him) negated those by his saying: "Ibrahim the Prophet never lied except in three lies, two of them concerning the cause of Allah: his saying ﴿I am sick﴾ [al-Saffat: 89], and his saying 'Rather, it was done by this, their biggest one,' and one concerning Sarah's affair." This is the wording of Muslim. As for his saying about the star, ﴿This is my lord﴾ [al-An'am: 78], it is not counted as a lie, and it does not fall under lying, because, Allah knows best, at the time he said it he was in childhood, and that is not a state of obligation. Or he said it to his people as a question, in the form of rebuke and denial, and the interrogative hamza was omitted. Or it was said as an argument against his people, to point out that what changes is not fit to be a lord. All these aspects have already been explained fully in *al-Anʿam*, and praise be to Allah.

**The third issue:** The judge Abu Bakr ibn al-ʿArabi said: In this hadith there is a great point that breaks the back. It is that he (peace be upon him) said: "Ibrahim did not lie except in three lies, two of which were only to protect the religion of Allah: his saying ﴿I am sick﴾ [al-Saffat: 89] and his saying 'Rather, it was done by this, their biggest one.'" He did not count his saying "This is my sister" as being for the sake of Allah, even though he used it to repel something disliked. But since Ibrahim (peace be upon him) had a share in it, namely the protection of his bed and the defence of his family, he did not put it in the cause of Allah. This is because nothing is placed alongside Allah and His cause except pure deeds free from the worldly impurities. Allusive speech that goes back to the self, when it is purified for the religion, belongs to Allah, glory be to Him, as He said: ﴿Is it not for Allah that sincere obedience is due?﴾ [al-Zumar: 3] (see vol. 15, p. 232 onward). If this had come from us, it would have been for Allah, but the station of Ibrahim required this. And Allah knows best.

**The fourth issue:** Our scholars said: lying is reporting about a thing contrary to what it is. The more apparent view is that Ibrahim's statement, in what Allah related about him (peace be upon him), was an allusive form of speech. Even though these were allusions, good deeds, arguments and indications for the creation, they lowered his rank and reduced his station compared with Muhammad, and the one who said them felt shy of them, as is reported in the hadith of intercession. The prophets fear what others do not fear, out of reverence for Allah. What would befit his rank in prophethood and friendship (*khullah*, the special intimate friendship with Allah) is that he should openly declare the truth and speak it plainly whatever the circumstances. But he was granted a concession, and he accepted the concession, so what happened happened, and the story is well known. For this reason it came in the hadith of intercession: "I was only taken as a close friend (*khalīl*) from behind, from behind" (*min warāʾ warāʾ*), with the accusative on *warāʾ* in both instances, being indeclinable like *khamsata ʿashar* (fifteen). Similarly they said *jāri bayta bayta*. In some copies of Muslim it occurs as "*min warāʾu min warāʾu*" with *min* repeated. In that case the indeclinability on the fatha is not permitted, and each of them is rather indeclinable on the damma, because it has been cut off from the genitive construction while the implied noun remains in mind, like *qablu* and *baʿdu*. If the implied noun is not intended, it is declined with tanwin, except that *warāʾ* is not inflected (not diptotic), because its *alif* is a feminine marker, since they said in its diminutive *wurayʾa*. Al-Jawhari said: this is anomalous. On this basis the fatha is valid in both instances even with *min* present. The meaning is: "I was a close friend who came later than others." From this it is derived that intimate friendship was not realised in its full perfection except for the one for whom the praised station (*al-maqam al-mahmud*) was established on that day, as has been mentioned before, and that is our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then they turned back to themselves﴾. That is, some of them turned to others, turning back like one who has been cut off from his argument and has perceived the soundness of his opponent's argument.

(So they said, "Indeed, it is you who are the wrongdoers.") That is, by worshipping one who cannot speak a single word and does not possess a moment's benefit for himself. How could he benefit his worshippers and ward off harm from them, when he cannot even turn the axe away from his own head?

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then they were overturned upon their heads﴾. That is, they returned to their ignorance and their worship, and they said, "You know that these do not speak." So he said, cutting off what they were babbling and silencing them concerning what they were fabricating: ﴿Do you then worship besides Allah that which can neither benefit you at all nor harm you? Uff to you and to what you worship besides Allah! Will you not then use your reason?﴾ "Uff" means: stench to you.

It has been said that ﴿they were overturned upon their heads﴾ means they lowered their heads in shame before Abraham. This is open to scrutiny, because it was not said as "nakkasū" (with a fatha on the kaf), but rather "nukkisū ʿalā ruʾūsihim" (with a damma on the nun and a kasra on the kaf, in the passive form). That means: they were returned to what they had been upon at the beginning. Likewise Ibn Abbas said: "Wretchedness overtook them, so they returned to their disbelief."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 68–69:

The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿They said: "Burn him!"﴾ When they were defeated by the proof, pride in sin seized them, and they turned to the path of brute force and domination, and they said: "Burn him!" It is related that the one who uttered this statement was a man from the Kurds, from the Bedouins of Persia, that is, from its desert regions; this was said by Ibn Umar, Mujahid and Ibn Juraij. It is said that his name was Hayzar [[Another view: his name was (Hayzan), as in the History and Tafsir of al-Tabari. Another view: (Hayyun).]], so Allah caused the earth to swallow him, and he continues sinking within it until the Day of Resurrection. It is also said that it was said by their king, Nimrod.

(And support your gods) by burning Ibrahim, because he reviles them and finds fault with them. It has come in a report that Nimrod built a lofty tower, eighty cubits long and forty cubits wide. Ibn Ishaq said: They gathered firewood for a month, then they lit it, and it blazed and intensified, so much so that a bird passing by its sides would be burnt from the intensity of its heat. Then they bound Ibrahim and placed him in the catapult (manjanīq) in fetters. It is said that Iblis made the catapult for them on that day. Then the heavens, the earth, and whoever is in them of the angels and all creation, except the two sacred creatures (humans and jinn), cried out with a single cry: "Our Lord! Ibrahim, there is no one on earth who worships You other than him, and he is being burned for Your sake, so permit us to support him." Allah, the Exalted, said: "If he seeks aid from any of you or calls upon him, then let him help him; I have indeed permitted him in that. And if he calls upon none other than Me, then I know him best, and I am his Protector." When they intended to cast him into the fire, the keepers of the water came to him, while he was in the air, and said: "O Ibrahim, if you wish, we will extinguish the fire with water." He said: "I have no need of you." Then the angel of the wind came to him and said: "If you wish, I will scatter the fire." He said: "No." Then he raised his head to the sky and said: "O Allah, You are the One in the heavens, and I am the one on earth; there is none who worships You other than me. Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs."

Ubayy ibn Ka'b, may Allah be pleased with him, related from the Prophet (ﷺ): "When they bound Ibrahim in order to throw him into the fire, he said: 'None has the right to be worshipped but You, glory be to You, Lord of the worlds, to You is all praise, and to You is all dominion, You have no partner.'" He said: Then they threw him into the catapult from a far distance, and Jibril met him and said: "O Ibrahim, do you have any need?" He said: "As for you, no." Jibril said: "Then ask your Lord." He said: "My asking is sufficient for me: His knowledge of my condition." Then Allah, the Exalted, who is the most truthful of speakers, said: (O fire, be coolness and safety upon Ibrahim). Some scholars said: Allah placed in it a coolness that removed its heat, and a heat that removed its coolness, so it became safety for him. Abu al-Aliyah said: Had He not said "coolness and safety," its coolness would have been harder on him than its heat; and had He not said "upon Ibrahim," its coolness would have remained forever. Some scholars mentioned: Allah sent down a carpet (zirbiyyah) [[The zirbiyyah: a rug or cushion; it is also said to be a cloth with a pile, and its letter zay is pronounced with three dots (ẓ-type variant).]] from Paradise and spread it within the Blazing Fire, and Allah sent angels: Jibril, Mikail, the angel of coldness and the angel of safety. Ali and Ibn Abbas said: Had its coolness not been followed by safety, Ibrahim would have died from its cold, and on that day no fire remained that was not extinguished, thinking that it was being targeted. Al-Suddi said: Allah commanded every piece of wood from a tree to return to its tree and drop its fruit. Ka'b and Qatadah said: The fire burned from Ibrahim only his bonds. He remained in the fire for seven days, and no one could approach the fire; then they came and found him standing, praying. Al-Minhal ibn Amr said Ibrahim said: "I never had days more blessed than the days I spent in the fire." Ka'b, Qatadah and al-Zuhri said: On that day no creature remained that did not try to extinguish the fire from him, except the gecko (wazagh), for it was blowing upon it; therefore the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) ordered its killing and named it "fuwaysiqah" (the vile little one). Shu'ayb al-Himmani said: Ibrahim was cast into the fire when he was sixteen years old. Ibn Juraij said: Ibrahim was cast into the fire when he was twenty-six years old. Al-Tha'labi mentioned the first, and al-Mawardi the second, and Allah knows best. Al-Kalbi said: The fires of the whole earth were cooled, so that they did not burn even a shin-bone. Nimrod saw him from the tower while he was sitting on a throne, being kept company by an angel of shade. He said: "What a Lord your Lord is! I will certainly offer Him four thousand cows," and he refrained from him.

**Al-Qurtubi's commentary (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 21, verses 70–73:**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They intended a scheme against him﴾, meaning Nimrod and his companions intended to scheme against him. (So We made them the greatest losers) [i.e. [[From b, j, z, t, k, y.]]] in their deeds, and We turned their scheme back upon them by empowering against them the weakest of Our creation. Ibn 'Abbas said: God empowered against them the weakest of His creatures, the mosquito. Nimrod did not cease until he saw the bones of his companions and his horses showing; they had eaten their flesh and drunk their blood. One mosquito entered his nostril and kept eating until it reached his brain. The person most honoured by him was the one who struck his head with an iron mallet. He remained in this state for about four hundred years.

[[We have already noted that some narrators lie about Ibn 'Abbas.]]

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We delivered him and Lot to the land which We had blessed for all the worlds﴾. He means: We delivered Abraham and Lot to [the land [[From b, j, z, t, k, y.]]] of Syria, while they had been in Iraq. [Abraham [[From k.]]], peace be upon him, had [Lot as his nephew [[So in k. In the other manuscripts: Lot. This is an error.]]], as said by Ibn 'Abbas. It was said that it is blessed because of its abundance of fertility, fruits and rivers, and because it is the place of origin of the prophets. Blessing (barakah) is the establishment of good, and from it comes "the camel knelt (baraka al-ba'ir)" when it stays in its place and does not move. Ibn 'Abbas said: the blessed land is Makkah. It was also said: it is Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), because God sent most of the prophets from it, and it is also very fertile and flourishing, with sweet water, and from it [water] spreads over the earth. Abu al-'Aliyah said: there is no sweet water except that it descends from the sky to the rock that is in Bayt al-Maqdis, and then it spreads across the earth. A similar statement is reported from Ka'b al-Ahbar. It was also said: the blessed land is Egypt.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We gave him Isaac and Jacob as a nafilah (an extra gift)﴾, meaning an addition, because he had prayed for Isaac, and Jacob was added without his asking, so that was a nafilah, i.e. an addition beyond what he requested, when he said: ﴿My Lord, grant me [a child] from among the righteous﴾ [al-Saffat: 100]. [[See vol. 15, p. 97 onward.]] A grandson is also called a nafilah, because he is an addition to the son.

(And We made them all righteous) meaning: We made each of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob righteous, acting in obedience to God. Making them righteous is achieved only by creating righteousness and obedience in them, and by creating the capacity for obedience. Then whatever the servant acquires is created by God, Exalted is He.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We made them leaders guiding by Our command﴾, meaning leaders who are followed in good deeds and acts of obedience. The meaning of "by Our command" is by what We revealed to them of revelation, command and prohibition, as if He said: guiding by Our Book. It was also said: the meaning is that they guide people to Our religion by Our command to them, by guiding creation and calling them to monotheism.

(And We inspired them to do good deeds) meaning that they should perform acts of obedience.

(And to establish prayer and to give zakah, and they were worshippers of Us) meaning obedient.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 21, verses 74–75:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Lot—We gave him judgment and knowledge﴾. "Ḥukm" (judgment) is prophethood, and "ʿilm" (knowledge) is understanding of the affairs of religion and that by which judgment is made between disputants. It was also said: "ʿilman" means understanding, and the meaning is one.

**Part 1 of 3**

There are twenty-six issues in this verse.

**First issue:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And David and Solomon, when they judged﴾. That is, mention them both when they judged. By His saying "when they judged" He did not mean that they jointly reached one ruling, even though He combined them in the statement, since two rulings on a single matter are not permissible. Each of them judged separately, and Solomon was the one who understood it through God's granting him understanding. Regarding "the field" (*al-harth*), scholars differ on two views. It was said that it was a crop, as Qatada said. It was also said that it was a vineyard whose clusters had grown, as Ibn Mas'ud and Shurayh said. *Al-harth* can be used for both, though for a crop it is a more distant metaphor.

**Second issue:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿when the sheep of the people strayed into it﴾. That is, they grazed in it at night. *Al-nafsh* is grazing at night. It is said: "Nafashat" (they grazed by night) and "hamalat" (they grazed by day) when they grazed without a shepherd. Their owner was "anfashahā" (he let them graze at night). A camel herd is called *nuffāsh*. In the hadith of Abdullah ibn Amr: "The grain in Paradise is like the paunch of a camel, it spends the night *nāfishan*," meaning grazing. This is related by al-Harawi. Ibn Sida said: *hamal* is not said of sheep; it is only said of camels.

**Third issue:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We were witnesses to their judgment﴾. This is evidence that the minimum of the plural is two. It was also said that what is meant is the two judges and the one judged against, which is why He said "their judgment."

**Fourth issue:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So We gave understanding of it to Solomon﴾. That is, We gave Solomon understanding of the case and the judgment, and He referred to it by a pronoun since what indicates it had already come before. Solomon's ruling was superior to his father's in that it secured for each of them the ability to keep his property, and each of them remained content with that. David, peace be upon him, judged that the sheep should be handed over to the owner of the field. Another group said that he in fact handed the sheep to the owner of the field and the field to the owner of the sheep.

Ibn 'Atiyya said:
On the first view, it resembles that he saw the sheep as equal to the produce that had been destroyed.
On the second view, he saw them as equal to the field and the produce. When the two litigants went out to Solomon, who used to sit at the door through which the litigants exited, and they used to enter to David through another door, he said:
"By what did the prophet of God, David, judge between you two?"
They said:
"He judged the sheep to the owner of the field."
He said: "Perhaps the ruling was other than this. Go back with me."
So he went to his father and said:
"O prophet of God, you judged such and such, but I saw what is more suitable for everyone."
He said:
"And what is it?"
He said:
"The sheep should be handed to the owner of the field so that he benefits from their milk, their fat and their wool, and the field should be handed to the owner of the sheep so that he may tend it. When the crop returns to the state in which the sheep damaged it in the coming year, each of them returns the other's property to its owner."
David said:
"You have been granted success, my son. May God never cut off your understanding."
And he judged as Solomon had judged. This is the view related by Ibn Mas'ud, Mujahid and others.

Al-Kalbi said:
David valued the sheep and the vineyard that the sheep had damaged, and the two values were equal, so he handed the sheep to the owner of the vineyard.
Al-Nahhas said the same, and said:
He judged the sheep to the owner of the field only because their price was close to it.
As for Solomon's ruling, it has been said:
The value of what the sheep took and the value of what the sheep destroyed were also equal.

**Fifth issue:** His saying: ﴿And to each We gave judgment and knowledge﴾. Some people interpreted this to mean that David, peace be upon him, did not err in this incident, but that in it he was given judgment and knowledge. They understood His saying "So We gave understanding of it to Solomon" as a virtue for him over David, and the virtue returns to David, since a father is pleased by his child's excellence over him.
Another group said: rather, he did not hit the desired target in this incident, and God only praised him for having judgment and knowledge to which people may refer in other incidents than this one.
Regarding this incident, Solomon was right and David was wrong, peace and blessings be upon them both. It is not impossible for prophets to make mistakes and errors just as others can, but they are not left to persist in them, whereas others may be left to persist in them.

When al-Walid demolished the church of Damascus, the king of the Romans wrote to him:
"You have demolished the church which your father saw fit to leave. If you are right, then your father was wrong, and if your father was right, then you were wrong."
Al-Walid replied with: ﴿And David and Solomon, when they judged concerning the field, when the sheep of the people strayed into it, and We were witnesses to their judgment. So We gave understanding of it to Solomon, and to each We gave judgment and knowledge﴾.

Some people said: David and Solomon, peace be upon them both, were two prophets who judged by what was revealed to them. David judged by revelation, and Solomon judged by a revelation by which God abrogated David's ruling (*naskh*, abrogation, meaning the replacement of one ruling by a later one). On this view, "So We gave understanding of it to Solomon" means by way of the revelation that abrogated what had been revealed to David, and Solomon was ordered to inform David of that. This is why He said: ﴿And to each We gave judgment and knowledge﴾.
This is the view of a group of scholars, including Ibn Furak.

The majority said: their judgment was by *ijtihad* (independent reasoned judgment), and this is:

**Sixth issue:** Scholars differed over whether prophets may exercise *ijtihad*. Some denied it. The critical scholars permitted it, because there is no rational impossibility in it, since it is a legitimate form of evidence, so there is no impossibility in prophets relying on it, just as if the Lord, glory be to Him, said to him: "When your assumption about such and such prevails, be certain that what prevails in your assumption is My ruling, and convey it to the community." This is not rationally impossible.
If it is said: it is evidence only when the text is absent, and they do not lack the text.
We reply: when the angel does not descend, the text is absent for them, and they become, in investigating the meanings of the texts they have, like other *mujtahids* (qualified jurists exercising ijtihad).
The difference between them and other *mujtahids* is that they are protected from error, from mistake, and from falling short in their *ijtihad*, whereas others are not.
Just as the majority held that all prophets, may God's blessings be upon them, are protected from error and mistake in their *ijtihad*.
Abu 'Ali ibn Abi Hurayra, from the companions of al-Shafi'i, held that our Prophet ﷺ is excepted from them in the permissibility of error upon them. He distinguished between him and other prophets by saying that there was no one after him who could correct his mistake, and therefore God protected him from it. But after other prophets there were those who could correct their mistakes.
It has also been said:
It applies generally to all prophets, and our Prophet and other prophets, may God's blessings be upon them, are equal in the permissibility of error, except that they are not left to persist in it. For this reason, correction by those who came after them was not required.
This is the Messenger of God ﷺ, when a woman asked him about the waiting period (*'idda*), and he said to her: "Observe it wherever you wish." Then he said to her: "Remain in your house until the decreed term reaches its end."
A man said to him: "Have you seen it? If I am killed patiently, seeking reward, will anything keep me from Paradise?"
He said: "No." Then he called him and said: "Except the debt, as Gabriel, peace be upon him, told me."

**Seventh issue:** Al-Hasan said:
"Were it not for this verse, I would have thought that the judges had perished. But He praised Solomon for his correctness, and excused David for his *ijtihad*."
People have differed about the *mujtahids* in the subsidiary matters (*furu'*) when they disagree. One group said:
"The truth lies on one side with God, and He has set up evidence for it and driven the *mujtahids* to search for it and to examine it. Whoever hits the desired target in the matter is correct absolutely, and has two rewards, one for the *ijtihad* and one for the correctness. Whoever does not hit it is correct in his *ijtihad* but wrong in that he did not hit the target, so he has a reward, but he is not excused."
This is Solomon, who hit the desired target, which was what he understood.
Another group held that the mistaken scholar has no sin for his error, though he is not excused.
Another group said:
"The truth lies on one side, but God did not set up evidence for it. Rather, He left the matter to the reasoning of the *mujtahids*. Whoever reaches it is correct, and whoever errs is excused and rewarded. He was not required to hit the target, but was only required to perform *ijtihad*."
But the majority of the People of the Sunnah, which is what is transmitted from Malik and his companions, may God be pleased with them, said:
"The truth in matters of subsidiary law lies on both sides, and every *mujtahid* is correct. What is sought is only the better option in his assumption, and every *mujtahid* has been led by his reasoning to the better option in his assumption. The evidence for this view is that the Companions, and those after them, let some of them maintain disagreement with others, and none of them saw it as necessary that one opinion be preferred over the opinion of its opponent."
From this is Malik's refusal, may God have mercy on him, to the caliph al-Mansur, Abu Ja'far, when he wanted to force people to follow the *Muwatta'*. So when a scholar says a thing about a matter that is permissible, that is the truth in what concerns that scholar before God and for everyone who follows his opinion, and likewise in the reverse case.
They said:
"Even if Solomon, peace be upon him, understood the most excellent and most correct judgment, the first is not an error. On this basis they interpret his saying, peace be upon him: 'If the scholar exercises *ijtihad* and errs,' meaning that he erred in the more excellent option."

**Eighth issue:** Muslim and others related from Amr ibn al-As that he heard the Messenger of God ﷺ say:
"If a judge judges, and exercises *ijtihad*, then is correct, he has two rewards. If he judges and exercises *ijtihad*, then errs, he has one reward."
This is the wording of the hadith in Muslim's book: "If he judges and exercises *ijtihad*." He mentioned judging before *ijtihad*, but the order should be reversed, since *ijtihad* precedes judgment. It is not permissible to judge before *ijtihad*, by consensus.
The meaning of this hadith is rather: "If he intends to judge," as He said: ﴿So when you recite the Qur'an, seek refuge﴾ [An-Nahl 16:98]. At that point he intends to exercise *ijtihad* on the incident.
This supports what the scholars of legal theory (*usuliyyun*) said: the *mujtahid* must renew his examination when an incident occurs, and must not rely on his earlier *ijtihad*, since it is possible that what appeared to him the first time may appear differently to him the second time. Unless he remembers the foundations of his earlier *ijtihad* and is inclined toward it, in which case he does not need to begin a new examination of another indicator.

**Ninth issue:** The reward for the mistaken judge applies only if he is learned in *ijtihad*, the Sunnah, analogy (*qiyas*), and the judgments of those who came before. This is because his *ijtihad* is an act of worship, and he is not rewarded for error, but only has his sin lifted. As for one who is not qualified for *ijtihad*, he is presumptuous and is not excused for error in judgment. Rather, the greatest burden is feared for him.
This is shown by another hadith, related by Abu Dawud: "Judges are three," and the hadith continues.
Ibn al-Mundhir said: a person is rewarded only for his *ijtihad* in seeking what is correct, not for error. Among what supports this is His saying: ﴿So We gave understanding of it to Solomon﴾, and the rest of the verse.
Al-Hasan said: He praised Solomon and did not blame David.

**Tenth issue:** Abu al-Tamm al-Maliki mentioned that the school of Malik holds that the truth lies in one of the opinions of the *mujtahids*, but not in the opinions of those who disagree. Most jurists also held this.
He said:
Ibn al-Qasim related that he asked Malik about the disagreement of the Companions, and he said: "Some were wrong and some were right, and the truth is not in all their opinions."

This view is the well-known opinion of Malik, and Muhammad ibn al-Husayn adopted it.

Those who held this view argued with the hadith of Abdullah ibn Amr. They said: It is an explicit text that among the mujtahidun and among the judges there is one who errs and one who is correct. They said: The claim that every mujtahid is correct leads to a thing being both lawful and unlawful, and obligatory and recommended.

The people of the first view argued with the hadith of Ibn Umar. He said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ called out to us on the day he returned from the Confederates (al-Ahzab): "None of you should pray the afternoon prayer except in the land of Banu Qurayza." Some people feared that the time would pass, so they prayed before reaching Banu Qurayza. Others said: "We will not pray except where the Messenger of Allah ﷺ commanded us, even if the time passes." He said: So he did not rebuke either of the two groups. They said: If one of the two groups had been in error, the Prophet ﷺ would have specified it.

It may be said: Perhaps he remained silent about identifying those who erred because they were not sinful but rewarded, so there was no need to name them.

And Allah knows best.

The question of ijtihad is long and branching, and this summary we have mentioned is sufficient for the meaning of the verse. And Allah is the One who grants success in guidance.

Eleventh: Connected to the verse is another matter: the judge's return, after his ruling, from one ijtihad to another that is more preponderant than the first. Dawud (peace be upon him) did this.

Our scholars, may Allah have mercy on them, differed on this. Abd al-Malik and Mutarrif said in al-Wadiha: "This is permitted to him as long as he remains in his jurisdiction. But if it is another jurisdiction, he may not do so; he is in the same position as other judges." This is the apparent view of Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, in al-Mudawwana.

Sahnun said, regarding his return from an ijtihad in which he had a view to another that he saw as more correct: "He is not permitted to do so." Ibn Abd al-Hakam also said this. Both said: "He begins the judgment anew with what is strong for him."

Sahnun said: "Unless he forgot what was stronger for him at that time, or erred and ruled according to something else, in which case he may annul it. But if he ruled according to what was strongest for him at that time, and then another view became stronger for him afterward, there is no way to annul the first ruling." Sahnun said this in the book of his son.

Ashhab said in the book of Ibn al-Mawwaz: "If his return to what is more correct concerns property, he may annul the first ruling; if it concerns divorce, marriage or manumission, he may not annul it."

I say: The judge's return from his ruling, when it becomes clear to him that the truth lies elsewhere, is preferable, as long as he remains in his jurisdiction.

Likewise is the letter of Umar to Abu Musa, may Allah be pleased with them both, which al-Daraqutni narrated. We have mentioned it in al-A'raf, but he did not distinguish. It is the proof for the apparent view of Malik.

The scholars have not differed that if a judge rules carelessly, or contrary to the people of knowledge, his ruling is rejected, if it was based on ijtihad. But as for one judge overturning the ruling of another judge, this is not permitted for him, because it involves great harm through annulling rulings, replacing the lawful with the unlawful, and failing to preserve the laws of Islam. No scholar has taken it upon himself to annul what another narrated; rather, a judge rules according to what has become clear to him.

Twelfth: Some people said: Dawud (peace be upon him) had not yet executed the judgment, and what others said became clear to him.

Others said: It was not a judgment but only a fatwa.

I say: Likewise it is interpreted regarding what Abu Hurayra narrated from him (peace be upon him), that he said: "While two women were with their two sons, a wolf came and took the son of one of them. She said to her companion: 'It was your son who was taken.' The other said: 'It was your son who was taken.' So they brought their dispute to Dawud, and he ruled for the elder. Then they went out to Sulayman ibn Dawud, peace be upon them, and informed him. He said: 'Bring me a knife, and I will cut him between you.' The younger said: 'No, may Allah have mercy on you, he is her son.' So he ruled for the younger." Abu Hurayra said: "I never heard of a knife except on that day; we used to say only al-mudya." Related by Muslim.

As for the view that this was a fatwa from Dawud, it is weak, because the Prophet ﷺ's fatwa is a judgment.

As for the other view, it is far-fetched, because He, the Exalted, said: "when they were judging concerning the field" (21:78), which clarifies that each of them had issued a judgment.

Likewise His words in the hadith: "so he ruled for the elder" indicate the enforcement and completion of the judgment.

Whoever said that it was part of Dawud's law to rule for the elder simply because she is the elder has gone too far, because age and youth in disputes are a pure irrelevancy, like length, shortness, blackness and whiteness, and that does not necessitate favoring one of the two litigants so that a ruling is given for or against him on that basis.

This is something that anyone who understands what the sacred laws came with would decide with certainty.

What should be said is: Dawud (peace be upon him) ruled for the elder only because of a cause that, in his view, required preferring her claim.

The hadith does not mention its specification, since there was no need for it. It is possible that the child was in her possession, and he knew the other was unable to produce evidence, so he ruled for her to keep things as they were.

This interpretation is the best of what has been said about this hadith.

It is also what the general principle of legal claims supports, in which differing among the sacred laws is unlikely.

It is not said: If Dawud ruled on a lawful basis, how was it permissible for Sulayman to annul his judgment? The answer: Sulayman (peace be upon him) did not touch his father's ruling by annulling it. Rather, he employed a subtle stratagem through which the truthfulness of the younger became evident to him. When he said, "Bring me the knife, I will cut him between you," the younger said, "No." Thus there appeared to him, from the sign of compassion in the younger and its absence in the elder, together with what other evidences combined with it, that he came to know her truthfulness, and so he ruled for her.

Perhaps he was among those permitted to judge by his own knowledge.

Al-Nasa'i titled this hadith "The judge's ruling by his knowledge."

He also titled it "The latitude for the judge to say to a thing he does not do, 'I will do it,' so that the truth becomes clear."

He also titled it "The judge's annulment is not to be ruled upon by another of his equal or superior."

Perhaps the elder woman acknowledged that the child belonged to the younger when she saw Sulayman's firmness and earnestness in the matter, so he ruled the child for the younger. This is like when a judge rules for the oath: when the one who was to swear went to swear, someone came forward who extracted from the denier an admission that required it, and he is judged by that admission both before and after the oath. This is not from the category of annulling the first ruling, but from the category of rulings changing according to the change of causes.

And Allah knows best.

From this hadith the jurisprudential lessons include: prophets were permitted to judge by ijtihad, which we have mentioned. It also includes: judges using stratagems by which rights are extracted, which comes from strength of intelligence and perceptiveness and experience with people's conditions. Among the God-fearing there may be religious insight and luminous discernment, and that is the bounty of Allah which He gives to whom He wills.

It also includes the proof for the one who says that the mother is to be attributed the child (istilhaq), though this is not the well-known position of Malik, and this is not the place to mention it.

In sum, Sulayman's judgment in this story is contained in His praise of him: "So We gave Sulayman the understanding of it."

Thirteenth: The discussion of the field and the judgment in this incident has already been mentioned in our law: that the owners of gardens must guard their walls and crops by day; then liability for destroyed items of the same kind is by like, and for items of value by their value.

The basis of this question in our law is what our Prophet ﷺ ruled concerning the camel of al-Bara ibn Azib.

Malik narrated it from Ibn Shihab, from Haram ibn Sa'd ibn Muhayyisa: that a camel of al-Bara entered a man's garden and caused damage in it. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ ruled that the people of the gardens must guard them at night, and that what the livestock destroy at night is a liability upon their owners.

All the narrators transmitted it this way as mursal. Likewise the companions of Ibn Shihab transmitted it from Ibn Shihab, except Ibn Uyayna, who narrated it from al-Zuhri, from Sa'id and Haram ibn Sa'd ibn Muhayyisa: "that a camel," and mentioned the same in meaning.

Ibn Abi Dhi'b narrated from Ibn Shihab that it reached him that al-Bara's camel entered a people's garden, like Malik's hadith exactly, except that he did not mention Haram ibn Sa'd ibn Muhayyisa or anyone else.

Abu Umar said: Ibn Abi Dhi'b did nothing of value, except that he corrupted its chain.

Abd al-Razzaq narrated it from Ma'mar, from al-Zuhri, from Haram ibn Muhayyisa, from his father, from the Prophet ﷺ, but Abd al-Razzaq was not followed in this, and they rejected his saying "from his father."

Ibn Jurayj narrated it from Ibn Shihab who said: "Abu Umama ibn Sahl ibn Hunayf narrated to me that a camel entered a people's garden and caused damage," so he attributed the hadith to Ibn Shihab from Abu Umama, and it is not mentioned that the camel belonged to al-Bara.

It is possible that the hadith came from Ibn Shihab from Ibn Muhayyisa, and from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, and from Abu Umama, and Allah knows best; he narrated it from whichever of them he met, and they are all trustworthy.

Abu Umar said: This hadith, although it is mursal, is a well-known hadith. The imams transmitted it as mursal, trustworthy narrators related it, the jurists of the Hijaz applied it and received it with acceptance, the practice in Medina has been according to it, and it is sufficient for you that the people of Medina and all the people of the Hijaz applied this hadith.

Fourteenth: Malik and the majority of imams went with the hadith of al-Bara. Abu Hanifa and his companions and a group of the Kufans held that this ruling was abrogated, and that if livestock destroy crops, whether at night or by day, the owner is not liable for anything. They extended its destruction to the general scope of his saying (peace and blessings be upon him): "The wound inflicted by an animal is unrecompensed" (jubar), and they analogized all its actions to its wounding.

It is said that no one preceded Abu Hanifa in this view, and there is no proof for him or for those who followed him in the hadith of the animal, nor in its being abrogating the hadith of al-Bara and contradicting it. The conditions of abrogation are absent, and contradiction is only valid if one of the two cannot be applied without negating the other. The hadith "the wound of the animal is unrecompensed" is a general text agreed upon, then the crops and gardens were specified from it by the hadith of al-Bara. For if the Prophet ﷺ had said in a single hadith: "The wound of the animal is unrecompensed by night, not by day, and for crops, gardens and tilled land," this would not be an impossible statement. How then can it be said that these are in contradiction?!

Rather, this belongs to the category of general and specific, as mentioned in the books of legal theory.

Fifteenth: If it is said: What is the wisdom in the Lawgiver distinguishing between night and day, when al-Layth ibn Sa'd said: "The owners of livestock are liable for everything they destroy, by night and by day, but not more than the value of the livestock"?

We say:

The difference between them is clear. Owners of livestock need to send their animals out to graze by day, and most of them consider that whoever has a crop tends to it by day and guards it from anyone who wants to harm it. So the guarding of crops by day was placed on the owners of the fields, because daytime is the time for earning a living, as Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And We made the day for livelihood﴾ [An-Naba 78:11] [[See vol. 19, p. 170.]]. When night comes, it is the time when every thing returns to its place and its rest, as Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Who is the god other than Allah who could bring you the night in which you rest?﴾ [Al-Qasas 28:72] [[See vol. 14, p. 308.]], and He says: ﴿And He made the night for rest﴾ [Al-An'am 6:96] [[See vol. 7, p. 44.]]. Owners of livestock bring their animals back to their places to guard them. If the owner of the animals neglects to bring them back to his home, or neglects to control them and keep them from roaming at night, so that they cause damage, then he is liable for that damage. Thus the ruling follows what is most equitable and lenient, and this is more gentle on both parties, easier on both groups, and better for the preservation of both properties. The dawn is clear to one who has two eyes, but only to one whose two senses are sound.

As for the statement of al-Layth: "He is not made liable for more than the value of the livestock," Abu 'Umar said: "I do not know from where al-Layth ibn Sa'd derived this, unless he made it an analogy with the slave who commits an offense: he is not ransomed for more than his value, and his master is not obliged to pay more than his value for the offense. But this analogy is weak," as he said in *al-Tamhid*. He said in *al-Istidhkar*: "He opposed the hadith about 'the wound caused by an animal is unpaid' (al-'Ajma' juruhuha jubar), and he opposed the she-camel of al-Bara'. A group of scholars preceded him in this, among them 'Ata'."

Ibn Jurayj said: "I asked 'Ata': 'Does livestock damaging a field by night or by day [make the owner liable]?'" He said: "Its owner is made liable and must pay compensation." I said: "Was there an enclosure around it or not?" He said: "Yes, he must pay compensation." I said: "What must he pay?" He said: "The value of what his donkey, his beast, and his livestock ate."

Ma'mar reported from Ibn Shubrumah: "The crop is assessed in the condition in which it was damaged, in dirhams."

It is also reported from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab and 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz (may Allah be pleased with them both): "The owner of the livestock is made liable whether by night or by day," but these reports are through chains that are not sound.

Sixteenth issue: Malik said: "The crop that livestock damaged at night is assessed on the basis of expectation and fear (of what it would have yielded)." He said: "Orchards that are guarded and those that are not guarded, and those that are enclosed and those that are not enclosed, are the same: their owners must compensate for what the animals damage at night, up to whatever amount it reaches, even if it exceeds their value." He said: "If an animal escapes at night and tramples a sleeping man, its owner is not made to pay anything. This applies only to the orchard, the crop and the field." Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam reported this from him.

Ibn al-Qasim said: "Whatever livestock damages at night is at the expense of its owner, even if it is many times its price, because the offense came from him when he did not tie it up. Livestock are not like slaves." Sahnun, Asbagh and Abu Zayd reported this from Ibn al-Qasim.

Seventeenth issue: The crop is not to be delayed to see whether it will grow or not, as is done with the young of a tree. 'Isa reported from Ibn al-Qasim: "Its value is assessed as if it could be sold." Ashhab and Ibn Nafi' said in *al-Majmu'a* quoting him: "Even if its ripeness has not appeared."

Ibn al-'Arabi said: "The first view is stronger, because that is its condition, so it is assessed as every destroyed thing is assessed in its condition."

Eighteenth issue: If the one whose property was damaged was not awarded anything until the crop grew back and was restored, then if there was some benefit from it, such as grazing or something else before that, the value of that benefit is deducted. If there was no benefit in it, then nothing is owed. Asbagh said: "The owner is made liable, because the destruction has occurred, and the restoration did not come from him, so it is not counted in his favour."

Nineteenth issue: It occurs in the book of Ibn Sahnun that the hadith was given only regarding the towns of Medina, which are walled gardens, but the lands that are continuous fields without enclosures, and orchards of the same kind, then the owners of livestock are made liable for what the animals damage by night or by day. It seems that he held that leaving animals unrestrained in such lands is a transgression, because they inevitably cause damage. This is a leaning toward the view of al-Layth.

Twentieth issue: Asbagh said about Medina: "The owners of livestock may not release their animals into farming villages without herders." The scholars built on this that a plot of land is either a plot of cultivation or a plot of pasture. If it is a plot of cultivation, then livestock may not enter it except livestock that needs it, and its owners must guard them; whatever they damage, their owner is liable, by night or by day. If it is a plot of pasture, then the one who farms in it must guard his crop, and the owners of livestock bear no responsibility.

Twenty-first issue: Livestock are of two kinds: *dawari* (those accustomed to damaging) and *harisa* (those that are guarded). Malik divided them accordingly. The *dawari* are those accustomed to harming crops [[In MS K: "crops."]] and fruits. Malik said: "They are to be exiled and sold in a land where there are no crops." Ibn al-Qasim transmitted this in *al-Kitab* and elsewhere. Ibn Habib said: "Even if their owner dislikes it. Malik also said the same about an animal that became accustomed to damaging crops: it is to be exiled and sold." But what can be guarded against is not ordered to be removed by its owner.

Twenty-second issue: Asbagh said: "Bees, pigeons, geese and chickens are like livestock: their owner is not prevented from keeping them, even if they cause damage. The people of the village must guard their crops." Ibn al-'Arabi said: "This report is weak and should not be considered. Whoever wishes to keep what benefits him and does not harm others is allowed to do so, but benefiting from what he keeps by harming someone is not permitted." The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "There shall be no harm nor reciprocating harm." Ibn al-Qasim's view about these *dawari* in Medina is that their owners bear no liability unless they were warned beforehand. Ibn al-'Arabi said: "I hold that they are liable even before a warning, if they are *dawari*."

Twenty-third issue: 'Abd al-Razzaq reported from Ma'mar, from Qatadah, from al-Sha'bi that a sheep fell into a weaver's yarn, and they brought the dispute to Shurayh. Al-Sha'bi said: "Look into it, for he will ask them whether it fell in at night or by day." They did so. Then he said: "If it was at night, it is liable; if it was by day, it is not liable." Then Shurayh recited: ﴿When the people's sheep strayed into it at night﴾ [Al-Anbiya 21:78], and said: "*Nafsh* is at night, and *hamal* is by day."

I say: From this chapter is his saying, peace be upon him: "The wound caused by an animal is unpaid" (al-'Ajma' juruhuha jubar), and so on. Ibn Shihab said: "*Jubar* means something that is wasted without compensation, and *al-'Ajma'* means the beast." Our scholars said: "The apparent meaning of his saying 'the wound caused by an animal is unpaid' is that whatever the beast alone destroys incurs no liability, and this is agreed upon. But if there was with it a leader, a driver, or a rider who directed it so that it destroyed something, the one who directed it bears the ruling of the destroyer. If the offense is a deliberate one punishable by retaliation, and the directing was intentional, then retaliation applies, and there is no disagreement about this, because the animal is like a tool. If it was not intentional, then blood money is due from the 'aqilah (the paternal kin who bear the liability). For property, compensation is paid from the wrongdoer's property."

Twenty-fourth issue: They differed regarding a case where an animal struck someone with its leg or tail. Malik, al-Layth and al-Awza'i did not make its owner liable, while al-Shafi'i, Ibn Abi Layla and Ibn Shubrumah did make him liable. They also differed about the *dariya* (the animal accustomed to harm). The majority held that it is like any other, while Malik and some of his companions made its owner liable.

Twenty-fifth issue: Sufyan ibn Husayn reported from al-Zuhri, from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "The Messenger of Allah, peace be upon him, said: 'The man is *jubar*'." Al-Daraqutni said: "No one narrated this except Sufyan ibn Husayn, and no one followed him in it. The memorizers who transmit from al-Zuhri opposed him: among them Malik, Ibn 'Uyaynah, Yunus, Ma'mar, Ibn Jurayj, al-Zubaydi, 'Uqayl and Layth ibn Sa'd, and others. All of them transmitted from al-Zuhri saying: 'The beast is *jubar*, the well is *jubar*, and the mine is *jubar*,' and they did not mention the leg. This is the correct version." Likewise, Abu Salih al-Sammān, 'Abd al-Rahman al-A'raj, Muhammad ibn Sirin and Muhammad ibn Ziyad and others transmitted it from Abu Hurayrah without mentioning "the leg is *jubar*," and this is what is preserved from Abu Hurayrah.

Twenty-sixth issue: His saying "the well is *jubar*" has also been narrated with the wording "the fire is *jubar*." Al-Daraqutni said: "Hamzah ibn al-Qasim al-Hashimi narrated to us: Hanbal ibn Ishaq narrated to us, who said: 'I heard Abu 'Abd Allah Ahmad ibn Hanbal say about the hadith of 'Abd al-Razzaq, the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, "the fire is *jubar*": it is nothing. It is not in the book; it is false, not sound.'" Muhammad ibn Makhlad narrated to us: Abu Ishaq Ibrahim ibn Hani' narrated to us, who said: "I heard Ahmad ibn Hanbal say: 'The people of Yemen write *al-nar* (fire) as *al-nir* and write *al-bi'r* (well)'," meaning similar to that. 'Abd al-Razzaq was only prompted (with the wording) "the fire is *jubar*." Al-Ramadi said: "'Abd al-Razzaq said: Ma'mar said: 'I do not think it is anything but a mistake'." Abu 'Umar said: "It has been narrated from the Prophet, peace be upon him, through the hadith of Ma'mar, from Hammam ibn Munabbih, from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet, peace be upon him, that he said: 'The fire is *jubar*'." Yahya ibn Ma'in said: "Its origin is 'the well,' but Ma'mar altered it." Abu 'Umar said: "Ibn Ma'in did not support this claim with any proof, and the reports of trustworthy narrators are not rejected in this way."

Waki' reported from 'Abd al-'Aziz ibn Husayn, from Yahya ibn Yahya al-Ghassani, who said: "A man burned his plot of cultivated land (*qarah*: a field), and a spark of fire came out and burned something belonging to his neighbour."
