He said: "Ibn Husayn wrote to 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz about it, and he wrote back to me: 'The Messenger of Allah, peace be upon him, said: "The beast is *jubar*," and I think that fire is *jubar*'." It has been narrated with "the grazing animal is *jubar*" in place of "the beast." This is what has been reported in the wording of this hadith, and each meaning has a sound wording mentioned in the explanation of the hadith and in the books of jurisprudence.

His exalted saying: ﴿And We subjected the mountains to glorify [Allah] along with Dawud﴾ [Al-Anbiya 21:79]. Wahb said: "Dawud used to pass by the mountains glorifying Allah, and the mountains would respond to him with glorification, and so did the birds." It was said: "Whenever Dawud felt a lull, he would command the mountains, and they would glorify Allah until he felt eager." This is why He said: "And We subjected," meaning: We made them such that they obey him when he commands them to glorify. It was also said: "Their traveling with him is their glorification," and *tasbih* (glorification) is derived from *sibahah* (swimming/gliding), the proof of which is His saying: ﴿O mountains, echo God's praises along with him﴾ [Saba 34:10] [[See vol. 14, p. 264 onward.]]. Qatadah said: "'Yusabbihna' means they pray along with him when he prays, and *tasbih* is prayer." Both interpretations are possible. This is an act of Allah the Exalted toward them, because mountains do not understand. Their glorification is a proof of Allah the Exalted's transcendence above the attributes of the incapable and the created.

**Part 1 of 3**

There are twenty-six issues in this verse.

**First issue:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And David and Solomon, when they judged﴾. That is, mention them both when they judged. By His saying "when they judged" He did not mean that they jointly reached one ruling, even though He combined them in the statement, since two rulings on a single matter are not permissible. Each of them judged separately, and Solomon was the one who understood it through God's granting him understanding. Regarding "the field" (*al-harth*), scholars differ on two views. It was said that it was a crop, as Qatada said. It was also said that it was a vineyard whose clusters had grown, as Ibn Mas'ud and Shurayh said. *Al-harth* can be used for both, though for a crop it is a more distant metaphor.

**Second issue:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿when the sheep of the people strayed into it﴾. That is, they grazed in it at night. *Al-nafsh* is grazing at night. It is said: "Nafashat" (they grazed by night) and "hamalat" (they grazed by day) when they grazed without a shepherd. Their owner was "anfashahā" (he let them graze at night). A camel herd is called *nuffāsh*. In the hadith of Abdullah ibn Amr: "The grain in Paradise is like the paunch of a camel, it spends the night *nāfishan*," meaning grazing. This is related by al-Harawi. Ibn Sida said: *hamal* is not said of sheep; it is only said of camels.

**Third issue:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We were witnesses to their judgment﴾. This is evidence that the minimum of the plural is two. It was also said that what is meant is the two judges and the one judged against, which is why He said "their judgment."

**Fourth issue:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So We gave understanding of it to Solomon﴾. That is, We gave Solomon understanding of the case and the judgment, and He referred to it by a pronoun since what indicates it had already come before. Solomon's ruling was superior to his father's in that it secured for each of them the ability to keep his property, and each of them remained content with that. David, peace be upon him, judged that the sheep should be handed over to the owner of the field. Another group said that he in fact handed the sheep to the owner of the field and the field to the owner of the sheep.

Ibn 'Atiyya said:
On the first view, it resembles that he saw the sheep as equal to the produce that had been destroyed.
On the second view, he saw them as equal to the field and the produce. When the two litigants went out to Solomon, who used to sit at the door through which the litigants exited, and they used to enter to David through another door, he said:
"By what did the prophet of God, David, judge between you two?"
They said:
"He judged the sheep to the owner of the field."
He said: "Perhaps the ruling was other than this. Go back with me."
So he went to his father and said:
"O prophet of God, you judged such and such, but I saw what is more suitable for everyone."
He said:
"And what is it?"
He said:
"The sheep should be handed to the owner of the field so that he benefits from their milk, their fat and their wool, and the field should be handed to the owner of the sheep so that he may tend it. When the crop returns to the state in which the sheep damaged it in the coming year, each of them returns the other's property to its owner."
David said:
"You have been granted success, my son. May God never cut off your understanding."
And he judged as Solomon had judged. This is the view related by Ibn Mas'ud, Mujahid and others.

Al-Kalbi said:
David valued the sheep and the vineyard that the sheep had damaged, and the two values were equal, so he handed the sheep to the owner of the vineyard.
Al-Nahhas said the same, and said:
He judged the sheep to the owner of the field only because their price was close to it.
As for Solomon's ruling, it has been said:
The value of what the sheep took and the value of what the sheep destroyed were also equal.

**Fifth issue:** His saying: ﴿And to each We gave judgment and knowledge﴾. Some people interpreted this to mean that David, peace be upon him, did not err in this incident, but that in it he was given judgment and knowledge. They understood His saying "So We gave understanding of it to Solomon" as a virtue for him over David, and the virtue returns to David, since a father is pleased by his child's excellence over him.
Another group said: rather, he did not hit the desired target in this incident, and God only praised him for having judgment and knowledge to which people may refer in other incidents than this one.
Regarding this incident, Solomon was right and David was wrong, peace and blessings be upon them both. It is not impossible for prophets to make mistakes and errors just as others can, but they are not left to persist in them, whereas others may be left to persist in them.

When al-Walid demolished the church of Damascus, the king of the Romans wrote to him:
"You have demolished the church which your father saw fit to leave. If you are right, then your father was wrong, and if your father was right, then you were wrong."
Al-Walid replied with: ﴿And David and Solomon, when they judged concerning the field, when the sheep of the people strayed into it, and We were witnesses to their judgment. So We gave understanding of it to Solomon, and to each We gave judgment and knowledge﴾.

Some people said: David and Solomon, peace be upon them both, were two prophets who judged by what was revealed to them. David judged by revelation, and Solomon judged by a revelation by which God abrogated David's ruling (*naskh*, abrogation, meaning the replacement of one ruling by a later one). On this view, "So We gave understanding of it to Solomon" means by way of the revelation that abrogated what had been revealed to David, and Solomon was ordered to inform David of that. This is why He said: ﴿And to each We gave judgment and knowledge﴾.
This is the view of a group of scholars, including Ibn Furak.

The majority said: their judgment was by *ijtihad* (independent reasoned judgment), and this is:

**Sixth issue:** Scholars differed over whether prophets may exercise *ijtihad*. Some denied it. The critical scholars permitted it, because there is no rational impossibility in it, since it is a legitimate form of evidence, so there is no impossibility in prophets relying on it, just as if the Lord, glory be to Him, said to him: "When your assumption about such and such prevails, be certain that what prevails in your assumption is My ruling, and convey it to the community." This is not rationally impossible.
If it is said: it is evidence only when the text is absent, and they do not lack the text.
We reply: when the angel does not descend, the text is absent for them, and they become, in investigating the meanings of the texts they have, like other *mujtahids* (qualified jurists exercising ijtihad).
The difference between them and other *mujtahids* is that they are protected from error, from mistake, and from falling short in their *ijtihad*, whereas others are not.
Just as the majority held that all prophets, may God's blessings be upon them, are protected from error and mistake in their *ijtihad*.
Abu 'Ali ibn Abi Hurayra, from the companions of al-Shafi'i, held that our Prophet ﷺ is excepted from them in the permissibility of error upon them. He distinguished between him and other prophets by saying that there was no one after him who could correct his mistake, and therefore God protected him from it. But after other prophets there were those who could correct their mistakes.
It has also been said:
It applies generally to all prophets, and our Prophet and other prophets, may God's blessings be upon them, are equal in the permissibility of error, except that they are not left to persist in it. For this reason, correction by those who came after them was not required.
This is the Messenger of God ﷺ, when a woman asked him about the waiting period (*'idda*), and he said to her: "Observe it wherever you wish." Then he said to her: "Remain in your house until the decreed term reaches its end."
A man said to him: "Have you seen it? If I am killed patiently, seeking reward, will anything keep me from Paradise?"
He said: "No." Then he called him and said: "Except the debt, as Gabriel, peace be upon him, told me."

**Seventh issue:** Al-Hasan said:
"Were it not for this verse, I would have thought that the judges had perished. But He praised Solomon for his correctness, and excused David for his *ijtihad*."
People have differed about the *mujtahids* in the subsidiary matters (*furu'*) when they disagree. One group said:
"The truth lies on one side with God, and He has set up evidence for it and driven the *mujtahids* to search for it and to examine it. Whoever hits the desired target in the matter is correct absolutely, and has two rewards, one for the *ijtihad* and one for the correctness. Whoever does not hit it is correct in his *ijtihad* but wrong in that he did not hit the target, so he has a reward, but he is not excused."
This is Solomon, who hit the desired target, which was what he understood.
Another group held that the mistaken scholar has no sin for his error, though he is not excused.
Another group said:
"The truth lies on one side, but God did not set up evidence for it. Rather, He left the matter to the reasoning of the *mujtahids*. Whoever reaches it is correct, and whoever errs is excused and rewarded. He was not required to hit the target, but was only required to perform *ijtihad*."
But the majority of the People of the Sunnah, which is what is transmitted from Malik and his companions, may God be pleased with them, said:
"The truth in matters of subsidiary law lies on both sides, and every *mujtahid* is correct. What is sought is only the better option in his assumption, and every *mujtahid* has been led by his reasoning to the better option in his assumption. The evidence for this view is that the Companions, and those after them, let some of them maintain disagreement with others, and none of them saw it as necessary that one opinion be preferred over the opinion of its opponent."
From this is Malik's refusal, may God have mercy on him, to the caliph al-Mansur, Abu Ja'far, when he wanted to force people to follow the *Muwatta'*. So when a scholar says a thing about a matter that is permissible, that is the truth in what concerns that scholar before God and for everyone who follows his opinion, and likewise in the reverse case.
They said:
"Even if Solomon, peace be upon him, understood the most excellent and most correct judgment, the first is not an error. On this basis they interpret his saying, peace be upon him: 'If the scholar exercises *ijtihad* and errs,' meaning that he erred in the more excellent option."

**Eighth issue:** Muslim and others related from Amr ibn al-As that he heard the Messenger of God ﷺ say:
"If a judge judges, and exercises *ijtihad*, then is correct, he has two rewards. If he judges and exercises *ijtihad*, then errs, he has one reward."
This is the wording of the hadith in Muslim's book: "If he judges and exercises *ijtihad*." He mentioned judging before *ijtihad*, but the order should be reversed, since *ijtihad* precedes judgment. It is not permissible to judge before *ijtihad*, by consensus.
The meaning of this hadith is rather: "If he intends to judge," as He said: ﴿So when you recite the Qur'an, seek refuge﴾ [An-Nahl 16:98]. At that point he intends to exercise *ijtihad* on the incident.
This supports what the scholars of legal theory (*usuliyyun*) said: the *mujtahid* must renew his examination when an incident occurs, and must not rely on his earlier *ijtihad*, since it is possible that what appeared to him the first time may appear differently to him the second time. Unless he remembers the foundations of his earlier *ijtihad* and is inclined toward it, in which case he does not need to begin a new examination of another indicator.

**Ninth issue:** The reward for the mistaken judge applies only if he is learned in *ijtihad*, the Sunnah, analogy (*qiyas*), and the judgments of those who came before. This is because his *ijtihad* is an act of worship, and he is not rewarded for error, but only has his sin lifted. As for one who is not qualified for *ijtihad*, he is presumptuous and is not excused for error in judgment. Rather, the greatest burden is feared for him.
This is shown by another hadith, related by Abu Dawud: "Judges are three," and the hadith continues.
Ibn al-Mundhir said: a person is rewarded only for his *ijtihad* in seeking what is correct, not for error. Among what supports this is His saying: ﴿So We gave understanding of it to Solomon﴾, and the rest of the verse.
Al-Hasan said: He praised Solomon and did not blame David.

**Tenth issue:** Abu al-Tamm al-Maliki mentioned that the school of Malik holds that the truth lies in one of the opinions of the *mujtahids*, but not in the opinions of those who disagree. Most jurists also held this.
He said:
Ibn al-Qasim related that he asked Malik about the disagreement of the Companions, and he said: "Some were wrong and some were right, and the truth is not in all their opinions."

This view is the well-known opinion of Malik, and Muhammad ibn al-Husayn adopted it.

Those who held this view argued with the hadith of Abdullah ibn Amr. They said: It is an explicit text that among the mujtahidun and among the judges there is one who errs and one who is correct. They said: The claim that every mujtahid is correct leads to a thing being both lawful and unlawful, and obligatory and recommended.

The people of the first view argued with the hadith of Ibn Umar. He said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ called out to us on the day he returned from the Confederates (al-Ahzab): "None of you should pray the afternoon prayer except in the land of Banu Qurayza." Some people feared that the time would pass, so they prayed before reaching Banu Qurayza. Others said: "We will not pray except where the Messenger of Allah ﷺ commanded us, even if the time passes." He said: So he did not rebuke either of the two groups. They said: If one of the two groups had been in error, the Prophet ﷺ would have specified it.

It may be said: Perhaps he remained silent about identifying those who erred because they were not sinful but rewarded, so there was no need to name them.

And Allah knows best.

The question of ijtihad is long and branching, and this summary we have mentioned is sufficient for the meaning of the verse. And Allah is the One who grants success in guidance.

Eleventh: Connected to the verse is another matter: the judge's return, after his ruling, from one ijtihad to another that is more preponderant than the first. Dawud (peace be upon him) did this.

Our scholars, may Allah have mercy on them, differed on this. Abd al-Malik and Mutarrif said in al-Wadiha: "This is permitted to him as long as he remains in his jurisdiction. But if it is another jurisdiction, he may not do so; he is in the same position as other judges." This is the apparent view of Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, in al-Mudawwana.

Sahnun said, regarding his return from an ijtihad in which he had a view to another that he saw as more correct: "He is not permitted to do so." Ibn Abd al-Hakam also said this. Both said: "He begins the judgment anew with what is strong for him."

Sahnun said: "Unless he forgot what was stronger for him at that time, or erred and ruled according to something else, in which case he may annul it. But if he ruled according to what was strongest for him at that time, and then another view became stronger for him afterward, there is no way to annul the first ruling." Sahnun said this in the book of his son.

Ashhab said in the book of Ibn al-Mawwaz: "If his return to what is more correct concerns property, he may annul the first ruling; if it concerns divorce, marriage or manumission, he may not annul it."

I say: The judge's return from his ruling, when it becomes clear to him that the truth lies elsewhere, is preferable, as long as he remains in his jurisdiction.

Likewise is the letter of Umar to Abu Musa, may Allah be pleased with them both, which al-Daraqutni narrated. We have mentioned it in al-A'raf, but he did not distinguish. It is the proof for the apparent view of Malik.

The scholars have not differed that if a judge rules carelessly, or contrary to the people of knowledge, his ruling is rejected, if it was based on ijtihad. But as for one judge overturning the ruling of another judge, this is not permitted for him, because it involves great harm through annulling rulings, replacing the lawful with the unlawful, and failing to preserve the laws of Islam. No scholar has taken it upon himself to annul what another narrated; rather, a judge rules according to what has become clear to him.

Twelfth: Some people said: Dawud (peace be upon him) had not yet executed the judgment, and what others said became clear to him.

Others said: It was not a judgment but only a fatwa.

I say: Likewise it is interpreted regarding what Abu Hurayra narrated from him (peace be upon him), that he said: "While two women were with their two sons, a wolf came and took the son of one of them. She said to her companion: 'It was your son who was taken.' The other said: 'It was your son who was taken.' So they brought their dispute to Dawud, and he ruled for the elder. Then they went out to Sulayman ibn Dawud, peace be upon them, and informed him. He said: 'Bring me a knife, and I will cut him between you.' The younger said: 'No, may Allah have mercy on you, he is her son.' So he ruled for the younger." Abu Hurayra said: "I never heard of a knife except on that day; we used to say only al-mudya." Related by Muslim.

As for the view that this was a fatwa from Dawud, it is weak, because the Prophet ﷺ's fatwa is a judgment.

As for the other view, it is far-fetched, because He, the Exalted, said: "when they were judging concerning the field" (21:78), which clarifies that each of them had issued a judgment.

Likewise His words in the hadith: "so he ruled for the elder" indicate the enforcement and completion of the judgment.

Whoever said that it was part of Dawud's law to rule for the elder simply because she is the elder has gone too far, because age and youth in disputes are a pure irrelevancy, like length, shortness, blackness and whiteness, and that does not necessitate favoring one of the two litigants so that a ruling is given for or against him on that basis.

This is something that anyone who understands what the sacred laws came with would decide with certainty.

What should be said is: Dawud (peace be upon him) ruled for the elder only because of a cause that, in his view, required preferring her claim.

The hadith does not mention its specification, since there was no need for it. It is possible that the child was in her possession, and he knew the other was unable to produce evidence, so he ruled for her to keep things as they were.

This interpretation is the best of what has been said about this hadith.

It is also what the general principle of legal claims supports, in which differing among the sacred laws is unlikely.

It is not said: If Dawud ruled on a lawful basis, how was it permissible for Sulayman to annul his judgment? The answer: Sulayman (peace be upon him) did not touch his father's ruling by annulling it. Rather, he employed a subtle stratagem through which the truthfulness of the younger became evident to him. When he said, "Bring me the knife, I will cut him between you," the younger said, "No." Thus there appeared to him, from the sign of compassion in the younger and its absence in the elder, together with what other evidences combined with it, that he came to know her truthfulness, and so he ruled for her.

Perhaps he was among those permitted to judge by his own knowledge.

Al-Nasa'i titled this hadith "The judge's ruling by his knowledge."

He also titled it "The latitude for the judge to say to a thing he does not do, 'I will do it,' so that the truth becomes clear."

He also titled it "The judge's annulment is not to be ruled upon by another of his equal or superior."

Perhaps the elder woman acknowledged that the child belonged to the younger when she saw Sulayman's firmness and earnestness in the matter, so he ruled the child for the younger. This is like when a judge rules for the oath: when the one who was to swear went to swear, someone came forward who extracted from the denier an admission that required it, and he is judged by that admission both before and after the oath. This is not from the category of annulling the first ruling, but from the category of rulings changing according to the change of causes.

And Allah knows best.

From this hadith the jurisprudential lessons include: prophets were permitted to judge by ijtihad, which we have mentioned. It also includes: judges using stratagems by which rights are extracted, which comes from strength of intelligence and perceptiveness and experience with people's conditions. Among the God-fearing there may be religious insight and luminous discernment, and that is the bounty of Allah which He gives to whom He wills.

It also includes the proof for the one who says that the mother is to be attributed the child (istilhaq), though this is not the well-known position of Malik, and this is not the place to mention it.

In sum, Sulayman's judgment in this story is contained in His praise of him: "So We gave Sulayman the understanding of it."

Thirteenth: The discussion of the field and the judgment in this incident has already been mentioned in our law: that the owners of gardens must guard their walls and crops by day; then liability for destroyed items of the same kind is by like, and for items of value by their value.

The basis of this question in our law is what our Prophet ﷺ ruled concerning the camel of al-Bara ibn Azib.

Malik narrated it from Ibn Shihab, from Haram ibn Sa'd ibn Muhayyisa: that a camel of al-Bara entered a man's garden and caused damage in it. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ ruled that the people of the gardens must guard them at night, and that what the livestock destroy at night is a liability upon their owners.

All the narrators transmitted it this way as mursal. Likewise the companions of Ibn Shihab transmitted it from Ibn Shihab, except Ibn Uyayna, who narrated it from al-Zuhri, from Sa'id and Haram ibn Sa'd ibn Muhayyisa: "that a camel," and mentioned the same in meaning.

Ibn Abi Dhi'b narrated from Ibn Shihab that it reached him that al-Bara's camel entered a people's garden, like Malik's hadith exactly, except that he did not mention Haram ibn Sa'd ibn Muhayyisa or anyone else.

Abu Umar said: Ibn Abi Dhi'b did nothing of value, except that he corrupted its chain.

Abd al-Razzaq narrated it from Ma'mar, from al-Zuhri, from Haram ibn Muhayyisa, from his father, from the Prophet ﷺ, but Abd al-Razzaq was not followed in this, and they rejected his saying "from his father."

Ibn Jurayj narrated it from Ibn Shihab who said: "Abu Umama ibn Sahl ibn Hunayf narrated to me that a camel entered a people's garden and caused damage," so he attributed the hadith to Ibn Shihab from Abu Umama, and it is not mentioned that the camel belonged to al-Bara.

It is possible that the hadith came from Ibn Shihab from Ibn Muhayyisa, and from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, and from Abu Umama, and Allah knows best; he narrated it from whichever of them he met, and they are all trustworthy.

Abu Umar said: This hadith, although it is mursal, is a well-known hadith. The imams transmitted it as mursal, trustworthy narrators related it, the jurists of the Hijaz applied it and received it with acceptance, the practice in Medina has been according to it, and it is sufficient for you that the people of Medina and all the people of the Hijaz applied this hadith.

Fourteenth: Malik and the majority of imams went with the hadith of al-Bara. Abu Hanifa and his companions and a group of the Kufans held that this ruling was abrogated, and that if livestock destroy crops, whether at night or by day, the owner is not liable for anything. They extended its destruction to the general scope of his saying (peace and blessings be upon him): "The wound inflicted by an animal is unrecompensed" (jubar), and they analogized all its actions to its wounding.

It is said that no one preceded Abu Hanifa in this view, and there is no proof for him or for those who followed him in the hadith of the animal, nor in its being abrogating the hadith of al-Bara and contradicting it. The conditions of abrogation are absent, and contradiction is only valid if one of the two cannot be applied without negating the other. The hadith "the wound of the animal is unrecompensed" is a general text agreed upon, then the crops and gardens were specified from it by the hadith of al-Bara. For if the Prophet ﷺ had said in a single hadith: "The wound of the animal is unrecompensed by night, not by day, and for crops, gardens and tilled land," this would not be an impossible statement. How then can it be said that these are in contradiction?!

Rather, this belongs to the category of general and specific, as mentioned in the books of legal theory.

Fifteenth: If it is said: What is the wisdom in the Lawgiver distinguishing between night and day, when al-Layth ibn Sa'd said: "The owners of livestock are liable for everything they destroy, by night and by day, but not more than the value of the livestock"?

We say:

The difference between them is clear. Owners of livestock need to send their animals out to graze by day, and most of them consider that whoever has a crop tends to it by day and guards it from anyone who wants to harm it. So the guarding of crops by day was placed on the owners of the fields, because daytime is the time for earning a living, as Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And We made the day for livelihood﴾ [An-Naba 78:11] [[See vol. 19, p. 170.]]. When night comes, it is the time when every thing returns to its place and its rest, as Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Who is the god other than Allah who could bring you the night in which you rest?﴾ [Al-Qasas 28:72] [[See vol. 14, p. 308.]], and He says: ﴿And He made the night for rest﴾ [Al-An'am 6:96] [[See vol. 7, p. 44.]]. Owners of livestock bring their animals back to their places to guard them. If the owner of the animals neglects to bring them back to his home, or neglects to control them and keep them from roaming at night, so that they cause damage, then he is liable for that damage. Thus the ruling follows what is most equitable and lenient, and this is more gentle on both parties, easier on both groups, and better for the preservation of both properties. The dawn is clear to one who has two eyes, but only to one whose two senses are sound.

As for the statement of al-Layth: "He is not made liable for more than the value of the livestock," Abu 'Umar said: "I do not know from where al-Layth ibn Sa'd derived this, unless he made it an analogy with the slave who commits an offense: he is not ransomed for more than his value, and his master is not obliged to pay more than his value for the offense. But this analogy is weak," as he said in *al-Tamhid*. He said in *al-Istidhkar*: "He opposed the hadith about 'the wound caused by an animal is unpaid' (al-'Ajma' juruhuha jubar), and he opposed the she-camel of al-Bara'. A group of scholars preceded him in this, among them 'Ata'."

Ibn Jurayj said: "I asked 'Ata': 'Does livestock damaging a field by night or by day [make the owner liable]?'" He said: "Its owner is made liable and must pay compensation." I said: "Was there an enclosure around it or not?" He said: "Yes, he must pay compensation." I said: "What must he pay?" He said: "The value of what his donkey, his beast, and his livestock ate."

Ma'mar reported from Ibn Shubrumah: "The crop is assessed in the condition in which it was damaged, in dirhams."

It is also reported from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab and 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz (may Allah be pleased with them both): "The owner of the livestock is made liable whether by night or by day," but these reports are through chains that are not sound.

Sixteenth issue: Malik said: "The crop that livestock damaged at night is assessed on the basis of expectation and fear (of what it would have yielded)." He said: "Orchards that are guarded and those that are not guarded, and those that are enclosed and those that are not enclosed, are the same: their owners must compensate for what the animals damage at night, up to whatever amount it reaches, even if it exceeds their value." He said: "If an animal escapes at night and tramples a sleeping man, its owner is not made to pay anything. This applies only to the orchard, the crop and the field." Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam reported this from him.

Ibn al-Qasim said: "Whatever livestock damages at night is at the expense of its owner, even if it is many times its price, because the offense came from him when he did not tie it up. Livestock are not like slaves." Sahnun, Asbagh and Abu Zayd reported this from Ibn al-Qasim.

Seventeenth issue: The crop is not to be delayed to see whether it will grow or not, as is done with the young of a tree. 'Isa reported from Ibn al-Qasim: "Its value is assessed as if it could be sold." Ashhab and Ibn Nafi' said in *al-Majmu'a* quoting him: "Even if its ripeness has not appeared."

Ibn al-'Arabi said: "The first view is stronger, because that is its condition, so it is assessed as every destroyed thing is assessed in its condition."

Eighteenth issue: If the one whose property was damaged was not awarded anything until the crop grew back and was restored, then if there was some benefit from it, such as grazing or something else before that, the value of that benefit is deducted. If there was no benefit in it, then nothing is owed. Asbagh said: "The owner is made liable, because the destruction has occurred, and the restoration did not come from him, so it is not counted in his favour."

Nineteenth issue: It occurs in the book of Ibn Sahnun that the hadith was given only regarding the towns of Medina, which are walled gardens, but the lands that are continuous fields without enclosures, and orchards of the same kind, then the owners of livestock are made liable for what the animals damage by night or by day. It seems that he held that leaving animals unrestrained in such lands is a transgression, because they inevitably cause damage. This is a leaning toward the view of al-Layth.

Twentieth issue: Asbagh said about Medina: "The owners of livestock may not release their animals into farming villages without herders." The scholars built on this that a plot of land is either a plot of cultivation or a plot of pasture. If it is a plot of cultivation, then livestock may not enter it except livestock that needs it, and its owners must guard them; whatever they damage, their owner is liable, by night or by day. If it is a plot of pasture, then the one who farms in it must guard his crop, and the owners of livestock bear no responsibility.

Twenty-first issue: Livestock are of two kinds: *dawari* (those accustomed to damaging) and *harisa* (those that are guarded). Malik divided them accordingly. The *dawari* are those accustomed to harming crops [[In MS K: "crops."]] and fruits. Malik said: "They are to be exiled and sold in a land where there are no crops." Ibn al-Qasim transmitted this in *al-Kitab* and elsewhere. Ibn Habib said: "Even if their owner dislikes it. Malik also said the same about an animal that became accustomed to damaging crops: it is to be exiled and sold." But what can be guarded against is not ordered to be removed by its owner.

Twenty-second issue: Asbagh said: "Bees, pigeons, geese and chickens are like livestock: their owner is not prevented from keeping them, even if they cause damage. The people of the village must guard their crops." Ibn al-'Arabi said: "This report is weak and should not be considered. Whoever wishes to keep what benefits him and does not harm others is allowed to do so, but benefiting from what he keeps by harming someone is not permitted." The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "There shall be no harm nor reciprocating harm." Ibn al-Qasim's view about these *dawari* in Medina is that their owners bear no liability unless they were warned beforehand. Ibn al-'Arabi said: "I hold that they are liable even before a warning, if they are *dawari*."

Twenty-third issue: 'Abd al-Razzaq reported from Ma'mar, from Qatadah, from al-Sha'bi that a sheep fell into a weaver's yarn, and they brought the dispute to Shurayh. Al-Sha'bi said: "Look into it, for he will ask them whether it fell in at night or by day." They did so. Then he said: "If it was at night, it is liable; if it was by day, it is not liable." Then Shurayh recited: ﴿When the people's sheep strayed into it at night﴾ [Al-Anbiya 21:78], and said: "*Nafsh* is at night, and *hamal* is by day."

I say: From this chapter is his saying, peace be upon him: "The wound caused by an animal is unpaid" (al-'Ajma' juruhuha jubar), and so on. Ibn Shihab said: "*Jubar* means something that is wasted without compensation, and *al-'Ajma'* means the beast." Our scholars said: "The apparent meaning of his saying 'the wound caused by an animal is unpaid' is that whatever the beast alone destroys incurs no liability, and this is agreed upon. But if there was with it a leader, a driver, or a rider who directed it so that it destroyed something, the one who directed it bears the ruling of the destroyer. If the offense is a deliberate one punishable by retaliation, and the directing was intentional, then retaliation applies, and there is no disagreement about this, because the animal is like a tool. If it was not intentional, then blood money is due from the 'aqilah (the paternal kin who bear the liability). For property, compensation is paid from the wrongdoer's property."

Twenty-fourth issue: They differed regarding a case where an animal struck someone with its leg or tail. Malik, al-Layth and al-Awza'i did not make its owner liable, while al-Shafi'i, Ibn Abi Layla and Ibn Shubrumah did make him liable. They also differed about the *dariya* (the animal accustomed to harm). The majority held that it is like any other, while Malik and some of his companions made its owner liable.

Twenty-fifth issue: Sufyan ibn Husayn reported from al-Zuhri, from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "The Messenger of Allah, peace be upon him, said: 'The man is *jubar*'." Al-Daraqutni said: "No one narrated this except Sufyan ibn Husayn, and no one followed him in it. The memorizers who transmit from al-Zuhri opposed him: among them Malik, Ibn 'Uyaynah, Yunus, Ma'mar, Ibn Jurayj, al-Zubaydi, 'Uqayl and Layth ibn Sa'd, and others. All of them transmitted from al-Zuhri saying: 'The beast is *jubar*, the well is *jubar*, and the mine is *jubar*,' and they did not mention the leg. This is the correct version." Likewise, Abu Salih al-Sammān, 'Abd al-Rahman al-A'raj, Muhammad ibn Sirin and Muhammad ibn Ziyad and others transmitted it from Abu Hurayrah without mentioning "the leg is *jubar*," and this is what is preserved from Abu Hurayrah.

Twenty-sixth issue: His saying "the well is *jubar*" has also been narrated with the wording "the fire is *jubar*." Al-Daraqutni said: "Hamzah ibn al-Qasim al-Hashimi narrated to us: Hanbal ibn Ishaq narrated to us, who said: 'I heard Abu 'Abd Allah Ahmad ibn Hanbal say about the hadith of 'Abd al-Razzaq, the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, "the fire is *jubar*": it is nothing. It is not in the book; it is false, not sound.'" Muhammad ibn Makhlad narrated to us: Abu Ishaq Ibrahim ibn Hani' narrated to us, who said: "I heard Ahmad ibn Hanbal say: 'The people of Yemen write *al-nar* (fire) as *al-nir* and write *al-bi'r* (well)'," meaning similar to that. 'Abd al-Razzaq was only prompted (with the wording) "the fire is *jubar*." Al-Ramadi said: "'Abd al-Razzaq said: Ma'mar said: 'I do not think it is anything but a mistake'." Abu 'Umar said: "It has been narrated from the Prophet, peace be upon him, through the hadith of Ma'mar, from Hammam ibn Munabbih, from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet, peace be upon him, that he said: 'The fire is *jubar*'." Yahya ibn Ma'in said: "Its origin is 'the well,' but Ma'mar altered it." Abu 'Umar said: "Ibn Ma'in did not support this claim with any proof, and the reports of trustworthy narrators are not rejected in this way."

Waki' reported from 'Abd al-'Aziz ibn Husayn, from Yahya ibn Yahya al-Ghassani, who said: "A man burned his plot of cultivated land (*qarah*: a field), and a spark of fire came out and burned something belonging to his neighbour." He said: "Ibn Husayn wrote to 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz about it, and he wrote back to me: 'The Messenger of Allah, peace be upon him, said: "The beast is *jubar*," and I think that fire is *jubar*'." It has been narrated with "the grazing animal is *jubar*" in place of "the beast." This is what has been reported in the wording of this hadith, and each meaning has a sound wording mentioned in the explanation of the hadith and in the books of jurisprudence.

His exalted saying: ﴿And We subjected the mountains to glorify [Allah] along with Dawud﴾ [Al-Anbiya 21:79]. Wahb said: "Dawud used to pass by the mountains glorifying Allah, and the mountains would respond to him with glorification, and so did the birds." It was said: "Whenever Dawud felt a lull, he would command the mountains, and they would glorify Allah until he felt eager." This is why He said: "And We subjected," meaning: We made them such that they obey him when he commands them to glorify. It was also said: "Their traveling with him is their glorification," and *tasbih* (glorification) is derived from *sibahah* (swimming/gliding), the proof of which is His saying: ﴿O mountains, echo God's praises along with him﴾ [Saba 34:10] [[See vol. 14, p. 264 onward.]]. Qatadah said: "'Yusabbihna' means they pray along with him when he prays, and *tasbih* is prayer." Both interpretations are possible. This is an act of Allah the Exalted toward them, because mountains do not understand. Their glorification is a proof of Allah the Exalted's transcendence above the attributes of the incapable and the created.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 80:

There are three issues in this.

The first: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We taught him the making of coats of mail for you﴾, meaning the making of armour (durue) by softening the iron for him. Al-libus (garment, armour) among the Arabs means all weapons: whether a coat of mail (dir'), a jawshan (light armour), a sword or a spear. Al-Hudhali [He is Abu Kabir al-Hudhali, whose name is Amir ibn al-Hulays, from a qasida whose opening is:

"Zuhayr, is there any turning back from old age,
or no way to the first youth?"

Al-bu'ays: the brave one. Al-rawq: the horn. Dhu ni'aj: meaning a bull, and al-ni'aj: wild cows.] said, describing a spear:

"And with me is a libus for the brave one, as if it were
a horn on the forehead of a startled bull of wild cows."

Al-libus is everything that is worn. Ibn al-Sikkit recited [The verse is by Buhays al-Fazari]:

"Wear for every situation its garment,
whether its ease or its hardship."

Here Allah, exalted is He, means the coat of mail, which is in the sense of the worn (al-malbus), like al-rakub (the mount) and al-halub (the milked). Qatadah said: The first to make coats of mail was Dawud. They were originally plates, so he was the first to link them and interlock them.

The second: His saying, exalted is He: (to protect you) [(liyuhsinakum) with the ya' is the reading of Nafi'.] meaning to safeguard you.

(from your violence) meaning from your war. It is also said: from the sword, the arrow and the spear, that is, from the instruments of your violence, so the modifier is omitted. Ibn Abbas said: "min ba'sikum" means from your weapons. Al-Dahhak said: from the war of your enemies. The meaning is one.

Al-Hasan, Abu Ja'far, Ibn Amir, Hafs and Rawh read "li-tuhsinakum" with the ta', in response to the craft (al-sun'ah) [So it is in B, J, Z, T, K and Y, and this is correct]. It is also said: it refers to the libus and the protection (al-mana'ah), which are the coats of mail. Shaybah, Abu Bakr, al-Mufaddal, Ruways and Ibn Abi Ishaq read "li-nuhsinakum" with the nun, in accordance with His saying: "and We taught him." The rest read it with the ya', making the verb refer to the libus, or the meaning being: that Allah may protect you.

(So will you be grateful?) meaning: for the facilitation of the blessing of coats of mail for you. It is also said: "So will you be grateful?" by obeying My messenger.

The third: This verse is a foundation for taking up crafts and means, and this is the view of people of intellect and understanding, not the view of the ignorant fools who claim that this was legislated only for the weak. The means is the sunnah of Allah in His creation. Whoever criticises this has criticised the Book and the Sunnah, and has attributed to those we have mentioned weakness and lack of dignity. Allah, exalted is He, has informed us about His prophet Dawud, peace be upon him, that he used to make coats of mail, and he also used to make palm-leaf baskets, and he used to eat from the work of his hands. Adam was a farmer, Nuh a carpenter, Luqman a tailor, and Talut a tanner. It is also said: a water-carrier. Thus a person restrains himself through a craft from people, and by it he repels harm and violence from himself.

In a hadith: "Allah loves the believer who earns through a trade, the weak one who is chaste, and He hates the beggar who importunes." Further explanation of this will come in surah al-Furqan [See vol. 13, p. 12 onward and p. 72]. It has been mentioned in more than one verse, and there is sufficiency in it, and praise be to Allah.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 21, verses 81–82:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And to Solomon [We subjected] the wind, blowing forcefully﴾. That is, We subjected to Solomon the wind, blowing forcefully, meaning violently gusting. It is said of it: "the wind became forceful (`asafat al-rih`)," meaning it grew strong, so it is a *rih `asif* and *`asuf*. In the dialect of the Banu Asad it is said: "the wind became forceful (`a`safat al-rih)," so it is *mu`sif* and *mu`sifa*. Al-`asf is chaff, and the intense wind was named after it, because the wind scatters it with the force of its blowing.

Abd al-Rahman al-A`raj, al-Sulami and Abu Bakr read "*wa-li-Sulayman al-rih*" with the *ha'* (of *al-rih*) in the nominative case (*raf`*), by way of *qat'* (a separate, independent clause) from what precedes it (*al-qat'*: treating the word as a new sentence rather than governed by the preceding phrase). The meaning is: "And for Solomon is the subjugation of the wind." It is a *mubtada'* (grammatical subject) and a *khabar* (predicate).

(﴿blowing by His command to the land which We had blessed﴾) That is, the land of al-Sham (Syria). It is related that it would carry him and his companions wherever he wished, and then return him to al-Sham. Wahb said: When Sulayman ibn Dawud went out to his assembly, the birds would gather around him, and the jinn and humans would stand for him until he sat upon his throne. He was a man who fought often in battle and did not stay behind from raiding. When he wished to campaign, he ordered wood to be stretched out, and people, animals and weapons of war were raised upon it. Then he commanded the violent wind, and it bore all of that, then he commanded the gentle breeze, and it carried it for a month in its outward journey and a month in its return, and this is the meaning of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿blowing by His command, gently, wherever he directed﴾. [See vol. 15 p. 198 onward.] [p. 36]. *Al-rukha'* means the mild, soft breeze.

(﴿And We were Knowers of all things﴾) That is, We knew everything that We did, with knowledge of its management.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And of the devils were those who dove for him﴾. That is, We subjected to him those who dove, meaning beneath the water, that is, they extracted pearls and jewels for him from the sea. *Al-ghawS* is descending beneath the water; one who has dived into the water is *ghaa'is*, and the one who attacks something is also *ghaa'is*. *Al-ghawwas* is one who dives into the sea for pearls, and the verbal noun is *al-ghiyasah*.

(﴿and did other work besides that﴾) That is, other than diving. This was said by al-Farra'. It was also said that it refers to the sanctuaries (*mihrab*), the statues (*tamathil*) and other things he subjected them to.

(﴿And We were Guardians over them﴾) That is, over their deeds. Al-Farra' said: guarding them from spoiling their work, or from stirring up any of the children of Adam in the time of Sulayman. It was also said: "guarding" them from fleeing or resisting, or that We kept them from departing from his command. It has been said that the bathhouses (*hammam*), the depilatory (*nawra*), the mills (*tawahin*), glassware (*qawarir*) and soap (*sabun*) are among the inventions of the devils.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 21, verses 83–84 (part 1 of 2):**

Allah's words: ﴿And [mention] Ayyub (Job), when he called to his Lord﴾, meaning: and mention Ayyub when he called to his Lord.

(﴿Indeed, adversity has touched me﴾), meaning: harm reached me in my body, and in my wealth and family. Ibn 'Abbas said: Ayyub was so named because he turned back (aba) to Allah the Exalted in every state. It is related that Ayyub (peace be upon him) was a man of the Romans, possessed of great wealth, righteous, pious, and merciful to the poor. He would sponsor orphans and widows, honour the guest, and provide for the wayfarer, and he was thankful for the blessings of Allah the Exalted. He entered with his people upon a mighty tyrant, and they petitioned him about a matter. Ayyub began to speak gently to him because of a field of crops he owned, so Allah tested him by taking away his wealth and his family, and with harm to his body, until his flesh fell away and his body became infested with worms. The people of his town then expelled him outside the town, and his wife would serve him. Al-Hasan said: he remained in this state for nine years and six months. When Allah intended to relieve him, Allah the Exalted said to him: ﴿Strike with your foot; this is a cool washing-place and a drink﴾ [Sad 38:42], in which is your cure. And I have granted you your family, your wealth, your children, and their like along with them.

What the exegetes have said about the story of Ayyub, regarding the Satan's domination over him, and the refutation of them, will come in Surah Sad [[See vol. 15, p. 207.]], if Allah wills.

There are fifteen opinions concerning Ayyub's saying: "Adversity has touched me":

The first: He rose to pray but could not stand up, so he said, "Adversity has touched me," informing of his condition, not complaining of his trial. This was related by Anas, traced to the Prophet (marfu', i.e., attributed to the Prophet ﷺ).

The second: It is an acknowledgment of inability, and so it does not contradict patience.

The third: He (glorified is He) caused it to be spoken on his tongue, so that it would serve as a proof for the afflicted after him in openly stating what befalls them.

The fourth: He caused it to be spoken on his tongue as a demonstration of the weakness of the human being in bearing trials.

The fifth: Revelation was cut off from him for forty days, so he feared being forsaken by his Lord, and said: "Adversity has touched me." This is the view of Ja'far ibn Muhammad.

The sixth: His students, who used to write down from him, when his condition reached what it reached, erased what they had written from him, and said: "This has no worth with Allah." So he complained of the harm in the loss of revelation and of religion from the hands of people. This has an unsound chain of transmission. And Allah knows best; this was said by Ibn al-'Arabi.

The seventh: A worm fell from his flesh, so he picked it up and returned it to its place, but it bit him, so he cried out, "Adversity has touched me," and it was said: "Do you [now] show impatience?" Ibn al-'Arabi said: This is very far-fetched, and in addition it requires a sound report, and there is no way to find one.

The eighth: The worms were consuming his body, and he was patient until a worm reached his heart and another his tongue, and so he said: "Adversity has touched me," because he was occupied from the remembrance of Allah. Ibn al-'Arabi said: How fine this would be, if it had a chain of transmission and were not a sweeping claim.

The ninth: He was uncertain about the cause of the trial sent upon him: whether it was discipline, or punishment, or specification, or purification, or a store [of reward], or cleansing. So he said: "Adversity has touched me," meaning: the harm of uncertainty concerning the reason for the trial. Ibn al-'Arabi said: This is an exaggeration that is not needed.

The tenth: It was said to him: "Ask Allah for well-being," and he said: "I remained in blessing for seventy years, and I remain in trial for seven years, and then I shall ask Him," and so he said: "Adversity has touched me." Ibn al-'Arabi said: This is possible, but no report has been authenticated concerning the duration of his stay, nor in this story.

The eleventh: His harm was the statement of Iblis to his wife: "Prostrate to me," and he feared that faith would be lost from her, so that she would perish and he would be left without a provider.

The twelfth: When the affliction appeared upon him, his people said: "He has disgusted us with his presence and his filth, so let him leave us." So his wife took him out to the outskirts of the town. Whenever they went out they would see him and consider themselves unlucky and inauspicious because of seeing him, and they said: "Let him be removed far away, out of our sight." So he went out to a distance from the town, and his wife would attend to him and bring him his food. They said: "She approaches him and mixes with us, and his harm returns to us through her." So they wanted to cut her off from him, and he said: "Adversity has touched me."

The thirteenth: 'Abdullah ibn 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr said: Ayyub had two brothers. They came to him and stood at a distance, unable to draw near him because of the stench of his smell. One of them said: "If Allah had known any good in Ayyub, He would not have afflicted him with this affliction." Nothing harder for him to hear than this word came to him. At that point he said: "Adversity has touched me." Then he said: "O Allah, if You know that I never slept full while I knew of a hungry person, then bear witness to me." Then a caller called out from the sky: "Indeed My servant has spoken the truth," and they were both listening, so they fell down in prostration.

The fourteenth: The meaning of "Adversity has touched me" is the gloating of enemies. For this reason it was said to him: "What was harder for you in your trial?" He said: "The gloating of enemies." Ibn al-'Arabi said: This is possible, for Kalim (Moses) was asked by his brother for well-being from this, and he said: ﴿Indeed, the people deemed me weak and almost killed me, so do not let the enemies gloat over me﴾ [al-A'raf 7:150] [[See vol. 7, p. 286 onward.]].

The fifteenth: His wife had long hair. When she was prevented from working for anyone on his account, from which she could benefit him, she cut off her hair and bought with it food from one who would connect her with others, and brought it to him. He used to rely on her hair in his movements and transfers, so when she was deprived of it and he wanted to move, he could not, and he said: "Adversity has touched me." It is also said: When she bought the food with her hair, Iblis came to him in the form of a man and said to him: "Your wife has committed adultery, so she was seized and her hair was shaved." So Ayyub swore that he would flog her, and the ordeal upon the heart of the woman was greater than the ordeal upon the heart of Ayyub.

I say: And a sixteenth opinion, mentioned by Ibn al-Mubarak: Yunus ibn Yazid informed us, from 'Uqayl, from Ibn Shihab, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ once mentioned Ayyub the Prophet (ﷺ) and the affliction that befell him, and the hadith continues. In it, some of his brothers who had been patient with him and kept his company said: "O Prophet of Allah, your matter has impressed me, and I mentioned it to your brother and companion: that He has afflicted you with the loss of family and wealth, and in your body for eighteen years, until you have reached what you see. Will He not have mercy on you and remove it from you? You have committed a sin that I do not think anyone has ever committed!" Then Ayyub (peace be upon him) said: "I do not know what the two of them are saying, except that my Lord, mighty and majestic, knows that I used to pass by two men who were quarrelling, and each swore by Allah, or by a group who were quarrelling; so I would return to my family and expiate their oaths, intending that no one should sin, and that no one should mention Him except in truth." Then he called to his Lord: "Indeed, adversity has touched me, and You are the Most Merciful of the merciful." His supplication was only a presentation he offered to Allah, blessed and exalted, informing Him of what had reached him, while being patient with whatever Allah, blessed and exalted, would do concerning him. And he (the narrator) mentioned the hadith.

A seventeenth opinion, which I heard but have not verified: a worm fell from his body, so he sought it to return it to its place, but did not find it, and so he said: "Adversity has touched me," because of what he had lost of the reward for the pain of that worm, and he wished that the reward should remain in full until the time of well-being. This is good, except that it requires a chain of transmission.

The scholars said: His saying "Adversity has touched me" was not impatience, because Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, We found him patient﴾ [Sad 38:44] [[See vol. 15, p. 212 onward.]]. Rather, it was a supplication from him, and impatience is in complaining to creation, not to Allah the Exalted, and supplication does not contradict contentment. Al-Tha'labi said: I heard our teacher Abu al-Qasim ibn Habib say: I attended a gathering in the palace of the sultan that was crowded with jurists and men of letters. I asked about this verse, after they had agreed that Ayyub's saying was a complaint, and Allah the Exalted had said: ﴿Indeed, We found him patient﴾ [Sad 38:44]. I said: This is not a complaint; it was a supplication, and its proof is (﴿So We responded to him﴾), and a response follows supplication, not complaint. They found this good and approved it. Al-Junayd was asked about this verse, and he said: He showed him the need of asking, so that He might bestow upon him by the generosity of giving.

Allah's words: ﴿So We removed what harm was upon him, and We gave him his family and their like along with them﴾. Mujahid and 'Ikrimah said: It was said to Ayyub (ﷺ): "We have given you your family in Paradise; if you wish, We will leave them for you in Paradise, and if you wish, We will give them to you in this world." Mujahid said: So Allah, mighty and majestic, left them for him in Paradise and gave him their like in this world. Al-Nahhas said: The chain of transmission for this from them both is sound. I say: Al-Mahdawi also related it from Ibn 'Abbas. And al-Dahhak said: 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud said: Ayyub's family had all died except his wife, and Allah, mighty and majestic, brought them back to life in less than the blink of an eye, and gave him their like along with them. And from Ibn 'Abbas also: his sons had died, and they were brought back to life for him, and there were born to him their like along with them. Qatadah, Ka'b al-Ahbar, al-Kalbi, and others said the same. Ibn Mas'ud said: His children died; they were seven sons and seven daughters. When he was healed, they were raised for him, and his wife bore him seven sons and seven daughters. Al-Tha'labi said: This opinion is closer to the apparent meaning of the verse. I say: Because they died as a trial before their appointed times, as was explained earlier in Surah al-Baqarah [[See vol. 3, p. 230.]], in the story of ﴿those who left their homes in their thousands, fearing death﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:243], and in the story of the seventy who were struck by the thunderbolt and died, then were brought back to life [[See vol. 1, p. 404, and vol. 7, p. 295.]]. That was because they died before their appointed times, and so it is here, and Allah knows best. According to the view of Mujahid and 'Ikrimah, the meaning would be: ﴿and We gave him his family﴾ in the Hereafter, ﴿and their like along with them﴾ in this world.

It is related in a report that when he struck the earth with his foot in a single strike, Allah sent Jibril (peace be upon him) to him, and a spring of hot water gushed forth. Jibril took him by the hand and shook him once, and the worms fell away from him. He then plunged into the water once, and his flesh grew back, and he returned to his home. Allah restored his family to him along with their like, and a cloud formed in the measure of the foundations of his house, and it rained for three days and nights locusts of gold. Jibril said to him: "Are you satisfied?" He said: "And who can be satisfied with the bounty of Allah?" Then Allah revealed to him: "I have praised you for patience before you fell into the trial and after it. And had I not placed beneath every hair of yours a patience, you would not have been patient."

(﴿As a mercy from Us﴾), meaning: We did that to him as a mercy from Us. And it was said: We tested him so that his reward would be magnified on the Day [of Judgment].

(And a reminder for the worshippers) — that is, a reminder for the servants of God. For when they recall the trial of Ayyub (Job), his patience under it, and the affliction he suffered, while he was the best of the people of his time, they prepare themselves to endure the hardships of this world in the manner that Ayyub did. This therefore serves as an admonition to them to persist in worship and to bear harm.

Scholars differ concerning the length of time he remained in affliction. Ibn Abbas said: the period of the affliction was seven years, seven months, seven days and seven nights. Wahb said: thirty years. Al-Hasan said: seven years and six months.

I (al-Qurtubi) say: and more sound than these, and God knows best, is eighteen years. This was narrated by Ibn Shihab from the Prophet (ﷺ), and Ibn al-Mubarak mentioned it, and it has already been discussed.

One of them said: "If Allah had known any good in Ayyub, He would not have afflicted him with this affliction." Nothing harder for him to hear than this word came to him. At that point he said: "Adversity has touched me." Then he said: "O Allah, if You know that I never slept full while I knew of a hungry person, then bear witness to me." Then a caller called out from the sky: "Indeed My servant has spoken the truth," and they were both listening, so they fell down in prostration.

The fourteenth: The meaning of "Adversity has touched me" is the gloating of enemies. For this reason it was said to him: "What was harder for you in your trial?" He said: "The gloating of enemies." Ibn al-'Arabi said: This is possible, for Kalim (Moses) was asked by his brother for well-being from this, and he said: ﴿Indeed, the people deemed me weak and almost killed me, so do not let the enemies gloat over me﴾ [al-A'raf 7:150] [[See vol. 7, p. 286 onward.]].

The fifteenth: His wife had long hair. When she was prevented from working for anyone on his account, from which she could benefit him, she cut off her hair and bought with it food from one who would connect her with others, and brought it to him. He used to rely on her hair in his movements and transfers, so when she was deprived of it and he wanted to move, he could not, and he said: "Adversity has touched me." It is also said: When she bought the food with her hair, Iblis came to him in the form of a man and said to him: "Your wife has committed adultery, so she was seized and her hair was shaved." So Ayyub swore that he would flog her, and the ordeal upon the heart of the woman was greater than the ordeal upon the heart of Ayyub.

I say: And a sixteenth opinion, mentioned by Ibn al-Mubarak: Yunus ibn Yazid informed us, from 'Uqayl, from Ibn Shihab, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ once mentioned Ayyub the Prophet (ﷺ) and the affliction that befell him, and the hadith continues. In it, some of his brothers who had been patient with him and kept his company said: "O Prophet of Allah, your matter has impressed me, and I mentioned it to your brother and companion: that He has afflicted you with the loss of family and wealth, and in your body for eighteen years, until you have reached what you see. Will He not have mercy on you and remove it from you? You have committed a sin that I do not think anyone has ever committed!" Then Ayyub (peace be upon him) said: "I do not know what the two of them are saying, except that my Lord, mighty and majestic, knows that I used to pass by two men who were quarrelling, and each swore by Allah, or by a group who were quarrelling; so I would return to my family and expiate their oaths, intending that no one should sin, and that no one should mention Him except in truth." Then he called to his Lord: "Indeed, adversity has touched me, and You are the Most Merciful of the merciful." His supplication was only a presentation he offered to Allah, blessed and exalted, informing Him of what had reached him, while being patient with whatever Allah, blessed and exalted, would do concerning him. And he (the narrator) mentioned the hadith.

A seventeenth opinion, which I heard but have not verified: a worm fell from his body, so he sought it to return it to its place, but did not find it, and so he said: "Adversity has touched me," because of what he had lost of the reward for the pain of that worm, and he wished that the reward should remain in full until the time of well-being. This is good, except that it requires a chain of transmission.

The scholars said: His saying "Adversity has touched me" was not impatience, because Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, We found him patient﴾ [Sad 38:44] [[See vol. 15, p. 212 onward.]]. Rather, it was a supplication from him, and impatience is in complaining to creation, not to Allah the Exalted, and supplication does not contradict contentment. Al-Tha'labi said: I heard our teacher Abu al-Qasim ibn Habib say: I attended a gathering in the palace of the sultan that was crowded with jurists and men of letters. I asked about this verse, after they had agreed that Ayyub's saying was a complaint, and Allah the Exalted had said: ﴿Indeed, We found him patient﴾ [Sad 38:44]. I said: This is not a complaint; it was a supplication, and its proof is (﴿So We responded to him﴾), and a response follows supplication, not complaint. They found this good and approved it. Al-Junayd was asked about this verse, and he said: He showed him the need of asking, so that He might bestow upon him by the generosity of giving.

Allah's words: ﴿So We removed what harm was upon him, and We gave him his family and their like along with them﴾. Mujahid and 'Ikrimah said: It was said to Ayyub (ﷺ): "We have given you your family in Paradise; if you wish, We will leave them for you in Paradise, and if you wish, We will give them to you in this world." Mujahid said: So Allah, mighty and majestic, left them for him in Paradise and gave him their like in this world. Al-Nahhas said: The chain of transmission for this from them both is sound. I say: Al-Mahdawi also related it from Ibn 'Abbas. And al-Dahhak said: 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud said: Ayyub's family had all died except his wife, and Allah, mighty and majestic, brought them back to life in less than the blink of an eye, and gave him their like along with them. And from Ibn 'Abbas also: his sons had died, and they were brought back to life for him, and there were born to him their like along with them. Qatadah, Ka'b al-Ahbar, al-Kalbi, and others said the same. Ibn Mas'ud said: His children died; they were seven sons and seven daughters. When he was healed, they were raised for him, and his wife bore him seven sons and seven daughters. Al-Tha'labi said: This opinion is closer to the apparent meaning of the verse. I say: Because they died as a trial before their appointed times, as was explained earlier in Surah al-Baqarah [[See vol. 3, p. 230.]], in the story of ﴿those who left their homes in their thousands, fearing death﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:243], and in the story of the seventy who were struck by the thunderbolt and died, then were brought back to life [[See vol. 1, p. 404, and vol. 7, p. 295.]]. That was because they died before their appointed times, and so it is here, and Allah knows best. According to the view of Mujahid and 'Ikrimah, the meaning would be: ﴿and We gave him his family﴾ in the Hereafter, ﴿and their like along with them﴾ in this world.

It is related in a report that when he struck the earth with his foot in a single strike, Allah sent Jibril (peace be upon him) to him, and a spring of hot water gushed forth. Jibril took him by the hand and shook him once, and the worms fell away from him. He then plunged into the water once, and his flesh grew back, and he returned to his home. Allah restored his family to him along with their like, and a cloud formed in the measure of the foundations of his house, and it rained for three days and nights locusts of gold. Jibril said to him: "Are you satisfied?" He said: "And who can be satisfied with the bounty of Allah?" Then Allah revealed to him: "I have praised you for patience before you fell into the trial and after it. And had I not placed beneath every hair of yours a patience, you would not have been patient."

(﴿As a mercy from Us﴾), meaning: We did that to him as a mercy from Us. And it was said: We tested him so that his reward would be magnified on the Day [of Judgment].

(And a reminder for the worshippers) — that is, a reminder for the servants of God. For when they recall the trial of Ayyub (Job), his patience under it, and the affliction he suffered, while he was the best of the people of his time, they prepare themselves to endure the hardships of this world in the manner that Ayyub did. This therefore serves as an admonition to them to persist in worship and to bear harm.

Scholars differ concerning the length of time he remained in affliction. Ibn Abbas said: the period of the affliction was seven years, seven months, seven days and seven nights. Wahb said: thirty years. Al-Hasan said: seven years and six months.

I (al-Qurtubi) say: and more sound than these, and God knows best, is eighteen years. This was narrated by Ibn Shihab from the Prophet (ﷺ), and Ibn al-Mubarak mentioned it, and it has already been discussed.

**Al-Qurtubi's commentary (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Qur'an) on Surah 21, verses 85–86:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And Isma'il and Idris﴾. He is Akhnukh (Enoch), and this has already been discussed. ﴿And Dhu'l-Kifl﴾, meaning: and mention them.

Al-Tirmidhi al-Hakim, in *Nawadir al-Usul* (*The Rare Traditions of the Principles*), and others narrated from Ibn 'Umar, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "There was among the Children of Israel a man called Dhu'l-Kifl, who did not refrain from any sin he committed. He pursued a woman and gave her sixty dinars [[in the texts of J, W, K and Ṣ]] [on condition that he would have intercourse with her] [[from B]]. When he sat with her in the position of a man with his wife, she trembled and wept. He said, 'What makes you weep?' She said, 'Because of this deed. By Allah, I have never done it before.' He said, 'Did I force you?' She said, 'No, but need compelled me to it.' He said, 'Go, it is yours. By Allah, I will never disobey Allah again after this.' Then he died that same night, and they found written on the door of his house: 'Indeed Allah has forgiven Dhu'l-Kifl.'"

Al-Tirmidhi (Abu 'Isa) also narrated it, and its wording is from Ibn 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with them both), who said: "I heard the Prophet (ﷺ) narrate a hadith which, if I had heard it only once or twice, [until he counted seven times,] I would not have narrated it. But I heard it more than that. I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'Dhu'l-Kifl, from the Children of Israel, did not refrain from any sin he committed. A woman came to him and he gave her sixty dinars on condition that he would lie with her. When he sat with her in the position of a man with his wife, she trembled and wept. He said, "What makes you weep? Did I force you?" She said, "No, but it is a deed I have never done before, and only need compelled me to it." He said, "You do this, though you have never done it?" Then he said, "Go, it is yours," and he said, "By Allah, I will never disobey Allah after this." He died that night, and in the morning it was written on his door: "Indeed Allah has forgiven Dhu'l-Kifl."' " He said: this is a hasan (good) hadith.

It is also said that al-Yasa' (Elisha), when he grew old, said: "If only I could appoint a man over the people so that I might see how he acts." He said: "Who will guarantee me three things: fasting by day, standing in prayer by night, and not becoming angry while judging?" A man from the descendants of al-'Is said, "I will." He dismissed him. Then he said the same thing the next day, and the man said, "I will." So he appointed him, and he fulfilled it. Allah praised him, and he was named Dhu'l-Kifl because he took on (takaffala) a responsibility. This was said by Abu Musa, Mujahid and Qatadah.

'Umar [[in the originals: 'Amr ibn 'Abd Allah; the correction is from al-Tahdhib]] ibn 'Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Harith said: Abu Musa said, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Dhu'l-Kifl was not a prophet, but he was a righteous servant who took on the task of a righteous man at his death. He used to pray one hundred prayers to Allah every day, so Allah praised him well."

Ka'b said: There was among the Children of Israel a disbelieving king. A righteous man passed through his land and said, "By Allah, I will not leave this land until I present Islam to this king." He presented it to him, and the king said, "What is my reward?" He said, "Paradise," and he described it to him. The king said, "Who will guarantee me this?" He said, "I will." The king embraced Islam, gave up his kingdom and devoted himself to obeying his Lord until he died. He was buried, and in the morning they found his hand protruding from the grave, and on it was a green piece of cloth on which was written in white light: "Indeed Allah has forgiven me, admitted me to Paradise, and fulfilled the guarantee of so-and-so." The people hastened to that man, asking him to take their oaths and to guarantee for them what he had guaranteed for the king. He did so, and they all believed, and he was named Dhu'l-Kifl.

It is also said: he was a chaste man who took responsibility for the affairs of everyone who fell into trouble, accusation or a legal claim, and Allah would rescue that person through his hands.

It is also said: he was named Dhu'l-Kifl because Allah, exalted is He, guaranteed for him, in his striving and his deeds, double the reward of the other prophets who were in his time.

The majority hold that he was not a prophet. Al-Hasan said: he was a prophet before Ilyas (Elijah). It is also said: he was Zakariyya (Zechariah), by his guardianship of Maryam (Mary).

﴿Each of them was among the patient﴾, meaning: patient in obeying Allah's command, in performing His worship, and in avoiding His disobedience.

﴿And We admitted them into Our mercy﴾, i.e., into Paradise. ﴿Indeed they were among the righteous﴾.
