Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 87–88 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And Dhu'l-Nun﴾ means: and remember Dhu'l-Nun (the Man of the Fish). It is a title (laqab) of Yunus ibn Matta, because the fish (nun) swallowed him. Al-nun is the fish (al-hut). In the hadith of Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him, that he saw a handsome child and said: "Blacken his nunah (the mark on the chin) so that the evil eye does not afflict him." Tha'lab related from Ibn al-A'rabi: al-nunah is the small pit (nuqbah) that is found on the chin of a young child. The meaning of dassimu is sawwidu (blacken).

﴿When he went off in anger﴾ Al-Hasan, al-Sha'bi and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: angry for the sake of his Lord, Mighty and Majestic. This was chosen by al-Tabari and al-Qutabi, and al-Mahdawi approved it, and it is related from Ibn Mas'ud. Al-Nahhas said: Some who do not know the language have denied it, but it is a correct view. The meaning is: angry on account of his Lord, just as you say: "I became angry for you," i.e., on your account. The believer becomes angry for Allah, Mighty and Majestic, when He is disobeyed. Most of the lexicographers hold that the Prophet's ﷺ saying to Aisha, "Stipulate for them the wala' (patronage)," is of this kind. Al-Qutabi strongly supported this view. In a report describing Yunus: he was narrow of chest, and when he bore the burdens of prophethood he gave way under them like a young camel (rabi') under a heavy load, so he went on his way like a runaway slave who flees. This anger was minor, and he did not become angry at Allah, but became angry for Allah when He lifted the punishment from them. Ibn Mas'ud said: he fled from his Lord, i.e., from the command of his Lord, until He commanded him to return to them after the punishment had been lifted from them. He had threatened his people with the descent of punishment at a known time, and he left them at that time; the punishment overshadowed them, they humbled themselves, and it was lifted from them. Yunus did not know of their repentance, and therefore he went off in anger, though it was incumbent upon him not to depart except by a specified permission. Al-Hasan said: Allah commanded him to go to his people, and he asked to be given time to prepare, so Allah hastened him until he asked to take a sandal to put on, but he was not given time, and it was said to him: "The matter is more urgent than that." He had a narrowness in his character, so he went off angry at his Lord. This is one view. The saying of al-Nahhas is the best of what has been said in its interpretation: he went off angry on account of his Lord, i.e., he became angry at his people on account of their disbelief in their Lord.

It was also said: he was at odds with his people when their affair dragged on for him and their obstinacy grew, so he left, fleeing with himself, and did not endure their harm, though Allah had commanded him to remain with them and to call them. His sin was his leaving them without permission from Allah. Its meaning is related from Ibn Abbas and al-Dahhak, and that Yunus was young and had not yet borne the burdens of prophethood. For this reason it was said to the Prophet ﷺ: ﴿And do not be like the companion of the fish﴾ [al-Qalam: 48]. Also from al-Dahhak: he went off angry at his people, because when they did not accept from him, though he was a messenger from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, they disbelieved in this, so it was obligatory for him to be angry with them, and everyone must be angry with whoever disobeys Allah, Mighty and Majestic. A group, including al-Akhfash, said: he only went off angry at the king who was over his people. Ibn Abbas said: Sha'ya the prophet and the king of his time, whose name was Hizqiya, wanted to send Yunus to the king of Nineveh, who had raided the Children of Israel and taken many of them captive, so that he would speak to him and send the Children of Israel with him. In that era the prophets received revelation, while the command and governance belonged to a king whom they had chosen, who acted upon the revelation of that prophet. Allah had revealed to Sha'ya: "Tell King Hizqiya to choose a strong, trustworthy prophet from the Children of Israel and send him to the people of Nineveh, to command them to release the Children of Israel, for I shall cast into the hearts of their kings and tyrants the release of them." Yunus said to Sha'ya: "Has Allah commanded you to send me out?" He said: "No." He said: "Has He named me to you?" He said: "No." He said: "Then here are prophets who are trustworthy and strong." They pressed him, so he went off angry at the prophet, the king and his people. He came to the Sea of the Romans, and of his story there is what there is; he was tested in the belly of the fish for abandoning the command of Sha'ya. For this reason Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿So the fish swallowed him while he was blameworthy﴾ [al-Saffat: 142]. The one who is blameworthy is one who does what he deserves blame for. What he did was either a minor sin or the leaving of the better course. It was also said: he went out when he was not a prophet at that time, but a king of the kings of the Children of Israel commanded him to go to Nineveh to call its people by the command of Sha'ya, and he disdained that his going to them should be by the command of anyone other than Allah, so he went off angry at the king. When he was saved from the belly of the fish, Allah sent him to his people, and he called them, and they believed in him. Al-Qushayri said: The more evident view is that this going off in anger occurred after Allah had sent him and after the punishment had been lifted from the people after it had overshadowed them, for he disliked the lifting of the punishment from them.

I say: This is the best of what has been said concerning it, as its explanation will come in "al-Saffat," Allah willing. It was also said: it was among the character of his people to kill whoever they found lying to them, so he feared that he would be killed, and he became angry and went out fleeing on his face until he boarded a ship, which stopped and did not sail. Its people said: "Is there a runaway slave among you?" He said: "I am he." Of his story there is what there is, and he was tested in the belly of the fish as a purification from the minor sin, just as He said about the people of Uhud: ﴿Until, when you lost heart﴾ [Al 'Imran: 152] to His saying: ﴿and that Allah might purify those who believed﴾ [Al 'Imran: 141]. So the disobediences of the prophets are forgiven, but a purification may occur, and this includes a deterrent against returning to it. A fourth view: he was not angry at his Lord, nor at his people, nor at the king; rather, it is from their saying "ghadiba" (he became angry) meaning "anafa" (he was disdainful). The form fa'ala may come from one party. The meaning is that when he promised his people the punishment and left them, they repented and the punishment was removed from them; when he returned and knew that they had not perished, he disdained that and fled. And this line of poetry is recited:
"And I am disdainful (aghdab) that Tamim be ridiculed in Darim."
That is, I am disdainful (anaf). But this is open to scrutiny, for it is said to the proponent of this view: that anger (mughadabah) of that kind, even if it was disdain, must be mixed with anger, and that anger, however subtle, how could it be found in one who... and you say he was not angry at his Lord nor at his people? The saying of the Exalted: ﴿So he thought that We would not decree against him, and called out in the darknesses﴾. It was said: its meaning is that Iblis made him slip, and it came into his thought that Allah would not be able to punish him. This is a rejected view, to be disavowed, because it is disbelief. It is related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, reported by al-Mahdawi, and al-Tha'labi from al-Hasan. Al-Tha'labi mentioned that 'Ata', Sa'id ibn Jubayr and many scholars said its meaning is: "So he thought that We would not constrict him." Al-Hasan said: it is from the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Allah extends provision to whom He wills and constricts (yaqdiru)﴾ [al-Ra'd: 26], i.e., constricts. And His saying: ﴿and whose provision is constricted for him﴾ [al-Talaq: 7]. I say: This is closer to the view of Sa'id and al-Hasan. Qadara, qudira, qatara and qutira have the same meaning: i.e., was constricted. This is the view of Ibn Abbas as reported by al-Mawardi and al-Mahdawi. It was also said: it is from al-qadar, which is decree and judgment, i.e., "so he thought that We would not decree against him with punishment," said by Qatadah, Mujahid and al-Farra'. It is derived from qadar meaning judgment, not qudrah (power) and capacity. It is related from Abu'l-Abbas Ahmad ibn Yahya Tha'lab that he said concerning the saying of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: "So he thought that We would not have power over him," it is from taqdir (decree), not from qudrah; it is said from it: qadara Allah lakal-khayr yaqduruhu qadran, meaning Allah decreed good for you. Tha'lab recited:
"Those evenings of al-Liwa will not return to us ever, as long as the sidr tree is green,
Nor will that time which passed come back. Blessed are You; what You decree, happens, and to You is thanks."
That is, what You decree and judge by occurs. Scholars take both of these interpretations. Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz and al-Zuhri read: "fa-zanna an lan nuqaddira alayhi" with a damma on the nun and shaddah on the dal, from taqdir. Al-Mawardi related this reading from Ibn Abbas. Ubayd ibn Umayr, Qatadah and al-A'raj read: "an lan yuqaddara alayhi," with a damma on the ya' and shaddah, as a passive verb. Ya'qub, Abdullah ibn Abi Ishaq, al-Hasan and Ibn Abbas also read: "yuqdaru alayhi," with a damma on the ya' and fathah on the dal, lightened, as a passive verb. From al-Hasan also: "fa-zanna an lan yaqdira alayhi." The rest read "naqdira," with a fathah on the nun and kasrah on the dal, and all of these carry the meaning of taqdir. I say: These two interpretations have been adopted by scholars regarding the saying of the man who had done no good at all for his family, and when he died they burned him: "By Allah, if Allah constricts (qadara) upon me..." in the hadith. According to the first interpretation, its sense is: "By Allah, if Allah constricts upon me, and exaggerates in calling me to account and recompenses me for my sins, that will certainly happen," and then he commanded that he be burned out of excessive fear. According to the second interpretation: i.e., if it has been decreed in the decree and judgment of Allah that He punish every guilty person for his crime, Allah will certainly punish me for my crimes and sins with a punishment that He will not inflict upon anyone else in the worlds. His hadith was recorded by the imams in the Muwatta' and elsewhere. That man was a believer who affirmed the oneness of Allah. In some of its chains it comes: "He had done no good except tawhid (affirming God's oneness)." And when Allah, the Exalted, said: "Why did you do this?" he said: "Out of fear of You, O Lord." Fear is not found except in a believer who affirms the truth, as Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Only those of His servants who have knowledge fear Allah﴾ [Fatir: 28]. This is the view of Sulayman [in the original, "Sulayman ibn al-Mu'tamir", which is an error; the correction is from Tahdhib al-Tahdhib] Abu'l-Mu'tamir. Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 21, verses 87–88 (part 2 of 2):

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And he called out in the darknesses: "There is no god but You; glory be to You. Indeed, I have been of the wrongdoers."﴾ In this there are two issues.

The first: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿he called out in the darknesses﴾. The scholars differed concerning what is meant by the plural "darknesses." A group, including Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah, said: the darkness of the night, the darkness of the sea, and the darkness of the fish. Ibn Abi al-Dunya mentioned: Yusuf ibn Musa narrated to us, from 'Ubayd Allah ibn Musa, from Isra'il, from Abu Ishaq, from 'Amr ibn Maymun, who said: 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud narrated to us in the House of Money (bayt al-mal), saying: When the fish swallowed Yunus, peace be upon him, it descended with him to the floor of the earth, and Yunus heard the glorification of the pebbles, and he called out in the darknesses, three darknesses: the darkness of the belly of the fish, the darkness of the night, and the darkness of the sea, "that there is no god but You; glory be to You. Indeed, I have been of the wrongdoers." ﴿So We cast him onto the open shore while he was ailing﴾ [al-Saffat: 145] like the state of a featherless fledgling that has been plucked. [See vol. 15, p. 127.] A group, including Salim ibn Abi al-Ja'd, said: the darkness of the sea, and the darkness of a fish that swallowed the first fish. It is also valid to express by "darknesses" the belly of the first fish alone, as He said: "in the depths of the well" [Yusuf: 10] [See vol. 9, p. 132.], and in all its directions there is darkness, so using the plural is acceptable. Al-Mawardi mentioned that it may be expressed by "darknesses" as the darkness of sin, the darkness of distress, and the darkness of loneliness.

It is narrated that God, Exalted is He, revealed to the fish: "Do not harm a single hair of him, for I have made your belly his prison, and I did not make him your food." It is also narrated that Yunus, peace be upon him, prostrated within the belly of the fish when he heard the glorification of the fish in the depths of the sea. Ibn Abi al-Dunya mentioned: al-'Abbas ibn Yazid al-'Abdi narrated to us: Ishaq [the text reads thus in the originals, and perhaps it is (Abd Allah ibn Idris), for the al-'Abdi narrated from that 'Abd Allah, as in Tahdhib al-Tahdhib] ibn Idris narrated to us, from Ja'far ibn Sulayman, from 'Awf, from Sa'id ibn Abi al-Hasan, who said: When the fish swallowed Yunus, peace be upon him, he thought he had died, so he stretched out his legs, and then he found that he had not died, so he returned to his habit of praying, and in his supplication he said: "And I have taken for You a place of worship where no one has taken one before."

Abu al-Ma'ali said: The saying of the Prophet ﷺ, "Do not prefer me over Yunus ibn Matta," means: for I, while I am at the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary, am not nearer to God than he is, while he is at the bottom of the sea in the belly of the fish. This indicates that the Creator, glory be to Him, is not in a direction. This meaning has already been discussed in al-Baqarah [See vol. 2, p. 308 onward.] and al-A'raf [See vol. 7, p. 180.]. "There is no god but You; glory be to You. Indeed, I have been of the wrongdoers": he means regarding what he opposed, namely leaving off persisting with his people and bearing patiently with them. It was also said: regarding leaving without being given permission. This was not a punishment from God, because prophets may not be punished; rather it was a purification (tamhis). Those who do not deserve punishment may be disciplined, such as children; al-Mawardi mentioned this. It was also said: "of the wrongdoers" refers to his supplication against his people for punishment. Nuh had also supplicated against his people, yet he was not seized. Al-Wasiti said regarding its meaning: he declared his Lord free of injustice and attributed the wrong to himself, in acknowledgment and admission of deserving it. A similar statement is the saying of Adam and Hawwa': ﴿Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves﴾ [al-A'raf: 23] [See vol. 7, p. 223 onward and p. 180.], since they were the cause of placing themselves in a place other than that in which they had been sent down.

The second: Abu Dawud narrated from Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "The supplication of Dhu al-Nun in the belly of the fish: 'There is no god but You; glory be to You. Indeed, I have been of the wrongdoers.' No Muslim man has ever called upon God with it for anything except that it was answered for him." It has been said that it is the Greatest Name of God. Sa'd also narrated it from the Prophet ﷺ. In the report: in this verse God stipulated for whoever calls upon Him that He will answer him as He answered him, and rescue him as He rescued him, and that is His saying: "Thus do We save the believers." Here there is no explicit supplication; rather it is the implication of his saying: "Indeed, I have been of the wrongdoers," for he acknowledged the wrong, and so it was an allusion.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Thus do We save the believers﴾, that is, We deliver them from their distress because of their deeds that preceded. This is His saying: ﴿Had he not been of those who glorify [God], he would have remained in its belly until the Day they are resurrected﴾ [al-Saffat: 143–144] [See vol. 15, p. 121.]. This is a preservation from God, Mighty and Majestic, for His servant Yunus: He safeguarded the right of his worship and preserved the obligation of the obedience that had preceded from him. Al-Ustadh Abu Ishaq said: Dhu al-Nun accompanied the fish for a few days, yet until the Day of Resurrection he is called Dhu al-Nun. So what do you think of a servant whom He worshipped for seventy years—would this be lost in His sight? It is not to be supposed of Him. "From the distress" means from the belly of the fish.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Thus do We save the believers﴾. The reading of the common people is with two nuns, from anja, yunji. Ibn 'Amir read "nujjiya" with a single nun, a doubled jim, and a sukun on the ya, as a past-tense verb with an implied verbal noun, meaning: "And thus the deliverance delivered the believers," just as you say: "Dariba Zaydan," meaning "the striking struck Zayd." And he recited:

"Had Qufayra (like Juhayna), the mother of al-Farazdaq, given birth to a whelp of a dog, the dogs would have been cursed by that whelp."

He meant: "cursing would have cursed by that whelp." Its ya was made quiescent according to the dialect of those who say baqiya and radiya without moving the ya. Al-Hasan read "wadharu ma baqiya mina al-riba" [al-Baqarah: 278] (see vol. 3, p. 362), finding it burdensome to move a ya preceded by a kasra. And he recited:

"The grey hair dyed my locks with reddening, and drove me toward the graves, the camel."
"Would that I knew, when the Resurrection rises and they are called to account, where the final destination is."

He made the ya quiescent in "du'iya" because it is burdensome to move it when a kasra precedes it; the agent of "hada" is "al-mashib" (the grey hair), meaning the grey hair drove the camel. "Would that I knew where the destination is." This is the interpretation of al-Farra', Abu 'Ubayd, and Tha'lab in approving this reading. Abu Hatim and al-Zajjaj rejected it and said: it is a grammatical error, because it puts in the accusative the object of what has not named its agent, whereas one should say: "nujjiya al-mu'minun," just as one says "kurrima al-salihun." It is not permissible to say "duriba Zaydan" meaning "dariba al-darbu Zaydan," because there is no benefit in it, since "darb" already indicates the striking. Such a verse may not be used as evidence against the Book of God. Abu 'Ubayd had another view, which al-Qutabi also held, namely that the nun was assimilated into the jim. Al-Nahhas said: this view is not permissible according to any of the grammarians, because the point of articulation of the nun is far from that of the jim, so it cannot be assimilated into it, and it is not permissible in "man ja'a bil-hasanati" [al-Qasas: 84; see vol. 7, p. 150] to read "majja'a bil-hasanati." Al-Nahhas said: I have not heard anything better on this than what I heard from 'Ali ibn Sulayman. He said: The original is "nunji," and one of the two nuns was deleted because they came together, just as one of two taa's is deleted when they come together, as in His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿and do not be divided﴾ [Al 'Imran: 103] (see vol. 4, p. 158), whose original is "tatafarraqu."

Muhammad ibn al-Sumayqa' and Abu al-'Aliya read: "wa-kadhalika najja al-mu'minin," meaning "God delivered the believers." It is a good reading.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 87–88 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And Dhu'l-Nun﴾ means: and remember Dhu'l-Nun (the Man of the Fish). It is a title (laqab) of Yunus ibn Matta, because the fish (nun) swallowed him. Al-nun is the fish (al-hut). In the hadith of Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him, that he saw a handsome child and said: "Blacken his nunah (the mark on the chin) so that the evil eye does not afflict him." Tha'lab related from Ibn al-A'rabi: al-nunah is the small pit (nuqbah) that is found on the chin of a young child. The meaning of dassimu is sawwidu (blacken).

﴿When he went off in anger﴾ Al-Hasan, al-Sha'bi and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: angry for the sake of his Lord, Mighty and Majestic. This was chosen by al-Tabari and al-Qutabi, and al-Mahdawi approved it, and it is related from Ibn Mas'ud. Al-Nahhas said: Some who do not know the language have denied it, but it is a correct view. The meaning is: angry on account of his Lord, just as you say: "I became angry for you," i.e., on your account. The believer becomes angry for Allah, Mighty and Majestic, when He is disobeyed. Most of the lexicographers hold that the Prophet's ﷺ saying to Aisha, "Stipulate for them the wala' (patronage)," is of this kind. Al-Qutabi strongly supported this view. In a report describing Yunus: he was narrow of chest, and when he bore the burdens of prophethood he gave way under them like a young camel (rabi') under a heavy load, so he went on his way like a runaway slave who flees. This anger was minor, and he did not become angry at Allah, but became angry for Allah when He lifted the punishment from them. Ibn Mas'ud said: he fled from his Lord, i.e., from the command of his Lord, until He commanded him to return to them after the punishment had been lifted from them. He had threatened his people with the descent of punishment at a known time, and he left them at that time; the punishment overshadowed them, they humbled themselves, and it was lifted from them. Yunus did not know of their repentance, and therefore he went off in anger, though it was incumbent upon him not to depart except by a specified permission. Al-Hasan said: Allah commanded him to go to his people, and he asked to be given time to prepare, so Allah hastened him until he asked to take a sandal to put on, but he was not given time, and it was said to him: "The matter is more urgent than that." He had a narrowness in his character, so he went off angry at his Lord. This is one view. The saying of al-Nahhas is the best of what has been said in its interpretation: he went off angry on account of his Lord, i.e., he became angry at his people on account of their disbelief in their Lord.

It was also said: he was at odds with his people when their affair dragged on for him and their obstinacy grew, so he left, fleeing with himself, and did not endure their harm, though Allah had commanded him to remain with them and to call them. His sin was his leaving them without permission from Allah. Its meaning is related from Ibn Abbas and al-Dahhak, and that Yunus was young and had not yet borne the burdens of prophethood. For this reason it was said to the Prophet ﷺ: ﴿And do not be like the companion of the fish﴾ [al-Qalam: 48]. Also from al-Dahhak: he went off angry at his people, because when they did not accept from him, though he was a messenger from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, they disbelieved in this, so it was obligatory for him to be angry with them, and everyone must be angry with whoever disobeys Allah, Mighty and Majestic. A group, including al-Akhfash, said: he only went off angry at the king who was over his people. Ibn Abbas said: Sha'ya the prophet and the king of his time, whose name was Hizqiya, wanted to send Yunus to the king of Nineveh, who had raided the Children of Israel and taken many of them captive, so that he would speak to him and send the Children of Israel with him. In that era the prophets received revelation, while the command and governance belonged to a king whom they had chosen, who acted upon the revelation of that prophet. Allah had revealed to Sha'ya: "Tell King Hizqiya to choose a strong, trustworthy prophet from the Children of Israel and send him to the people of Nineveh, to command them to release the Children of Israel, for I shall cast into the hearts of their kings and tyrants the release of them." Yunus said to Sha'ya: "Has Allah commanded you to send me out?" He said: "No." He said: "Has He named me to you?" He said: "No." He said: "Then here are prophets who are trustworthy and strong." They pressed him, so he went off angry at the prophet, the king and his people. He came to the Sea of the Romans, and of his story there is what there is; he was tested in the belly of the fish for abandoning the command of Sha'ya. For this reason Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿So the fish swallowed him while he was blameworthy﴾ [al-Saffat: 142]. The one who is blameworthy is one who does what he deserves blame for. What he did was either a minor sin or the leaving of the better course. It was also said: he went out when he was not a prophet at that time, but a king of the kings of the Children of Israel commanded him to go to Nineveh to call its people by the command of Sha'ya, and he disdained that his going to them should be by the command of anyone other than Allah, so he went off angry at the king. When he was saved from the belly of the fish, Allah sent him to his people, and he called them, and they believed in him. Al-Qushayri said: The more evident view is that this going off in anger occurred after Allah had sent him and after the punishment had been lifted from the people after it had overshadowed them, for he disliked the lifting of the punishment from them.

I say: This is the best of what has been said concerning it, as its explanation will come in "al-Saffat," Allah willing. It was also said: it was among the character of his people to kill whoever they found lying to them, so he feared that he would be killed, and he became angry and went out fleeing on his face until he boarded a ship, which stopped and did not sail. Its people said: "Is there a runaway slave among you?" He said: "I am he." Of his story there is what there is, and he was tested in the belly of the fish as a purification from the minor sin, just as He said about the people of Uhud: ﴿Until, when you lost heart﴾ [Al 'Imran: 152] to His saying: ﴿and that Allah might purify those who believed﴾ [Al 'Imran: 141]. So the disobediences of the prophets are forgiven, but a purification may occur, and this includes a deterrent against returning to it. A fourth view: he was not angry at his Lord, nor at his people, nor at the king; rather, it is from their saying "ghadiba" (he became angry) meaning "anafa" (he was disdainful). The form fa'ala may come from one party. The meaning is that when he promised his people the punishment and left them, they repented and the punishment was removed from them; when he returned and knew that they had not perished, he disdained that and fled. And this line of poetry is recited:
"And I am disdainful (aghdab) that Tamim be ridiculed in Darim."
That is, I am disdainful (anaf). But this is open to scrutiny, for it is said to the proponent of this view: that anger (mughadabah) of that kind, even if it was disdain, must be mixed with anger, and that anger, however subtle, how could it be found in one who... and you say he was not angry at his Lord nor at his people? The saying of the Exalted: ﴿So he thought that We would not decree against him, and called out in the darknesses﴾. It was said: its meaning is that Iblis made him slip, and it came into his thought that Allah would not be able to punish him. This is a rejected view, to be disavowed, because it is disbelief. It is related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, reported by al-Mahdawi, and al-Tha'labi from al-Hasan. Al-Tha'labi mentioned that 'Ata', Sa'id ibn Jubayr and many scholars said its meaning is: "So he thought that We would not constrict him." Al-Hasan said: it is from the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Allah extends provision to whom He wills and constricts (yaqdiru)﴾ [al-Ra'd: 26], i.e., constricts. And His saying: ﴿and whose provision is constricted for him﴾ [al-Talaq: 7]. I say: This is closer to the view of Sa'id and al-Hasan. Qadara, qudira, qatara and qutira have the same meaning: i.e., was constricted. This is the view of Ibn Abbas as reported by al-Mawardi and al-Mahdawi. It was also said: it is from al-qadar, which is decree and judgment, i.e., "so he thought that We would not decree against him with punishment," said by Qatadah, Mujahid and al-Farra'. It is derived from qadar meaning judgment, not qudrah (power) and capacity. It is related from Abu'l-Abbas Ahmad ibn Yahya Tha'lab that he said concerning the saying of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: "So he thought that We would not have power over him," it is from taqdir (decree), not from qudrah; it is said from it: qadara Allah lakal-khayr yaqduruhu qadran, meaning Allah decreed good for you. Tha'lab recited:
"Those evenings of al-Liwa will not return to us ever, as long as the sidr tree is green,
Nor will that time which passed come back. Blessed are You; what You decree, happens, and to You is thanks."
That is, what You decree and judge by occurs. Scholars take both of these interpretations. Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz and al-Zuhri read: "fa-zanna an lan nuqaddira alayhi" with a damma on the nun and shaddah on the dal, from taqdir. Al-Mawardi related this reading from Ibn Abbas. Ubayd ibn Umayr, Qatadah and al-A'raj read: "an lan yuqaddara alayhi," with a damma on the ya' and shaddah, as a passive verb. Ya'qub, Abdullah ibn Abi Ishaq, al-Hasan and Ibn Abbas also read: "yuqdaru alayhi," with a damma on the ya' and fathah on the dal, lightened, as a passive verb. From al-Hasan also: "fa-zanna an lan yaqdira alayhi." The rest read "naqdira," with a fathah on the nun and kasrah on the dal, and all of these carry the meaning of taqdir. I say: These two interpretations have been adopted by scholars regarding the saying of the man who had done no good at all for his family, and when he died they burned him: "By Allah, if Allah constricts (qadara) upon me..." in the hadith. According to the first interpretation, its sense is: "By Allah, if Allah constricts upon me, and exaggerates in calling me to account and recompenses me for my sins, that will certainly happen," and then he commanded that he be burned out of excessive fear. According to the second interpretation: i.e., if it has been decreed in the decree and judgment of Allah that He punish every guilty person for his crime, Allah will certainly punish me for my crimes and sins with a punishment that He will not inflict upon anyone else in the worlds. His hadith was recorded by the imams in the Muwatta' and elsewhere. That man was a believer who affirmed the oneness of Allah. In some of its chains it comes: "He had done no good except tawhid (affirming God's oneness)." And when Allah, the Exalted, said: "Why did you do this?" he said: "Out of fear of You, O Lord." Fear is not found except in a believer who affirms the truth, as Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Only those of His servants who have knowledge fear Allah﴾ [Fatir: 28]. It has also been said: the meaning of "fa-zanna an lan nuqdira alayhi" is the interrogative, and its sense is "afa-zanna" (so did he think?), the alif of interrogation being dropped for brevity. This is the view of Sulayman [in the original, "Sulayman ibn al-Mu'tamir", which is an error; the correction is from Tahdhib al-Tahdhib] Abu'l-Mu'tamir. Al-Qadi Mundhir ibn Sa'id related that some read: "afazanna" with an alif.

Ibn 'Amir read "nujjiya" with a single nun, a doubled jim, and a sukun on the ya, as a past-tense verb with an implied verbal noun, meaning: "And thus the deliverance delivered the believers," just as you say: "Dariba Zaydan," meaning "the striking struck Zayd." And he recited:

"Had Qufayra (like Juhayna), the mother of al-Farazdaq, given birth to a whelp of a dog, the dogs would have been cursed by that whelp."

He meant: "cursing would have cursed by that whelp." Its ya was made quiescent according to the dialect of those who say baqiya and radiya without moving the ya. Al-Hasan read "wadharu ma baqiya mina al-riba" [al-Baqarah: 278] (see vol. 3, p. 362), finding it burdensome to move a ya preceded by a kasra. And he recited:

"The grey hair dyed my locks with reddening, and drove me toward the graves, the camel."
"Would that I knew, when the Resurrection rises and they are called to account, where the final destination is."

He made the ya quiescent in "du'iya" because it is burdensome to move it when a kasra precedes it; the agent of "hada" is "al-mashib" (the grey hair), meaning the grey hair drove the camel. "Would that I knew where the destination is." This is the interpretation of al-Farra', Abu 'Ubayd, and Tha'lab in approving this reading. Abu Hatim and al-Zajjaj rejected it and said: it is a grammatical error, because it puts in the accusative the object of what has not named its agent, whereas one should say: "nujjiya al-mu'minun," just as one says "kurrima al-salihun." It is not permissible to say "duriba Zaydan" meaning "dariba al-darbu Zaydan," because there is no benefit in it, since "darb" already indicates the striking. Such a verse may not be used as evidence against the Book of God. Abu 'Ubayd had another view, which al-Qutabi also held, namely that the nun was assimilated into the jim. Al-Nahhas said: this view is not permissible according to any of the grammarians, because the point of articulation of the nun is far from that of the jim, so it cannot be assimilated into it, and it is not permissible in "man ja'a bil-hasanati" [al-Qasas: 84; see vol. 7, p. 150] to read "majja'a bil-hasanati." Al-Nahhas said: I have not heard anything better on this than what I heard from 'Ali ibn Sulayman. He said: The original is "nunji," and one of the two nuns was deleted because they came together, just as one of two taa's is deleted when they come together, as in His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿and do not be divided﴾ [Al 'Imran: 103] (see vol. 4, p. 158), whose original is "tatafarraqu."

Muhammad ibn al-Sumayqa' and Abu al-'Aliya read: "wa-kadhalika najja al-mu'minin," meaning "God delivered the believers." It is a good reading.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (*al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran*) on Surah 21, verses 89–90:**

The Most High said: ﴿And Zakariyya, when he called upon his Lord﴾. That is, "and mention Zakariyya." His story has already been mentioned in *Al 'Imran* [[See vol. 4, p. 74 onward.]].

(﴿My Lord, do not leave me alone (without an heir)﴾): that is, alone, with no child of mine. This has already been discussed.

(﴿And You are the best of inheritors﴾): that is, the best of those who remain after everyone who dies. He said "and You are the best of inheritors" because of His words earlier: ﴿who will inherit me﴾ [Maryam: 6]. The meaning is: I know that You do not neglect Your religion, but do not cut off this virtue, which is the upholding of the affairs of the religion, from my descendants. This was explained earlier in *Maryam* [[See p. 81 of this volume.]].

The Most High said: (﴿So We answered him﴾), that is, We answered his supplication. (﴿And We gave him Yahya﴾), whose mention has already been given in full. (﴿And We made his wife fit for him﴾). Qatadah, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and most of the exegetes said: she had been barren, and she was made fertile. Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ata' said: she had a bad character and a long tongue, so Allah the Most High corrected her and made her good-natured. I say: it is possible that she combined both meanings, so that she became good-natured and fertile. (﴿Indeed they﴾), meaning the prophets named in this surah, (﴿used to hasten to good deeds﴾). It has also been said that the pronoun refers to Zakariyya, his wife and Yahya.

The Most High said: ﴿And they used to call on Us with hope and fear﴾. In this there are two issues.

The first: the Most High's words ﴿and they used to call on Us with hope and fear﴾ mean that they turned to Us and called upon Us both in times of ease and in times of hardship. It has also been said that the meaning is that they called upon Us at the time of their worship, while in a state of desire and hope and of awe and fear, because desire and awe accompany each other. It has also been said that *raghab* is raising the palms of the hands with their insides toward the sky, and *rahab* is raising their backs; this was said by Khusayf. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the summary of this is that the usual manner of every human supplicant is to make use of his hands. *Raghab*, as seeking, is when it is fitting to turn the inside of the palm toward the one from whom one seeks, since that is the place of giving or of receiving. *Rahab*, as the averting of harm, is when it is fitting to cast that aside, and the gesture of removing and warding off is by shaking the hand or the like.

The second: al-Tirmidhi narrated from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) that he said: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) raised his hands in supplication, he would not lower them until he wiped his face with them." The disagreement about raising the hands has already been discussed in *al-A'raf* [[See vol. 7, p. 224 onward.]], and we mentioned this hadith and others there. According to the view that the hands are raised, people differed about the manner of it and its direction. Some preferred to spread both palms, raising them opposite the chest with their insides facing the face; this was narrated from Ibn 'Umar and Ibn 'Abbas. 'Ali used to supplicate with the insides of his palms, and it was narrated from Anas likewise, and this is the apparent meaning of the hadith of al-Tirmidhi. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "When you ask Allah, ask Him with the insides of your palms, and do not ask Him with their backs, and wipe your faces with them." It was narrated from Ibn 'Umar and Ibn al-Zubayr that they raised them up to the face, and they relied on the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stood at 'Arafah and began to supplicate, and he made the backs of his palms face his face, and he raised them above his nipples and below his shoulders. It has also been said: until he brought them level with his face, with their backs facing his face.

Abu Ja'far al-Tabari said: The correct position is to say that all these reports narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) agree and do not differ in meaning, and it is possible that they were from the Prophet (ﷺ) because of the differing states of supplication, as Ibn 'Abbas said: "If one of you points with a single finger, that is sincerity (*ikhlas*); if he raises his hands opposite his chest, that is supplication (*du'a'*); and if he raises them until they pass above his head with their backs facing his face, that is supplication with humble entreaty (*ibtihal*)." Al-Tabari said: Qatadah narrated from Anas, who said: "I saw the Prophet (ﷺ) supplicating with the backs of his palms and their insides."

*Raghaban wa rahaban* (رَغَباً وَرَهَباً) are in the accusative, either as a verbal noun (*masdar*), meaning they desire with desire and fear with fear; or as an object of purpose, meaning for desire and for fear; or as a circumstantial state (*hal*).

Talhah ibn Musarrif recited *wa yad'unana* (وَيَدْعُونَا) with a single *nun*. Al-A'mash recited *raghaban wa rahaban* with a *damma* on the *ra'* and a sukun on the *ghayn* and the *ha'*, like *al-saqam* and *al-bakhl*, and *al-'adam* and *al-darb*; both are dialectal forms. Ibn Wassab and al-A'mash also recited *raghaban wa rahaban* with a *fatha* on the *ra'* and lightening of the *ghayn* and the *ha'*; these are two forms, like *nahr* and *nahar*, and *sakhr* and *sakhar*. This recitation has also been narrated from Abu 'Amr.

(﴿And they used to be humble before Us﴾): that is, humble and submissive.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 91:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And she who guarded her chastity﴾, meaning: and mention Mary, who guarded her chastity. He mentioned her, though she is not among the prophets, so that the mention of Jesus, peace be upon him, would be complete. For this reason He said: ﴿And We made her and her son a sign for all the worlds﴾, and He did not say "two signs," because the meaning of the statement is: We made their state, their affair and their story a sign for all the worlds. Al-Zajjaj said: the sign in them is one, because she bore him without a male. According to the school of Sibawayh, the construction is: "We made her a sign for the worlds and We made her son a sign for the worlds," then it was elided. According to the school of al-Farra', it is: "We made her a sign for the worlds and her son," like His saying, may His praise be exalted: ﴿And God and His Messenger have more right that they should please Him﴾ (see vol. 8, p. 193 ff.).

It has been said that among her signs is that she was the first woman whose vow was accepted in the place of worship (mutaʿabbad). Among them is that God, mighty and majestic, nourished her with a provision from Himself that He did not send through the hand of any of His servants. It has also been said that she never took a breast to suckle.

"Ahsanat" means she was chaste and abstained from immorality. It has been said that the intended meaning of "farj" (the opening) is the opening of the shirt, i.e., no suspicion clung to her garment, meaning her garments were pure. The openings of a shirt are four: the two sleeves, the upper and the lower. Al-Suhayli said: let your thought not go to anything other than this, for it is a subtle allusion, since the Qur'an is more exalted in meaning, more precise in wording, more delicate in indication and more beautiful in expression than to intend what the ignorant imagination goes to, especially since the breathing was from the Holy Spirit by the command of the Holy One. So attribute the holiness to the Holy One, and free the sanctified, purified one from false suspicion and conjecture.

﴿So We breathed into her of Our spirit﴾, meaning: We commanded Gabriel, and he breathed into her shift, and by that breathing We caused the Messiah to come into being in her womb. This has already been discussed in "al-Nisa'" (see vol. 6, p. 22 ff.) and "Maryam," so there is no point in repeating it.

﴿A sign﴾, meaning: a token and a wonder for creation, and a mark of the prophethood of Jesus, and an indication of the reach of Our power over whatever We will.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 92:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, this community of yours is one community﴾. When He mentioned the prophets, He said: these are all united upon tawhid (monotheism). So the word "ummah" (community) here means the religion, which is Islam; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and others. As for the polytheists, they have opposed all of them.

(﴿And I am your Lord﴾) meaning: your God, alone.

(﴿So worship Me﴾) meaning: single Me out for worship. 'Isa ibn 'Umar and Ibn Abi Ishaq recited: "inna hadhihi ummatukum ummatun wahidah" (with ummatun in the nominative), and Husayn related it from Abu 'Amr. The rest recited "ummatan wahidatan" (with the accusative), as a circumstantial/emphatic accusative (nasb 'ala al-qat') due to the indefinite noun coming after the completion of the sentence, as said by al-Farra'. Al-Zajjaj said: "ummatan" is in the accusative as a state (hal), meaning: while it is united upon the truth; that is, "this is your community as long as it is one community and you are united upon tawhid. But if you split and oppose one another, then whoever opposes the truth is not among the people of the true religion." It is like when you say: "So-and-so is my friend, chaste," meaning: as long as he is chaste; if he abandons chastity, he is no longer my friend.

As for the nominative, it is permissible that it be in apposition (badal) to "ummatukum," or by supposing an omitted subject, meaning: "Indeed, this is your community; this is one community." Or it may be a second predicate (khabar ba'd khabar). And if "ummatakum" were put in the accusative as an apposition to "hadhihi," it would be permissible, and "ummatan wahidatan" would then be the predicate of "inna."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 93–94:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And they cut their affair into pieces among themselves﴾, meaning they became divided in religion, said al-Kalbi. Al-Akhfash said: they differed concerning it. The intended people are the polytheists, whom He censures for opposing the truth and for taking gods besides Allah. Al-Azhari said: that is, they scattered in their affair, so "amrahum" is in the accusative by the omission of "fi" (in). Thus the verb "mutaqatti'" (cut up) is intransitive according to this view, and transitive according to the first view. The intended meaning is all of creation, that is, they made their affair in their religions into pieces and divided it among themselves: so there is the monotheist, the Jew, the Christian, and the worshipper of a king or an idol.

(﴿Every one of them shall be returned to Us﴾) meaning, to Our judgment, so that We may recompense them.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So whoever does righteous deeds while he is a believer﴾. The "min" (some of) here is partitive, not for genus, since no mukallaf (responsible person) is able to perform all acts of obedience, both obligatory and voluntary. So the meaning is: whoever does some of the acts of obedience, obligatory or voluntary, while he is a monotheist and Muslim. Ibn 'Abbas said: "believing in Muhammad (ﷺ)."

(﴿so there will be no denial of his effort﴾) meaning, there is no repudiation of his deed, that is, its reward will not be lost nor concealed. Kufr (disbelief) is its opposite, faith (iman). Kufr also means ingratitude for a blessing, which is the opposite of shukr (gratitude). One says "kafarahu kufuran wa kufranan." In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud it is "fa-la kufra li-sa'yihi."

(﴿And indeed, We are recording it for him﴾) preserving his deed for him. Its parallel is His saying: ﴿Indeed, I will not waste the work of any worker among you, whether male or female﴾ [Al 'Imran: 195], meaning all of that is preserved so that He may recompense for it.

**Al-Qurtubi's commentary (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 21, verses 95–97:**

His saying, the Exalted: (﴿And it is forbidden for a town which We have destroyed that they should not return﴾). The reading of Zayd ibn Thabit and the people of Madinah is "وَحَرامٌ" (*wa-ḥarām*), and this is the choice of Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim. The people of Kufa read "وَحِرْمٌ" (*wa-ḥirm*), and this is reported from 'Ali, Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them all. Both are dialectal variants, like *ḥill* and *ḥalāl* (both meaning "lawful"). It is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas and Sa'id ibn Jubayr as "وَحَرِمَ" (*wa-ḥarima*), with a fatḥah on the ḥā' and the mīm and a kasrah on the rā'. Also from Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrimah and Abu al-'Aliyah: "وَحَرُمَ" (*wa-ḥaruma*), with a ḍammah on the rā' and a fatḥah on the ḥā' and the mīm. Also from Ibn 'Abbas: "وَحَرَمَ" (*wa-ḥarama*), and from him also "وَحَرَّمَ" (*wa-ḥarrama*) and "وَحُرِّمَ" (*wa-ḥurrima*). Also from 'Ikrimah: "وحرم". From Qatadah and Matar al-Warraq: "وَحَرْمٌ" (*wa-ḥarm*). These make nine readings. Al-Sulami read "عَلَى قَرْيَةٍ أَهْلَكْتُهَا" (*'alā qaryatin ahlaktuhā*, in the first person).

Scholars differ concerning the "لَا" (*lā*, "not") in His saying "لَا يَرْجِعُونَ" (*lā yarji'ūn*, "they will not return"). It was said that it is *ṣila* (a redundant particle), reported from Ibn 'Abbas and chosen by Abu 'Ubayd. The meaning would be: "And it is forbidden for a town which We have destroyed that they should return after destruction." It was also said that it is not redundant but is an established part of the sentence, and that *ḥarām* here carries the sense of *wājib* (obligatory), meaning "it is obligatory for a town," as al-Khansa' said:

*"Indeed, I do not see anyone weeping over his grief for the rest of time except that I weep for Sakhr."*

She means her brother. On this view the "لَا" is established. Al-Nahhas said: "The verse is problematic. Among the finest and most sublime things said about it is what was transmitted by Ibn 'Uyaynah, Ibn 'Ulayyah, Hushaym, Ibn Idris, Muhammad ibn Fudayl, Sulayman ibn Hayyan, and Mu'alla, from Dawud ibn Abi Hind, from 'Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding the saying of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: 'And it is forbidden for a town which We have destroyed.' He said: *wajaba* (it became obligatory) that they will not return; he said: they will not repent."

[[In the originals: Salim ibn Hayyan, and so in al-Tahdhib with a fatḥah, but perhaps the correct form is Sulayman, as in al-Tahdhib too, since he is the narrator from Ibn Abi Hind. And Allah knows best.]]

Abu Ja'far (al-Nahhas) said: The derivation of this is clear in the language, and its explanation is that *ḥurrima al-shay'* means it was forbidden and prevented, just as *uḥilla* means it was permitted and not prevented. So when "ḥarām" and "ḥirm" have the meaning of *wājib*, its meaning is that the exit from it has been constricted and prevented, and so it enters the category of the prohibited by this. As for the view of Abu 'Ubaydah that "lā" is superfluous, a group of scholars rejected it, because it is not added in a position like this, nor in anything where there is a difficulty. Even if it were superfluous, the interpretation would still be remote: if it means "forbidden for a town which We have destroyed that they should return to the world," this has no benefit; and if it means repentance, repentance is not forbidden.

It was also said that there is an implied element in the speech, meaning: "And it is forbidden for a town which We have decreed to be uprooted, or whose hearts We have sealed, that any deed of theirs be accepted, because they will not return, i.e., they will not repent." This was said by al-Zajjaj and Abu 'Ali, and "lā" is not superfluous. This is the meaning of the saying of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Until, when Gog and Magog are let loose﴾. Their case has already been discussed. In the speech there is an ellipsis, meaning: "until, when the barrier of Gog and Magog is opened," like ﴿and ask the town﴾ [Yusuf: 82].[[See vol. 9, p. 245 onward.]]

(﴿And they will swarm from every slope﴾). Ibn 'Abbas said: "They will come from every elevation." Both are dialectal variants, like *ḥill* and *ḥalāl* (both meaning "lawful"). Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 98:

There are four issues in this.

The first: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, you and what you worship besides Allah are the fuel of Hell﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: "It is a verse about which people will not ask me! I do not know whether they recognised it and therefore did not ask about it, or they were ignorant of it and so did not ask about it." It was said: "And what is it?" He said: "'Indeed, you and what you worship besides Allah are the fuel (ḥaṣab) of Hell; you will be entering it.'" When it was revealed, it weighed heavily on the disbelievers of Quraysh, and they said: "He has reviled our gods." They went to Ibn al-Zib'ara and informed him. He said: "If I had been present, I would have answered him." They said: "And what would you have said to him?" He said: "I would have said to him: 'This is the Messiah, whom the Christians worship; the Jews worship 'Uzayr. Are these two also in the fuel of Hell?'" Quraysh were amazed at his statement, and they saw that Muhammad had been defeated. Then Allah, exalted is He, revealed: ﴿Indeed, those for whom the best reward has preceded from Us will be kept far from it﴾ [al-Anbiya: 101]. And concerning him was revealed: ﴿And when the son of Mary is cited as an example, behold, your people turn away from it [in dismay]﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 57], meaning Ibn al-Zib'ara. "Yaṣiddūn" is read with a kasra on the ṣād, meaning they clamour (yaḍijjūn). It will come later. [See vol. 16, p. 201.]

The second: This verse is a basis for the view that generality (al-'umum) exists and that it has specific forms (ṣiyagh makhsusa), contrary to those who say there is no form established to indicate it. That view is invalid in light of what this verse and others indicate. Thus 'Abdullah ibn al-Zib'ara, in his pre-Islamic time, understood "mā" to include everything that was worshipped, and Quraysh, who are the eloquent Arabs and the most articulate speakers, agreed with him on this. Had it not been for generality, it would not have been valid to make an exception from it, and since that exception was found, it indicates generality. This is clear.

The third: The common reading is with the unpointed ṣād (ḥaṣab), meaning: "Indeed you, O assembly of disbelievers, and the idols you worship besides Allah, are the fuel of Hell." This was said by Ibn 'Abbas. Mujahid, 'Ikrima and Qatada said: its firewood. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib and 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with them both, read "ḥaṭab Jahannam" with a ṭā'. Ibn 'Abbas read "ḥaḍab" with a pointed ḍād. Al-Farra' said: he means al-ḥaṣab. He said: it has been mentioned to us that ḥaḍab in the language of the people of Yemen means firewood, and everything with which you stir up and kindle a fire is ḥaḍab, as mentioned by al-Jawhari. And the place where fire is kindled is miḥḍab. Abu 'Ubayda said regarding the words of Allah, exalted is He, "ḥaṣab Jahannam": everything you throw into the fire, you have thrown it as ḥaṣab into it.

It appears from this verse that the people among the disbelievers and the idols they worship are firewood for Hell. A parallel to this verse is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So fear the Fire whose fuel is men and stones﴾ [al-Baqara: 24]. It was said that the stones are stones of sulphur, as previously mentioned in al-Baqara [see vol. 1, p. 235 onward], and that the fire is not a punishment or retribution for the idols, since they have committed no sin; rather, it is a punishment upon those who worshipped them: they are first punished with remorse, then they are gathered into the Fire, so its fire will be fiercer than every fire, and then they will be tormented by it. It was also said: they will be heated and attached to them as an increase in their torment. It was also said: they were placed in the Fire only as a rebuke to their worship.

The fourth: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿you will be entering it﴾, meaning: you will be entering therein. The address is to the polytheists who worship idols, meaning: you and what you worship will enter it together with the idols. It is also permissible to say that the address is to the idols and their worshippers, because although idols are inanimate objects, they may be referred to with pronouns used for human beings. The scholars said: 'Isa, 'Uzayr and the angels, may Allah's blessings be upon them, are not included in this, because "mā" is for non-human beings; had He intended them, He would have said "man" (whoever). Al-Zajjaj said: and because the addressees of this verse are the polytheists of Mecca and not others.

The commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 21, verses 99–100:

Allah's words: ﴿If these were gods, they would not have entered it﴾. That is, if the idols were gods, their worshippers would not have entered the Fire. It was also said: the worshippers and the worshipped did not enter it. This is why He said: ﴿And all of them will abide therein forever﴾.

Allah's words: ﴿For them therein is a zafir (a groaning, sighing sound)﴾. That is, for those who entered the Fire among the disbelievers and the devils. As for the idols, that depends on the disagreement about them: does Allah bring them to life and punish them so that they have a zafir, or not? There are two opinions. The zafir is the sound of the breath of one in distress, coming out from the heart. It has already been discussed in "Hud" [[See vol. 9, p. 78 onward.]].

(﴿And they therein will not hear﴾). It was said: there is an omission in the speech, and the meaning is: ﴿they therein will not hear anything﴾, because they will be gathered deaf, as Allah said: ﴿And We will gather them on the Day of Resurrection upon their faces, blind, mute, and deaf﴾ [[See vol. 10, p. 333.]] [al-Isra: 97]. Hearing things brings comfort and solace, so Allah denied the disbelievers that in the Fire. It was also said: they will not hear what would please them, but they will hear the voice of whoever is in charge of punishing them from the guardians (al-zabaniyah). It was also said: when it is said to them, ﴿Be silenced therein and do not speak to Me﴾ [[See vol. 12, p. 153.]] [al-Mu'minun: 108], they then become deaf and mute, as Ibn Mas'ud said: when those who will abide forever in Hell remain in Jahannam, they will be placed in coffins of fire, then the coffins will be placed inside other coffins with nails of fire, so they will hear nothing, and none of them will see that there are in the Fire people who are being punished other than himself.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 21, verses 101–103:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those for whom the best reward has already preceded from Us﴾, meaning Paradise, ﴿will be kept far from it﴾, meaning from the Fire. So the meaning of the statement is an exception. For this reason some scholars said: "Inna" here carries the meaning of "illa" (except), and there is no other instance of this in the Qur'an. Muhammad ibn Hatib said: I heard Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, recite this verse from the pulpit, "Indeed, those for whom the best reward has already preceded from Us," and he said: I heard the Prophet (ﷺ) say: "Indeed, Uthman is among them."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They will not hear its faintest sound﴾, meaning the sound of the Fire and the movement of its flame. The *hasis* and the *hiss* both mean movement. Ibn Jurayj narrated from Ata', who said: Abu Rashid al-Haruri said to Ibn Abbas: "They will not hear its faintest sound." Ibn Abbas said: Are you mad? Then where is the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿And there is not one of you but will pass over it﴾ [See p. 135 and p. 152 of this part], and His saying: ﴿So He will lead them into the Fire﴾ [See vol. 9, p. 93 onward] [Hud: 98], and His saying: ﴿Driven to Hell as a thirsty herd﴾ [See p. 152 and p. 149 of this part] [Maryam: 86]. Indeed, it was among the supplications of those who passed before us: "O Allah, bring me out of the Fire safely, and admit me into Paradise victorious." Abu Uthman al-Nahdi said: On the Sirat there are serpents that sting the people of the Fire, and they say: "Hass! Hass!" It was also said: When the people of Paradise enter Paradise, they will not hear the sound of the people of the Fire, whereas before that they would hear it. And Allah knows best. ﴿And they will abide forever in that which their souls desire﴾, meaning they will remain forever in what the souls desire and the eyes delight in. He said: ﴿And for you therein is whatever your souls desire, and for you therein is whatever you request﴾ [See vol. 15, p. 357] [Fussilat: 31].

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The greatest terror will not grieve them﴾. Abu Ja'far and Ibn Muhaysin recited "la yahzunuhum" with a damma on the yaa and a kasra on the zaay. The rest recited it with a fatha on the yaa and a damma on the zaay. Al-Yazidi said: *hazanahu* is the dialect of Quraysh, and *ahzanahu* is the dialect of Tamim, and both have been recited. The greatest terror is the horrors of the Day of Resurrection and of the Resurrection, according to Ibn Abbas. Al-Hasan said: It is the time when the servants are commanded toward the Fire. Ibn Jurayj, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Dahhak said: It is when the Fire closes over its people and death is slaughtered between Paradise and the Fire. Dhu al-Nun al-Misri said: It is severance and separation. And from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Three people on the Day of Resurrection will be upon a dune of the most fragrant musk, and the greatest terror will not grieve them: a man who led a people in prayer seeking reward, and they were pleased with him; a man who called the adhan for a people seeking reward; and a man who was tested with the worldly servitude yet it did not distract him from obedience to his Lord." Abu Salama ibn Abd al-Rahman said: I passed by a man who was beating a boy of his, and the boy gestured to me for help, so I spoke to his master until he pardoned him. Then I met Abu Sa'id al-Khudri and told him, and he said: "O son of my brother, whoever relieves a distressed person, Allah will free him from the Fire on the Day of the Greatest Terror. I heard that from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)."

﴿And the angels will receive them﴾, meaning the angels will meet them at the gates of Paradise, congratulating them and saying to them: ﴿This is your Day, which you were promised﴾. It was also said: the angels of mercy will receive them when they come out of their graves, according to Ibn Abbas. "This is your Day," meaning and they will say to them, so it is elided. "Which you were promised": in this there is honour.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 104:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿On the day We roll up the heaven﴾. Abu Ja'far ibn al-Qa'qa', Shaybah ibn Nisah, al-A'raj and al-Zuhri read "tuṭwā" with a damma on the taʾ, and "al-samā'u" in the nominative, as the verb in the passive voice (ʿalā mā lam yusamma fāʿiluh, "with an unnamed agent"). Mujahid read "yaṭwī," meaning God rolls up the heaven. The rest read "naṭwī" with the first-person plural of majesty (nūn al-ʿaẓamah). The accusative of "yawma" is either in apposition (badal) to the omitted pronoun in the relative clause (ṣilah, the clause that completes a relative pronoun), with the sense: "that which you were promised, the day We roll up the heaven." Or it is governed by "nuʿīduh" in His saying: "As We began the first creation, We will repeat it." Or it is governed by His saying "lā yaḥzunuhum," meaning: "the great terror will not grieve them on the day We roll up the heaven." Or it is by the implied verb "wa-dhkur" (and remember). By "the heaven" He means the category (al-jins), and the evidence is: ﴿The heavens will be rolled up in His right hand﴾ [al-Zumar: 67]. ["See vol. 15, p. 277 onward."]

"Like the rolling of the scroll for the books." [(al-Kitab) in the singular is the reading of Nafi'.] Ibn ʿAbbas and Mujahid said: that is, like the rolling of the page over what is written on it, so the lam (in "li-l-kutub") means "over" (ʿalā). It is also reported from Ibn ʿAbbas that the scroll is the name of the scribe of the Messenger of God ﷺ, but this is not strong, because the scribes of the Messenger of God ﷺ are well known and this man is not among them, nor is there among his Companions anyone named al-Sijill. Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn ʿUmar and al-Suddi also said: "al-Sijill" is an angel, who rolls up the books of the children of Adam when they are raised to him. It is said that he is in the third heaven, to which the deeds of the servants are raised; the guardian angels appointed over creation raise them to him every Thursday and Monday. Among his helpers, they mentioned, were Harut and Marut. "Al-sijill" is the document, a word derived from "al-sijalah," which is writing. Its root is from "al-sajl," which is the bucket. You say: "I competed with the man (sājaltu al-rajul)" when you drew a bucket and he drew a bucket. Then the term was borrowed, so that writing back and forth and exchange of documents was called "musājalah." It is said: "The judge recorded (sajjala al-ḥākim) a registration (tasjīl)." Al-Fadl ibn al-ʿAbbas ibn ʿUtbah ibn Abi Lahab said:

"Whoever competes with me will compete with a noble man,
who fills the bucket up to the knot of the rope."

[Al-kurab: a rope tied to the sides of the bucket, then doubled, then tripled, so that it is the part that reaches the water, and the large rope does not rot.]

Then this word was patterned on the form fiʿil, like ḥimir, ṭimir and bili. Abu Zur'ah ibn ʿAmr ibn Jarir read: "ka-ṭayyi al-sujull" with a damma on the sin and the jim, and a shaddah on the lam. Al-A'mash and Talhah read: "ka-ṭayyi al-sijil" with a fatha on the sin, a sukun on the jim and a light lam (no shaddah). Al-Nahhas said: the meaning is one, God willing. The pause (tamām) is at His saying "li-l-kitab." The rolling (al-ṭayy) in this verse may have two meanings. The first: folding, which is the opposite of unfolding (al-nashr), as God said: ﴿The heavens will be rolled up in His right hand﴾ [al-Zumar: 67]. The second: concealing, obscuring and erasing, because God erases and effaces their traces and dims their stars.

God said: ﴿When the sun is wrapped up, and when the stars fall﴾ [al-Takwir: 1-2], ﴿and when the sky is stripped away﴾ [al-Takwir: 11]. ["See vol. 19, p. 225 and p. 47."] "li-l-kitab" and the sentence is complete. The reading of al-A'mash, Hafs, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Yahya and Khalaf is "li-l-kutub" in the plural. Then He resumed the speech, saying: "As We began the first creation, We will repeat it," meaning: We will gather them barefoot, naked and uncircumcised, as they were brought forth in the wombs. Al-Nasa'i related from Ibn ʿAbbas, from the Prophet ﷺ, that he said: "People will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection naked, barefoot and uncircumcised. The first of creation to be clothed on the Day of Resurrection will be Ibrahim, peace be upon him." Then he recited: "As We began the first creation, We will repeat it." Muslim also related it from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ stood among us with an exhortation and said: "O people, you will be gathered to God barefoot, naked and uncircumcised, ﴿As We began the first creation, We will repeat it; that is a promise upon Us; indeed We will be doing it﴾. Verily, the first of creation to be clothed on the Day of Resurrection will be Ibrahim, peace be upon him." And he mentioned the hadith. We have covered this subject fully in our book "al-Tadhkirah." Sufyan al-Thawri mentioned, from Salamah ibn Kuhayl, from Abu al-Za'ra', from ʿAbd Allah ibn Mas'ud, who said: God, mighty and majestic, will send water from beneath the Throne like the semen of men, and from it their flesh and bodies will grow, as the earth grows by the moisture. And he recited: "As We began the first creation, We will repeat it." Ibn ʿAbbas said: the meaning is: We will destroy everything and annihilate it, as it was the first time. ["This statement needs reflection, as al-Alusi said."] According to this, the speech is connected to His saying "the day We roll up the heaven," meaning: We roll it up and then return it to destruction and annihilation, so it is nothing. It was also said: We annihilate the heaven, then We restore it another time after its folding and disappearance, as in His saying: ﴿The day the earth will be changed into other than the earth, and the heavens﴾ [Ibrahim: 48]. ["See vol. 9, p. 383."] The first opinion is more sound, and it is the parallel of His saying: ﴿And you have indeed come to Us alone, as We created you the first time﴾ [al-An'am: 94], and His saying, mighty and majestic: ﴿They will be presented before your Lord in rows: "You have indeed come to Us as We created you the first time."﴾ ["See vol. 10, p. 417."]

"Wa'dan" is in the accusative as an absolute object (maṣdar), meaning: He promised a promise, "upon Us" its fulfilment and keeping, namely of the resurrection and the restoration. So there is an omission in the speech. Then He confirmed that with His saying, may His praise be exalted: "indeed We will be doing it." Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning of "innā kunnā fāʿilīn" is: indeed We have been able to do what We will. It was also said: "innā kunnā fāʿilīn" means what We promised you. This is like His saying: ﴿His promise was ever to be fulfilled﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 18]. It was also said: "kāna" is for reporting what has preceded from His decree. And it was said: it is a filler (ṣilah).

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 21, verses 105–106:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We had written in the Zabur﴾. The Zabur and the Kitab are one and the same; for this reason it is permissible to call the Tawrah and the Injil a Zabur. One says "zabartu," meaning "I wrote," and its plural is zubur. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "al-Zabur" refers to the Tawrah, the Injil and the Qur'an.

(After the Reminder) which is in heaven, (that the earth) the earth of Paradise, (shall be inherited by My righteous servants). This was narrated by Sufyan from al-A'mash from Sa'id ibn Jubayr. Al-Sha'bi said: "al-Zabur" is the Zabur of Dawud, and "al-Dhikr" is the Tawrah of Musa, peace be upon him. Mujahid and Ibn Zayd said: "al-Zabur" is the books of the prophets, peace be upon them, and "al-Dhikr" is Umm al-Kitab which is with Allah in heaven. Ibn 'Abbas said: "al-Zabur" is the books which Allah sent down after Musa to His prophets, and "al-Dhikr" is the Tawrah revealed to Musa. Hamzah read "fi al-Zabur" with a dammah on the zay, as the plural of zubur. "That the earth shall be inherited by My righteous servants": the best of what has been said about it is that it means the earth of Paradise, as Sa'id ibn Jubayr said, because the earth of this world has been inherited by the righteous and others besides them. This is also the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and others. Mujahid and Abu al-'Aliyah said: the evidence for this interpretation is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And they will say, "Praise be to Allah, who has fulfilled His promise to us and made us inherit the earth"﴾ [[See vol. 15, p. 284 onward.]] [al-Zumar: 74]. And from Ibn 'Abbas: it is the holy land. And also from him: it is the land of the disbelieving nations, which the community of Muhammad ﷺ inherits through conquests. It was also said that what is meant is the Children of Israel, by the evidence of His saying: ﴿And We made the people who had been oppressed inherit the eastern and western parts of the land which We had blessed﴾ [[See vol. 7, p. 272.]] [al-A'raf: 137]. Most exegetes hold that the righteous servants refers to the community of Muhammad ﷺ. Hamzah read "ibadi al-salihun" with the yā' silent.

(Indeed in this) i.e., in what has been mentioned in this surah of admonition and warning. It was also said: indeed in the Qur'an (is a message for a people who worship). Abu Hurayrah and Sufyan al-Thawri said: they are the people of the five prayers. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "'abidin" means obedient. And the 'abid is one who is humbled and submissive. Al-Qushayri said: it is not far-fetched that every rational person is included in this, for by nature he is humbled before the Creator, and if he were to reflect upon the Qur'an and act upon it, that would lead him to Paradise. Ibn 'Abbas also said: they are the community of Muhammad ﷺ who perform the five prayers and fast the month of Ramadan. This is the very same as the first view.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We had written in the Zabur﴾. The Zabur and the Kitab are one and the same; for this reason it is permissible to call the Tawrah and the Injil a Zabur. One says "zabartu," meaning "I wrote," and its plural is zubur. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "al-Zabur" refers to the Tawrah, the Injil and the Qur'an.

Al-Sha'bi said: "al-Zabur" is the Zabur of Dawud, and "al-Dhikr" is the Tawrah of Musa, peace be upon him. Mujahid and Ibn Zayd said: "al-Zabur" is the books of the prophets, peace be upon them, and "al-Dhikr" is Umm al-Kitab which is with Allah in heaven. Ibn 'Abbas said: "al-Zabur" is the books which Allah sent down after Musa to His prophets, and "al-Dhikr" is the Tawrah revealed to Musa. **Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 21, verses 107–109:**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We have not sent you except as a mercy to the worlds﴾. Sa'id ibn Jubayr narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Muhammad ﷺ was a mercy to all people. Whoever believed in him and affirmed him was made happy, and whoever did not believe in him was kept safe from what befell the nations of punishment by sinking into the earth and by drowning." Ibn Zayd said: "By 'the worlds' He meant only the believers."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: It is only revealed to me that your God is one God﴾. Therefore, associating partners with Him is not permissible.

(So will you submit?) That is, will you yield to the Oneness of God, exalted is He? I.e., then submit. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So will you desist?﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 91], meaning: desist. [See vol. 6, p. 285 onwards.]

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But if they turn away﴾, meaning: if they turn away from Islam. (Then say: I have announced to you on equal terms.) That is, I have informed you, with clarity, that we and you are at war, and there is no peace between us. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if you fear treachery from a people, then throw back to them [their covenant] on equal terms﴾ [al-Anfal: 58], meaning: inform them that you have broken the covenant openly, so that you and they are on equal footing, and neither party is bound by a covenant toward the other. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is, I have informed you of what is revealed to me on an equal footing in knowledge of it, and I have not disclosed to anyone something I have concealed from others. [See vol. 8, p. 31.]

(And I do not know) "In" here is a negation meaning "ma," i.e., and I do not know.

(Whether what you are promised is near or far) This means: the appointed time of the Day of Resurrection, which no one knows, neither a prophet sent nor an honored angel. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas. It has also been said: I have announced war to you, but I do not know when I will be permitted to fight you.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 21, verses 110–112:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, He knows what is spoken aloud and knows what you conceal﴾, meaning, of shirk, and He is the One who will recompense for it.

(And I do not know) meaning, perhaps the respite (may be) ﴿a trial for you﴾, meaning a test, so that He may see how you act, and He is the All-Knowing.

(And provision for a time) It was said: until the end of the term. It is narrated that the Prophet ﷺ saw in his dream the Banu Umayyah ruling over people, and al-Hakam came out from his presence, so he informed the Banu Umayyah of that. They said to him: "Return and ask him when that will happen." So Allah, Exalted is He, revealed: ﴿And I do not know whether it is near or far, that which you are promised﴾ and ﴿And I do not know; perhaps it is a trial for you and a provision for a time﴾, saying to His Prophet, peace be upon him: "Say to them that."

His saying, Exalted is He: (He said [[(Qul) in the imperative form is the reading of Nafi'.]] ﴿My Lord, judge with truth﴾). He concluded the surah by commanding the Prophet ﷺ to entrust the matter to Him and to expect relief from Him, meaning: judge between me and these deniers, and grant me victory over them. Sa'id narrated from Qatadah who said: The prophets used to say: ﴿Our Lord, decide between us and our people with truth﴾ [al-A'raf: 89], so the Prophet ﷺ was commanded to say: "My Lord, judge with truth." Whenever he met the enemy, he would say, while knowing that he was upon the truth and his enemy upon falsehood: "My Lord, judge with truth", meaning, decide by it. Abu 'Ubaydah said: the attribute here is placed in the position of the qualified noun, and the implied meaning is: "My Lord, judge by Your true judgment." And "Rabb" is in the accusative position, because it is a vocative construction with an annexed noun. Abu Ja'far ibn al-Qa'qa' and Ibn Muhaysin read: "Qul Rubbu uhkum bil-haqq" with a damma on the ba'. Al-Nahhas said: This is a grammatical error according to the grammarians; it is not permitted according to them to say "rajulu aqbil" until you say "ya rajulu aqbil" or something similar. Al-Dahhak, Talhah and Ya'qub read: "Qala Rabbi ahkamu bil-haqq" with an alif cut, the kaf fathah and the mim dammah, meaning: Muhammad said, "My Lord is more just in truth than any judge." Al-Jahdari read "Qul Rabbi ahkama," in the sense of: He has judged the matters with truth.

(And our Lord is the Most Merciful, the One whose help is sought against what you describe) meaning, what you describe of disbelief and denial. Al-Mufaddal and al-Sulami read "ʿalā mā yaṣifūn" with the ya', as a report. The rest read with the ta', as address. And Allah knows best.

End of the eleventh part of the Tafsir of al-Qurtubi, followed, God willing, by the twelfth part, beginning with: (Surat al-Hajj).
